_ SIX LITTLE WORDS. ix words concentrate my attention day by day— I shall, I must, I can, I will, I dare, I may. I shall, is God's command upon my heart engraved, The aim in seeking which my soul from self is saved. I must, that is the boundary that shuts me in From nature's worldly lusts that lead to sin. I can, is but the limit of my borrowed power, The deed, the readiness, the art, the science dower. I will, the highest coronet that decks my brow— Freedom's own seal which liberates the spirit now. 'I dare, its fellow, the inscription on the seal Which bats the door of freedom for the public weal. Between me and futurity there lies I may, Which shuts me in, uncertain of my way. I shall, I must, I can, I will, I dare, I may, These six concentrate my attention every day. Only with God's instruction when I pray. I shall, I must, I can. I will, I dare, I may. ...--.From the German.

N ED. A SIZEIY IN RHYME. Night after night: Then, wan and white, Eyes haggard, wild, Went home to see His wife and child In misery, Starving and cold! Yet such a hold Had gambling got— So bright the cup, That give it up Poor Ned could not, But dreamt that still Some chance would fill His hands with gold. So, day by day, From child, and wife, And man, the-life Ebbed fast away. At last one night Luck took a turn! Ned's hopes came right: Fate, cold and stern, Passed by or slept! At one swift bound Ned's shilling leapt Into a,pound, The pound to ten! And then, Life bright with joy, Which seemed so black, He hurried back To wife and boy, To find them—dead! Poor ! night His brain gave way, The doctors said: And well it might! And then to-day, A year ago, When winter snow Hid all the way, Ned thought, they say, That wife and child From heaven above Looked down and smiled With eyes of love! And with a cry Of joy, too deep For words to toll, Ned fell asleep 1 GEORGH WHATIIERLEY.

Ned? Ned's dead! 'Mid winter snow, A year ago This very day, Ned passed away! And better so. ' Why should he die? Why better so? You want to know? I'll tell you why. You knew poor Ned? Knew that his life Was just a strife For daily bread? Three years agone, Thinking that what He knew was not ! Enough for one Might do for two— As men will do, - In bat-blind way— Ned took a wife, . And all his life Was glad that day! And for awhile Beamed Fortune's smile; ' Plenty of.work, Plenty to ; Then, all too soon, Came the sad end! Trade was depressed, And work was scant; And to the nest Came care and want. And with them, tot, Ned's first-born child A blessing? True, Had Fortune smiled— . A blessing rare! But uuw, alas! It brought new care, New pangs !--well, there, It came to pass (The tale's soon told) That one by one Ned's sticks were sold! Work there was none! Then, in despair, Ned gambled, lost The few poor coins Earned at high cost Throughout the day! Threwilhem away

In private and in public the surest way to avoid em- barrassment, perplexity, trouble, and annoyance is to tell the truth, to admit an error if one has been com- mitted, and insist upon a clear understandable ex- planation ,of any question that arises between two or more, and about which there may be honestly two dif- fering opinions. ON THE TARESHOLD.—There is one point in every life at which all things appear in their true colours. It is the point .6f death. All illusions vanish there. There are no falsesestimates of deeds in the light of that hour. The things we shall wish then that we had done are things we ought to have done. The things that will look fair and lovely as we it in the gloaming of life's day are the things that are truly lovely. The things that will shame us then are the things that God condemns, and -which we aught not to have done. A Thearrrieue CUSTO3I.—In the mountains of the Tyrol it is the custom of the women and children to come out when it is bedtime and sine their national songs, until they hear their husbands, fathers, and brothers answer them from the hills on their return home. On the shores of the Adriatic such a custom prevails. There the wives of the fishermen come down about sunset and sing a melody. After singing the first stanza they listen awhile for the answering strain from off the water, and con- tinue to sing and listen till the well-known voices come borne on the tide, telling that the loved ones are almost home. How sweet to the weary fisherman, as the shadows gather round him, must be the songs of the loved ones at home, who sing to cheer him; and how they strengthen and tighten the bonds that bind together these humble dwellerS by the sea. THE MIND AND THE LIFE.—The mind is largely dependent for its strength and clearness of vision upon the purity of he life. It is true that a man should know what is right in order to do right; but it is also true that he must be in the habit of doing-right in order to make such knowledge of any practical value. For example one who is accustomed to live wisely and to avoid whatever he believes injurious learns one day through a reliable source that a certain article of diet of *which he is fond,.er a certain habit that he has acquired, is deleterous, and he at once discontinues it. Another ac- -customed to self-indulgence, receives the same instruc- tion. and makes no change in his conduct. The intellect •or each has been appealed to alike, and their knowledge of the points in question is equal; but in the one case the habitof right-doing makes it operative, but in the ,order the habit of wrong-doing makes it inoperative. ,THE PARCHMENT RECORDS OF Ersesasen.—The Rolls and Records of early Parliamentary proceedings in England -are unequalled in the world for antiquity, beauty, and .correctness. They consist generally of several skins or 'sheets of parchment or vellum, each sheet being about three feet long, Aanci often nine to fourteen inches in -width. They are either all fastened together at one end, 2so as to form a kind of book, or are stretched end to end, so as to constitute an extended roll. Some of the records of the former of these two kinds contain so manyselsins of parchment that they form a huge roll equal in size to a large Cheshire cheese, and requring the strength of two men to lift them. Some of those on the continuous plan are also said to be of immense size; ones,of modern date, is 900 feet in length, and employs a man three hours to unreil dt. "Domesday Book" is shaped like a book, and is much more convenient to open than others. Many other legal documents, to an immense amount, are "filed," or fastened together by a string passing through them. Some of the Records and Rolls are written in Latin, some in Norman French, andl • some in English. "MOTHERS APRON STRINGS.".--" Charley ! Charley !" clear and sweet as a note struck from a silver bell, the voice rippled, over the country. "That's mother," cried one of the boys, and he instantly threw &yen his bat and picked up his jacket and cap. •" Don't go yet! Have it out !" "Finish the game! Try it again?" cried the players in noisy .chorus. "I must go—right off—this mute. I told her I'd come whenever she called." Make believe you didn't hear!" they exclaimed. "But I did hear." "She won't know you did." "But I know it,-and— " "Let him go," iaid a bystander; "you can't do anything with him; he is tied to his metheris apron strings." "That's so," said Charies, "and it's to what every boy cught to be tied, and in a hard 'knot, too." "I wouldn't he such a baby as to run the minute ..9he carted." "I don't call it babyish to keep one's word to his mother,' answered the obedient boy, a beautiful light glosvine in his blue eyes_ "I call that manly, and the boy who doesn't keep his word to her will never keep it to any one else—you see if he does," and he hurried away to his cottage borne. Thirty years have passed since the boys played on the common. Chancy Gray is a prosperous business Tan in a great city, and his mer- cantile friends say of him that his word "is bond." We ask him how he acquired such a reputation. "I never broke my word when a boy, no matter how great the temptation, arid the habits formed then have clung to Lee

'4‘ Ah,'David," said a Scottish parish minister to one of his parishioners whom he had met on the road enjoying his evening pipe, "I am astonished at a man of your eense clinging sae tenaciously to such a filthy habit as smoking—you who are f}n elder and looked on as a pillar of the kirk. Do you expect to go to heaven when you die, David, with such a vile habit!" "I'll no seek the tak' my pipe wi' me when my time comes," calmly replied the reproved elder. "But you know, David, that nothing unclean can enter heaven, and there is nothing so unclean as the breath of a smoker." "Ay, ay," was the reply, •" but I expeck that my last breath 'll be my last smoke, so that baith pipe and breath will be left ahint at the hinder ea'."

WONDERFUL SHIRTS.—A funny story has just been published of Edison. The report was recently circulated that he invented a wondrous shirt. It consisted of thin pieces of gelatine, each piece to be taken off when soiled, and one shirt was guaranteed to last for a year. The story, after circulating in many places, at last found its way to Brazil. "The gullibility of the South American may be appreciated," said Mr. Edison in a recent inter- view;" when it is known that soon after the shirt story met their eyes the Brazilians began to send me drafts land-cheques for shirts. An idiotic diamond dealer sent Ime a draft for £lOO on the Bank of England. He wrote that he didn't know how much the shirts were, but he did not think they ought to cost over £lOO apiece." FAILURE AND DurrY.—The unsuccessful striver in any department of life may lose his property, his situation, his means of livelihood; all his plans may come to naught, and all his efforts be frustrated; but, until he lose his courage, he has not lost all. Instead of sitting down idle to mourn over dead hopes, let him apply himself vigourously to the nearest duty, and his spirits and his fortune will alike arise triumphant from the ashes of the past. Even small disappointments, and vexations, such as assail us continually, lose half their sting 1 such treatment. The more we brood upon - - them the more afflictive they become; but, busily ..aployed in the nearest duty, we forget their sharpness, and learn unconciously VI-bear them with firmness.: The Khedive of Egypt has a country palace at Helwan, fifteen miles from Cairo. There are celebrated sulphur springs at Helwan, and all the tourists who flock to the laud of the Pharaohs during the winter months spend a short while at these springs. His Highness was taking a walk alone near the palace, and was closely followed by two very determined-looking ladies. The royal person- age seemed annoyed at the intrusion, and suddenly turned, seemingly to escape them, in an opposite direc- tion. The ladies, however, were not to be thwarted, and striding up to the Khedive with a Fifth Avenue swing, lone of them said, "Aren't you the Khedive?" His Highness politely replied, " I am." The ladies said "We thought so ." and then, with a smile, "We are from New 'York." The very innocent Sovereign said, "I thought so," and bowing, walked away." WA,GNERIAN. A renowned Viennese opera basso has just died of paralysis of the brain, induced by overwork- ing himself in mastering Wagnerian parts. His disease stud decease are not to be wondered at. A critic once said of Wagner's pieces:—" As far as I could understand, itibegan with: music suggestive of a naelie and fight of aboriginal savages, and ended with an intensified de- scription of modern civilisation, which culminates in tall disasters and big accidents; then comes a general and indiscriminate smash of railway passengers and car- riages, till at length all are promiscuously rolled over a high bridge into a boiling flood, and are swept away by the roaring torrent." A few years ago, when the Wagner craze was booming round gaily, a young lady with whom we were acquainted went mad on the Bayreuth master's music. We visited her the other day at a private asy- lum. She was still squalling notes from his celebrated air, ." Dasdtunezekatzdiedton," in G6iterddnanterung.— Fax.

' OUR TEUTONIC ORIGIN.—Sad as it is to confess it, ' the truth must nevertheless be told, that our beasts and birds, our plants and flowers, are for the most part of purely Teutonic origin. Even as the rude and hard- headed Anglo-Saion•has driven the gentle, poetical, and imaginative Celt ever westward before him into the hills and the sea, so the rude and vigorous Germanic beasts and weeds have driven the gentler and softer southern typesinto Wales, Cornwall, Galloway and Connemara. It is to the Central European population that we owe or owed the red deer, the wild boar, the bear, the wolf, the beaver, the fox, the badger, the otter, and the squirrel. It is to the Central European flora that we owe the larger part of the most familiar plants in all eastern and south-eastern England. They crossed in bands over the old land belt before Britain was finally isulated, and they have gone on steadily ever since, with true Teutonic per- sistence, overrunning the land and pushing slowly west- ward, like all other German bands before or since, to the detriment and discomfort of the previous inhabitants. Let us humbly 'remember-that we are all of us at bottom foreigners alike, but that it is the Teutonic English, the people from the old Low Dutch fatherland by the Elbe, who have finally given to this isle its name of England, and to every one of us, Celt or Teuton, their own Teu- tonic name of Englishman. We are at best, as an irate Teuton once remarked," nozzing but zegond-hand Cher- mans." In the words of a distinguished modern philolo- gist of our own blood, " English is Dutch, spoken with a Welsh accent."—Carnhill Magazine. How PRESIDENT LINCOLN EARNED RIS FIRST DOLLAR. —One morning, when a few gentlemen, making whom was Mr. Seward, had met in the Executive Chamber without official business, and were telling of the past, President Lincoln said ; "Seward, you never heard, did you, how I earned my first dollar !" "No," said Seward. "Well," replied he," I was about eighteen years of age, ssa lnoa South tebhse the eeg e sd c,r ua nobodyl3you know, pheeorpe.lew B who what uot do oe nhoattdhoewy call n succeededladown n d ani nd raising, chiefly by my labour, sufficient produce, as I thought, to justify me in taking it down the river to sell. After much persuasion I had got the consent of my mother to go, and had constructed a flat-boat large enough to take a few barrels of things we had gathered down to'New Orleans, A steamer was going down the river. We have, as you know, no wharves on the western ' streams, and the custom was, if passengers were at any of the landings, they were to go out in a boats, the steamer stopping and taking them on board. I was contemplating my new boat and wondering whethei I could make it stronger or improve it in any part, when two men came down, to the shore in carriages with trunks, and, looking at the different boat, singled out mine and asked, Who owns this?' I answered modestly, I do, -‘ Will you,' said one of them, 'take us and our trunks out to the steamer?' Certainly,' said I. I was very glad to have the chance of earning something, and suppossed that each of them would give me a couple of bits. The trunks were put on my boats,"the passengers seated themselves on them, and I sculled them out to the steamer. They got on board and I lifted their trunks and put them on the deck. The steamer was about to put on steam again' when I called out, 'You have forgotten to pay me.' Each of them took from his pocket a silver half-dollar, and threw it an the bottom of my boat. I could scarcely believe my eyes as I picked up the money. You may think it was a very little thing, and in these days it seems to me like a trifle, but it was a most important incident in my life. I could scarcely credit that I, a poor boy, had earned one dollar in less than a day; that by honest work I had earned one dollar, the world seemed wider and fairer before me. I was a more hopeful and thoughtful boy from that tiroe,"

MR&DOW GRASS.—" P. S. A." says—" A meadow has become quite objectionable for pasturage, owing to the enormous increase of yellow clover. It has received , dressings of mixed road scrapings, lime, and house sewerage. I am not allowed to plough it up. Will ammonia be of any use ?" Nitrate of soda or sulphate of ammonia-1 cwt. an acre of either twice a year in grow- ing weather—will help the grass. To DESTROY THISTLES.—Like very many farmers, I have been much troubled with the thistle pest, particu- larly in fields where sheep have been f,d. About a year I ago it struck me that something could be invented to exterminate them, and I killed a great many by cutting them off at the roots and then pouring carbolic acid and water on the cut places. This was a slow process, how- ever, and could not be adopted on a large scale; so I /invented a spud which, being hollow, I filled with car- bolic acid and water, and as the thistle is cut a few drops of the acid get squirted on the roots. This duly , kills the plant. In two days the reots are withered and I dead.—Tantara.

MILK STANDARDS.—NeaTIy threP years 870 the Society of Public Analysts appointed a special, committee to go into the whole question of milk analysis and milk standards. This committee devoted more than two years, not to mere discussion, but to active work on milk analysis, makin,a vast number of analyses by various methods. After"duly considering the whole subject, and after several general meetings of the society for its more open discussion, a report was adopted describing the processes of analyses recommended by the committee as the most accurate and reliable, and recommending a limit of 8.50 per cent. of solids not fat, and 3 per cent. of fat. I use the word "limit" advisedly, because a "limit" is not exactly a "standard." Average milk has a much higher "standard," but it is the "limit" (often miscalled a "standard") that determines the decision of the analyst as to watering and skimming. It is gratify- ing that the figures recommended for adoption by the Society of Public Analysts are now independently recom- mended by eminent authorities in practical dairying:— Bernard Dyer, F.C.S., F.1.C., Hon. Secretary of the Society of Public Analysts. FARMERS AND MANUFACTURERS' GOODS.—As the prac- tice of analysing manures and feeding stuffs supplied to farmers becomes more general, it is to be hoped that fair dealing on the part of the vendors of such articles will soon free the trade from the stigma that rests upon it in common with many others. At a meeting a week or two i ago of a Farmers' Protection Association n the North of England, the report of the analyst to the association re- vealed some disgraceful practices in trade, such as are now and again brought to light by-the reports emanating from the Royal Agricultural Society's officers. On the occasion just alluded to, the reports of the analyst were discussed, and it appeared that several samples of cake were found to be crushed from badly-dressed seed, con- taining upwards of three per cent. of sand. Further, a number of analytical valuations of bone manure, as fol- lows, showed the following results :—No. 1, selling at £7, was found to be worth £3 2s. Ed. per ton only; No. 2, selling at £7 ss. per ton, £3 I7s. 6d: only; No. 3, selling at £6 per ton, £2 16s. only; while No. 4, which sold at £7 per ton, was found to be worth but £4 10s. ; and a sample of blood-bone manure, sold at £4, was worth just half.. Another sample of manure was found to contain upwards of eighteen per cent.,of sand. Resolutions were passed at the meeting requesting the hon. secretary to take the necessary steps to compel full compensation being made to the members 'interested, in accordance with the analytical valuation. NORTH LANCASHIRE NOTE6.—We usually look to Com- mence the cutting of seed grasses in the middle of June, but owing to the backward spring, the end of the month was reached without a commencement. A fortnight of fine weather in the beginning of July enabled all seed grasses to be housed in the best condition, and excellent crops. A few early meadows were cut and housed. A showery season then set in, and continued to Us: end of July, and as on most farms extra hands are engaged at so much per month—this year about 1.65. per week, with food and lodging—the hay harvest has been both expen- sive and annoying, for the weather was showery, never long enough fair to permit carting the hay. On Sun- days, July 25th and August Ist, hay-making was prose- cuted on many farms. The cut hay has been a bit "weathered," but is not seriously injured, and as last week was fine all the cut grass has been housed, and on most farms a finish made with cutting. The yield is everywhere good, and present appearance of the after- grasses is most promising.—Root Crops: Before the rains came, root crops were at a standstill; now the earlier- sown swedes are meeting in the rows, rooting well, and look like making good crops. There is nothing so salu- tary ifs showers for ridding either mangolds or swedes from their enemies. Mangolds are now recovering from the maggot attack, and are rooting nicely. Cabbages and carrots look like good crops, and potatoes are very regular in the rows; the rains have come before the time when they might have br9ught disease to the tubers, the tops are fine, and we may anticipate a good yield—Cereals: Wheat is year by year less grown, and the area of barley is decreasing, consequent upon the abolition of the malt tax. As a consequence, the area of oats has increased. At present oats are looking fairly well on good soils, the straw having lengthened out con- siderably, and the crop is promising. As yet all cereals are upstanding, the rains and winds having done but the minimum of damage to the crops.—Produee : Beef does not improve much in price, but mutton has advanced. Butter, too, sells better, and the agitation for a drop in the price of milk has subsided. Trade depression does but deepen, and until the iron trade improves, agricul- tural produce will not make any sensible advance.—R. THE COLLIE AT WORK.—A tourist in the Western Highlands sends the following graphic account of a Scotch shepherd and his dog to a London daily; so well is the scene portrayed that one seems to see the whole proceeding. On his way from Loch Rama to the little village of Corrie he falls in with a shepherd, whom he finds very civil, and who does not refuse a " wee drap " from a tourist's companion; and after a little talk he says, "If you'll bide a wee till I coont my sheep, I'll walk wi' ye as far as Corrie." And, more for the sake of seeing a clever performance by dogs, writes the tour- ist, than of enjoying his company,' assent, and seat my- self on the grassy bank of the 'roadside, Close to the boulder on which he is standing. "They are black- faced sheep and bothersome a wee," he explains, "and one o' my dogs is but a whelp, so must be canny wi' them. I- would rather lose a ewe than spoil a young dog. You may see them fairly on the hillside if ye look through your spy glass. They are handy things, spy glasses; but we have to trust to the naked ee." And was it true that he proposed to count those sheep away up among the rocks? and how long would it be neces- sary to wait for his company in that case? "Bide a wee, mon;" says the shepherd, and, putting the fore-fingers of both hands into a very capacious mouth, he gives a screaming whistle that a curlew might envy. This is intended as a kind of gun from the flag ship to call at- tention to signals; for ere the echoes have died away our friend has converted himself into a semaphore, and is waving his crook downwards to the right. Favoured with a glance through the binocular, I make out the dogs, also perched on the tops of rocks and apparently watching every motion of their master. The signals being understood, their action is soon made apparent. Looking right against the face of the steep mountain, which is furrowed with huge clefts, the shepherd ob- serves sheep which his dogs cannot possibly see. Some below them to the right, some below them to the left, and each and all nibbling busily at the green shoots which grow so sparingly on the thinly-clad soil. A scream of the whistle, when one or other of the dogs is I s een to go wrong, at once brings them to "attention," and in fancy we can see their keen, intelligent eyes.as they stand with ears at full cock watching the waving of the crook. At last all of the lots are gathered into, one flock, and this is soon brought, after much barking, close up to where we are seated. From lcng practice the clever little animals contrive to let the sheep pass one by one, though occasionally two and three make a race for it, and get off together. The shepherd counts them, however, and when the last two or three go off down- hill with a skip, all are declared to be there The moun- tain roll-call has been read satisfactorily; not a single member of the flock has been found missing. OPENING OF THE CHESHIRE DAIRY INSTITUTE.—Aston Hall, Worleston, which has been adapted as an institute to provide facilities for practical lessons in the improve- ment of cheese and butter-making in Cheshire. was form- ally opened on Tuesday by a public meeting and ad- dresses on dairy subjects. The project promises to supply a long-felt want in the county. Already a num- ber of. pupils have been secured. Several county land- lords are paying fees for their tenants. The annual report stated that during the brief interval the institute had been opened the 'directors had received much encouragement and support. After an address by Col. Humberston, Lord Egerton of Tatton, who was ieceived with applause, said he had come there in order to ac- quaint himself with what was being done and to see if the movement could be adopted in any other portion of Cheshire. (Hear, hear.) He believed they would all ash:llft that in these days, if they were to succeed, they must turn out a good article. A great deal of complaint had been made lately about bad prices, but these had to some extent been caused by cheese unfortunately not being of the first quality. Therefore he thought it was not only wise, but absolutely necessary, that efforts should be made by means of that institute to raise the standard of cheese-making to the highest-class. How was that to be done? Possibly there might be certain disadvantages in carrying out the scheme, but he under- stood that they already had in the institute those who wished to learn and those who were competent to teach. (Hear, hear.) It was right that an institution of that kind should not proceed from the landlords of the county, but from the class whom it was designed to benefit. They must interest themselves in it. THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. THE PRESERVATION OF EGGS.—II. Eggs can be kept in a cool place for a considerable period without any special preservative, and we have 'known eggs so kept quite good for cooking at the end of three months. But this system depends most of all upon the place, that it is not applicable to every one. There can be no question that if any one has an ice cellar, some portion of which can be given up to keep- ing eggs, they do not need any other preservative, and we believe that frozen eggs retain more of their original qualities than those kept by means of any of the .pre- parations which have already been described. The reason for this is not far to seek. When an egg is frozen every- thing is held in suspension, and no process of change or decay goes on. Therefore, we should advise those who ; have a cellar of this description to use the opportunities ' at their disposal, as they need not trouble themselves any more about the matter. All that will be needed is to fit up some shelves in which are perforated holes large enough for the eggs to stand up in but not to go through, Or coarse wire lattice may be used of a mesh that will effect the same purpose. The disadvantage of this sys- tem is, that if the eggs are not properly disfrozen they crack, and it is often difficult to avoid their cracking in any case. They should be very gradually brought to their normal condition, first by placing in an atmosphere but very few degrees warmer than the cellar', and, after giving two or three hours there, gradually placing in yet warmer air until the ordinary temperature has been reached. There are many poultry-keepers who only wish to pre- serve the surplus eggs for a few weeks, and in this case it,is not necessary to use any preservative, or even to freeze them. All that is requisite is to have a cool cel- lar, larder, or closet fitted with the perforated shelves already described. The eggs should be placed broad end downwards on these shelves, but they may with advan- tage be turned about twice a week, keeping them, how- ever, almost all of the time with the broad end down- wards. The reason for this is that when so kept the air space does not increase in size, and the egg seems to keep better. It is a very good plan to arrange the eggs in uniform rows from front to back, so that these laid first can be used first. We once knew a poultry-keeper who bad stoneware mugs for keeping his eggs in. These would each contain atput a hundred, and the eggs were placed in regularly every day as they were laid. As soon as one was full it was emptied into another mug, so that the first laid were in that case at the top. This gentle- man never appeared to take any especial care in the matter, and yet his eggs were wonderfully fresh when three and four months old; but he had a very cool cel- lar where the mugs were kept, and that must have been the reason. Without a cool place it could not have beeh done in such a free and easy fashion. That was the secret of his success. Claim has been made that eggs can be preserved if the air ooming to them is first filtered so as to remove all germs therefrom. In this way the eggs are packed in cotton wool or padding, and it is claimed that this suc- ceeds very well indeed. We have never tried the pro- cess, and therefore cannot speak of it, but are not in- clined to place much reliance upon it, for the reason that it is not enough in egg preservation to keep germs away that are without, as in most eggs there are the germs of decay within the egg itself. Still this is only theory, and we should be very glad to have some well authenticated experiments recorded. Gypsum is said to be a good preservative of eggs. They should be packed in finely pulverised gypsum, and the only experiment recorded showed that they kept for six months. But this was in a cool place, and the cold air may have had just as much to do with the effective preservation as the gypsum. In fact it is most desirable that whatever process is adopted the storage should be a cold one. This we regard as of supreme importance, and to our mind it explains the reason why some pro- cesses succeed at one time and in one place and fail at another. In this matter of egg preservation'there is a consider- ation that has never yet had its weight, namely, the fer- tility or infertility of the eggs to be preserved. We have only 'once seen it suggested that infertile eggs might keep much better than those which have the germ of life within them. But a little consideration will show that this may be a most important matter. The idea was suggested to our own mind by thinking over the fact that infertile eggs never go rotten when sat upon by hens. They dry up and become fusty, but it is only the fertile egg that actually goes rotten. In the former there is no germ of life to die and beeome putrid. In the lat- ter it is the death of the living organism which causes the rottenness. This germ must have actualflife within it, for the life cannot be put there after the egg has been laid, and the presence of life gives all the elements for putridity. We have met those who have declared they can tell whether an egg is fertile or not before it is sat upon, and several times the experiment have shown the test to turn out right. The way in which this is done is by placing the broad end of an egg into the mouth, and, with the lips around it, breathing 'thereon, If after doing so the egg does not -seem cold, or, to put it in a better way, appears to give back warmth, then it is fertile; but if, on the other hand, it takes all the heat without giving back any, then it is infertile. Often have we proved this test to be correct, but we should scarcely like to depend entirely upon it in the case or valuable eggs. But whether there be any truth in it or not we do not feel that there need be any doubt that the preservation of eggs may depend greatly upon whether they are fertile or infertile. As already explained, the former have within them the germs of rottenness, and the latter have not. Therefore, we should strongly advise those who intend putting eggs down for the winter to only use in- fertile ones. Though we cannot go so far as to lay down as a fixed yule that for which we have been here con- tending, yet there is so much of reason and of proba- bility in It that we feel quite justified in going as far as we have done. There can in no case be any advantage in preserving fertile eggs, for they can never be used for hatching, and there is little or no difficulty in arranging that the eggs be infertile. To summarise the methods of egg preservation, we should be inclined to place the lime water system first, as best for practical purposes, whether for home use or for sale. It involves the least expense and the leait trolible. The egg is least changed when preserved in lime water, as there is little or no evaporation. Next to that, we should be included to think that the freezing process would come, but it would not be suitable for those who produce eggs for the market, and the expense would be too great if an ice chamber bed to be specially erected; therefore, it is only available in a very few in- stances. The other methods given can be adopted if preferred, but some of them, at least, are more of in• teresting experiments than practical. We lay very great stress upon the question of fertility or non-fertility, for we believe that unfertile eggs will keep where fertile ones will not.

Most probably some of the earlier pullets will soon begin to lay. There may be some of the January and February hatched pullets laying already, but we do not care to force them on too soon, as they never make such fine birds as when allowed to mature properly. It is to be preferred that pullets should commeve laying about the end of September or the beginning of October, if possible, as eggs are then getting scarce in consequence of most of the old birds in the moult, and they are then more likely to continue laying right through the winter. , If the pullets are showing signs of laying it will be better to put them off by:moving them from one run to an- other, for as a rule this keeps them back and does no harm in any way. Unless this is done there is danger that the earlier hatched birds will moult in the autumn.

The "Five Ails" was at one time a very common tavern sign in England. It consisted of five human figures, each accompanied by a motto. The first was a king in full regalia, with the legend "I govern all "; the second a bishop in pontificals, with the motto "I pray for all"; the third a lawyer in his gown, with the motto, "I plead for all "; the fourth a soldier in regimentals, with the motto "I fight for all "; and the fifth a poor countryman with scythe and rake, having for motto, "I pay for all." COURTESY IN THE 110IISEHOLD.—TO abbreviate and neglect the forms of politeness is really to diminish the settlements and the needs of the heart. As soon as one ceases to express outwardly even the most essential sentiments, these sentiments become weakened to a certain degree in the soul; they lose something of their delicacy and of their energy. The cultivation of the forms of politeness must be begun in family life between husbands and wives, parents and children, brothers and sisters. Till courtesy is honoured in the household, it will not appear elsewhere.

LUBRICATED SIGNAL WIRES.—An American railway company now uses signal wires running in tubes filled with petroleum oil. Some of the wires are 1,100 feet long, and are easily operated. The pipes are laid on stakes driven into the ground Bft. apart, and are 41n. in diameter inside; whilst the wire is 3-16 in. in diameter. The pipes run parallel to the railway, and follow the curves as well as the straight parts of the lines. ILLUMINATING A POND.—In the new Cirque Nautique of Faris, the ring -Where equestrian and other ordinary circus entertainments are performed during the earlier part of the ,evening, is submerged by means of machinery, the floor being lowered and its place occupied by water. This water is illuminated in the middle by a powerful electric arc light under the surface, and the swimming peformers appear like fishes in a luminous sea, or better still, like mermen and mermaids. EXCAVATIONS IN MRXICO.—M. Charnay's excavations at Popocatepetl in the course of his scientific mission to Mexico and Central America, at the cost of the French Government and Mr. Lorillard, of New York, have pro- duced valuable results. At a height of 13,000 feet above the level of the sea he obtained 370 objects from an ancient Indian cemetery, the interments in which consisted entirely of young persons, not a single bone being that of an adult. It is suggested that the burials mark the site of one of the high places upon which in- fant human sacrifices were offered to the god Tlaloc, representations of whom are frequent among the objects discovered.

THE CHINTISEI LARIL—Among the trophies brought home by the French army from the Eastern expedition is a specimen of a bird, rarely if at all seen in Europe. This is the :celebrated Chinese, or rather Manchoorian, lark. Ho is a larger bird than his European congener; his notes are more brilliant, and his natural repertoire, if the expression may be used, is more extensive. put the most noticeable feature is his wonderful promptness and skill of mimicry, deserving indeed in this respect the title of a genuine mocking bird, imitating most natural sounds which he hears, the notes and songs of other birds, the cawing of crows, the crowing of cocks, bray- ing of the donkey, even the barking of dogs. The Chinese turn this faculty to account, and train the lark to sing many airs. _

How LIGHTNING WORKS.—OR the 27th of July a party of engineers and workmen had an excellent opportunity of observing the way in which a thunder cloud dis- charges its electricity. They had just completed the fitting of a lightning conductor at the shelter hut on the Mythen, in Schwyz. A heavy storm was seen approach- ing from three different points, and they took refuge in the hut. Through a hole in the wall they could see the conductor. From time to time small bluish flames ap- peared hovering on it; then the lightning flash would be seen descending alone- the conductor into the earth, fol- lowed almost instantaneously by the thunder crash. More than twenty times they watched the phenomena regularly suceeeding each other; then there was an electrical discharge of such violence that there seemed to be a recoil, and two of the party felt the shock from be- low up to their hips, and one fancied that both his legs were shot off. The party was so terrified that they quitted the hut and descended the mountain amid blinding snow, as thick as if it were the middle of winter, varied by thunder and lightning. ELECTRIC BOAT.—The Spark, which has recently been launched at the Royal Gunpowder Factory, Waltham Abbey, is an electric boat about 25ft..10ng and sft. beam. It was designed by the superintendent, Colonel W. H. Noble, R. A., mainly as a means of lighting up some of the powder houses in the factory which are at a con- siderable distance from the dynamos used for general electric lighting purposes. The details of construction have been worked out by Mr. Thomas Webb, the chief engineer in the gunpowder works, who has given much attention to the subject of electric lighting. The light- ing and motive powers of the boat are derived from a battery of accumulator cells, stowed under cover amid- ships, and a small li-horse power motor, which turns the shaft to which the screw propeller is attached. The accumulator cells were supplied by the Electrical Power Storage Company, of which Mr. Drake is manager, and are those known as No. 23, 5, type. Each cell consists of a wooden (teak) box, "q inches in length by 8+ inches in width by 10+ inches in height, and weighs 4.51 b. com- plete. Inside the box are a number of lead plates of special form surrounded by acidulated water, which is poured in throueh a small hole in the top of the box. Two strips of lead project about a couple of inches from the top of the box; these are the positive and negative poles, and, by attaching the positive pole of one box to the negative pole of another, and so on, a number of boxes are coupled together so as to form a battery. When a current of electricity is passed into a battery of this construction certain chemical changes take Place and the battery becomes capable of retaining, or rather absorbing, the electric energy due to such a current and of subsequently discharging or giving it out in the form of light, heat, or power as required. In fact, a certain quantity of electro-motive force is, so to speak, bottled up, and a battery of accumulator cells thus takes the place of a gasometer as regards lighting, and of a steam boiler as regards n-otive power. The total number of cells in Colonel Noble's boat is 30. and these are connected together as above described and stowed away under a kind of deck in the centre of the boat. To charge the battery the boat is brought up one of the factory canals alongside the "Dynamo-house" and the two wires lead- ing from this electric generator are attached respectively to the positive and negative poles of the battery. The dynamo, which is driven by a steam engine, is then started and a charge of electricity is run into the bat- tery until the acidulated water assumes a milky appear- ance and begins to give off gas bubbles. The battery has now taken in as much electro-motive force as it is cap- able of absorbing, and the poles are disconnected from the dynamo. The boat is now ready for use, and the poles are connected with the motor or dynamo electric discharger in the stern through a "reversing switch," controlled by a handle which when turned in one direc- tion causes the motor to act and the screw to go ahead, and in the other direction to go astern. Now, if it be desired to light up any powder house the boat is run alongside, the poles disconnected from the motor and reconnected to the wires which communicate with the electric incandescent lamps in the house. Most dan- gerous operations are carried on in many of these houses, and hitherto no light of any description was permitted even to approach them. The consequence was that as soon as it became dark all work had to cease. With the aid, however, of the electric light accumulator boat and special safety lamps work can now be carried on by night as well as by day. The speed of Colonel Noble's boat is from five to six knots an hour' and, so far as can be judged from the trials made up to date, it is a perfect success.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

The match between England and Auqralia ended disas- trously for our visitors, on Saturday. Ibis defeat of the Antipodeans, the third this season by representative English teams, proves most decidedly that Mr. Scott's men are far inferior to those sent over in past years, and that the Aus- tralians do not pull together as many of the preceding elevens have done. It ought, however, to be borne in mind that in this match the Colonists were without the services of two of their best bowlers. The hero of the match was undoubtedly W. G. Grace, with his magnificent score of 170, the highest he has ever made against an Australian eleven. His total was put together with remarkably good cricket, though at the commencement he ought to have been got out more than once. His most noticeable mistake was at the time he had scored six, when he ought to have been easily caught. The Surrey batsman, W. W. Read, played the best innings on the English side, his 94 being hit off without a mistake; while Briggs, the Lancastrian, played a lively innings for 53. The collapse of the visitors came as a surprise on everybody. With the exception of Palmer and Trum )1e none of them were able to stand up to the bowling. Lohmann, the Surrey professional, who had been a failure in the other two matches, made capital amends by securing 7 wickets for 36 runs, and received quite an ovation at the conclusion of the innings. Briggs also bowled remarkably well, capturing 3 wickets for 28 runs. In their second essay, on Saturday, the "cornstalks" made a better stand, but It was of no avail, the match closing in a win for Eng- land by an innings and 217 runs. At Derby, on Tuesday, the home county suffered a crush- ing defeat at the hands of Lancashire by ten wickets, a result in a great measure due to the remarkable bowling of Watson. The •Lancashire innings, in which five wickets had fallen overnight for 65 rune, closed for 119, which gave them an advantage of 35 runs. Against this Derbyshire did so badly, that with four wickets down for eight runs it seemed that they might even be beaten in an innings. A useful 17 by Mr. Docker, did much to avert this die. grace, and in the end the total reached 43, which left Lan- cashire 9to get to win. These were quickly obtained by Barlow and Brig,ga, and Lancashire won as stated. Yorkshire, after a long run of bad luck this season, re- gained some of their lost laurels on Wednesday, by deci- sively beating Middlesex, on the Horton Park Avenue Ground, at Bradford. Up to this match the once powerful' not thern eleven had only beaten one first-class county this year, but on the present occasion they were seen at their beet, and outplayed the metropolitan county at all points of the game.

Though the Sussex men lost five wickets on Wednesdar morning in making the 49 runs wanted to beat Surrey, the' result of the match was never in doubt. Su,sea gained a thoroughly well-deserved victory by four 'wickets. Previ• ous to Wednesday, Sussex had not beaten Surrey for some considerable time, and the success will therefore be all the more welcome. The Surrey men bowled and fielded al' mirably, and did their best to save a hopeless game. On Wednesday, on the College Ground at Cheltanhrl, the Australians beat Gloucestershire ly 26 runs, this being their first success since they defeated Yorkshire at Shef- field on the 14th of July. At the close of Tuesday's play Gloucestershire had seven wickets to go down and wanted 1102 runs to win the match. On a very slow and rather dif- ficult wicket this taek proved too heavy, the innings being finished off for the addition of 75 uns to the previous total. The match ended in a victory for the Australians by 26 runs. Altogether it was a very interesting game, and the Australians may be congratulated on their success. The bowling was fine on both sides, but there was a number of mistakes in the field. Spofforth's five wickets in Glouces- tershire's second innings COM him 09 runs, but his record for the whole of the match was an excellent one—ten wickets for 106 runs. Palmer, Garrett, and Trumble also bowled remarkably well, the latter faking two wickets at the end of the match for six runs.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

Shallots have now completed their growth, and the bulbs should be taken up and spread out in an open, airy position, in order to get them thoroughly dry before being stored for the winter. After they are cleaned they may be placed in cupboards or drawers, or tied up le bags and suspended from the roof of a dry but not tOO warm room, so as not to excite premature growth. Herbs for drying should be cut on a dry, sunny day, and the sorts spread separately on pieces of paper. After they are thoroughly dry they are usually tied iu bunchet and suspended from the kitchen ceiling, either exposed,. or wrapped in a sheet of paper. Many are in too man haste to pack them up, and the consequence is that when the bunches are taken down for use they are found quite mouldy, and to use them would spoil the flavour of any dish. They no doubt appeared dry at the dme they were tied, and their leaves probably were so, but the stems of such as Mint and Sage contain much stP that is not dissipated as readily as from leave and when the herb is tied in a bunch its chances of esc iping art lessened, which accounts for the mouldy appearance .91: the herbs when untied. However carefully herbs Sre harvested in this way they are sure to lose their arointe and unless very carefully tied in bags they accumul2o a quantity of dust that may be seen flying in clouds aS the bunches are takeridown. We prefer to place thera in bottles, and as the herbs dry the leaves are rubbed between the hands and pieces of branches picked out, se nothing should be stored that is not fit for use. Battluag should not take place till there is ample evidence t.110,_, they are thoroughly dry, and to ensure this they mign"' be spread on paper and placed in the oven in the even- ing when the heat is on the decline, and allowed to re' main there till the morning with the door slightly open to allow any moisture that may be present to escaPt When it is necessary to open the bottles to use some ot the contents they should be corked up again at once. Treated in this way, it will be found that whatever r& mains in them twelve months hence will be as fragrant as it was on the day when it was first put in. It should be observed that all herbs have matured and are at tir best when they commence t: flower.—Raspberry: 'the young canes should be. tied up loosely to their parens to protect them from being damaged by winds or by the movements of those who have to go amongst them IP pick the fruit. The season has been decidedly in favour of this fruit, which is very fine and abundant. The picir ing has been going on for three weeks, and will from present appearance find agreeable occupation for some time yet.-- Lettuce : To ensure a stock of these to plant out in the Spring. it is necessary to make more than one sowing, me much depends upon the nature of the weather for the next two months; and a sowing made now, for instances if followed by fine growing weather, would most prote• ably be too forward to stand a severe winter, whilst one' made a fortnight hence would survive. Lettuce soyrn now, and taken care of during the winter, means having them fit for use in June instead of July, if Spring.sosvn ones are relied upon; for it often occurs that the seedn cannot be sown before May, and even then its progress in slow. The best sorts to resist the cold and wet of winter are the brown Bath cos and hardy hammersmith, and if they are sown thinly and not allowed to become crowded at any stage of their growth they pass through most winters uninjured. Tile FRONT GARDEN.—The sooner carnations nee layered the better, Othat they may have time to form' sufficient roots to carry them through the winter.. In wet, heavy soils, in cold districts, bothl old and young plants are apt to perish in winter; hence the importanee of annual propatation. To make doubly sure, many pot up a few of even the common kinds, and preserve tbern in a frame, to avoid losing the stock. Gardens in the country are subject to have the carnations in them de• stroyed in a night by a rabbit or a hare nibbling the heart out of each growth, rendering it useless. We have' frequently suffered in this way, and had we not taken the above precaution our stock would have been lost. Everything should be in readiness before: layering in actually commenced,. and, first of all, a barrow loth--O whatever quantity may be required—of soil, composed of loam, leaf mould, and sand, nassed through a half - inch sieve, should be placed round each parent plant after the layers are dressed, so that when they are cat they have only to be pegged down into it. The pegs may be convoyed from one root to another in a basket or flower pot, or the requisite number thrown down at each place, so that there may be no necessity to move before eaeh:lot is completed. The soil should be well , raised into a mound round the plant, and slightly pressed with the hands, in order that those layers that remain out for the winter may stand drier than if on the level, as well as provide depth of better soil for the young - roots. Water is best withheld for a day or two, so tlxit the mounds may have an opportunity to heal. THR WlNDOW.—Propagating Pelargoniums: As the plants are cut down—which should be done well late the brown wood of this year's growth—the ripest poPs tions should be selected for cuttings, and cut in lengtbS of three or four inches, then placed round the inner side lof small pots, previously filled with sandy soil madit moderately firm. The pots should be thoroughly cleansed and well drained, by placing a crock or piece of oyster shell large enough to cover the bottom, and on this an inch of broken crocks, covered with moss or half-decayed leaves, to prevent the smaller particles of soil mixing with them and obstructing the free passage of water. The pots may stand in the open air providing they ails afforded some protection from heavy rain. If kept in the window, no more water must be given until they form roots than will prevent the soil becoming dustsdrY.

Honest industry is always rewarded. No young' man need complain of being kept poor if he rolls up' his sleeves and goes cheerfully to work. One man rebuke i another for smoking. The culprit replied that he used the weed in moderation. "What do you call moderation?" inquired the other. "WY sir," said the offender, "one cigar at a time." "Sarah Jane, what book is that you're reading So steadily all the time ?" It's a novel, by Dumas, the elder." "Don't tell me! Dumas the elder? What church could he be elder in and write novels, I shoug like to know ?"

A gentleman on a steamboat asked the steward, when he came round to collect the passage-money (one shilling) if there was no danger of being blown up. The steward promptly replied. "No sir, not in the least we can't afford to blow people up at a shilling a head." At a Boston theatre, after the impressive performance of Booth's "Hamlet," attention was drawn to the effusive delight of a young lady who was thus trying apparentlY to show her gratitude to the gentleman upon whose arm she was resting—" I've had a real good time, Georgeiw said she, "and it is a real lovely. play; it's so full of quotations."

- "Do you not think," said Dorothea to Ezekiel, "that there is something soft and tender in the fall of the beautiful snow?" Ezekiel scratched his head, and re- plied, "There is something soft and tender in the fall of a single snowflake, but when it comes to crawling out in the morning and shovelling away a big drift it's simp,/ disgusting." Richard Cceur de Lion was the most stylish man in England of his time. When he put on his tin helmet and cast-iron ulster, and a pair of steel boots, and picked up a club with an iron knob and a steel spike in the ena, fashionable society considered him just "dressed to kill!' And so he was. And one time, when he was dressed up that way, a fellow killed him. X. had been away from England for what seemed ages, and when his friend Y. met him on the sunny side Of Pall Mall, last week, he (Y.) exclaimed almost involun- tarily, " What ! is it you, X.? Good gracious! hoW. altered you are; you look quite old, don't you know.' "Well," returned X., calmly, "seeing that I was born early in this century, if I wasn't old by this time, why,i should be dead." •

• A lady wrote to a clever authoress to beg her to pre' cure a tutor for her son, one endowed with every imagin- able qualification of mind and heart. Her friend replied, "My dear am looking for a tutor such as you have described; but I have not as yet been happy enough te, meet him. I shall continue my search with unabated zeal, and I promise you that as soon as I have found hill 2 I will—marry him!" There is no happiness in the world equal to 010 of blessing others. Not only by giving money tP the needy, help to the sick, food to the hungry, .15 this blessing compassed; we gain it as we give 4* by sympathy, by affection, by seeing that which le best in our friends and shutting our eyes to glat which is worst, by taking joy in their good thug even when our own portion is scant and poor. CAPTURE OF AN IMMENSE WHALE—three Lewis fisher- men, from Kerobost, Bernara, have captured an irornenSe whale, 50 feet long. The animal' had stranded in a email creek, probably in pursuing herrings. The fishermen cut a deep hole through the blubber into the animal's fish, also pierced both eyes until the blood spurted freely. animal lingered for a few night., its death throes he 1. described as most terrible, the poor creature breaking 011 large pieces of rock in its agony. The whale had be sporting in adjacent waters for a fortnight previously. A Stornoway firm has purchased the carcase.

TROOPS FOR BURMAH. CALCUTTA., SUNDAY . —The following corps are placed nn - der orders for ,Burmah, to arrive there by October 20:— Ito. 1 Mountain Battery, eastern division • No. 9 Moun- tain Battery, northern division'; 2nd Battalion Queen's Ist Rifle Brigade. 2nd Munster Fosiliers. 7th Bengal Cav- alry, let Madras Lancers, let Bembav,Lancers, Ist and sth Bengal Infantry, Ist Beloochias, one Madras infantry regi- ment, and 3rd Infantry Hyderabad contingent. The whole force in Burnish, which will then number over 30,000, will be under the command of Sir Herbert Macpherson. Several new brigades will be formed, one .of which will be corn- =sided by Colonel Lockhart, lately in charge of the Ghilgit Mission. A division under General 'John Gordon will proba- bly operate from the Manipur side. FRIDAY.—A general order has beeliseued to the army in India announcing that the ,Viceroy is satisfied that the charges brought apirot Colonel Hooper, late Provost Marshal at Mandalay, of photogeanhing condemned crimi- nals at the moment of execution, and of causing a prisoner to confess under threat of death, have been established. The order adds that Colonel Hooper's conduct reflects dis- credit on the British army, and that the Viceroy woul. have been justified in recommending his dismissal from the service, but having regard to his past career thinks a public reprimand will be sufficient. Colonel Hooper has tseigned. KURDISH RAIDS ON THE RUSSIAN FRONTIER. TIBRERZ. SUNDAY.—SOItitt severe fighting has taken p(ace between the Persians and the insurgent Mangoor Kurds at Lablijan. The Mangoors lost 84 men and took refuge in Turkey. Oorurnia reports that large parties of TuPitish Kurds are crossing the frontier te pillage, the bor- der villages. Persia °elle on Turkey to stop these periodical invasions. and not to harbour the insurgents. THE SOUDAN.—SUPPOSED ARAB MARAUDERS. CAIRO, MONDAY.--SM v.ll hands of Arabe, eupposed to be marauders, are reported to haveatuddenly attacked the out- Doasts at Wady lialfa, but were reoulsed. It is saia that several prisoners were taken. WEDNESDAY.—The friendlies have made a raid.j ag•aiset the rebelle, killing and wounding SO of them They have also cAptured several head of cattle. It is rep )rted Osinan Digna has escaped from Tamil, and is proceeding to Khartoum, his followers having dispersed. WORKING MEN'S DEMONSTRATION IN BELGIUM. Banssers, SUNDAI.—To-dity's demonstration here of the working-classes was remarozably enthusiastic and at the same time moat orderly. Between forty and fifty thousand people arrived before ten o'clock thiA morning, and were formed into a procession six abreast. This marching column was ninety minutes passing a given point, and was about two miles long, taking four hours to perambulatelthe city. Numerous banners were carried on which were inscribed demands for "universal suffrage" and " amnesty " for all fellow-workers who bad fallen into the clutches of the law. The streets were crowded with spectators. The puede and the " demonstrators " were cheered frequently. The " Mar- seillaise " and patriotic airs were sung and played during the who!e of the time taken in passing through the streets, the head of the procession being preceded by the National flag draped in black. Many red banners and caps of liberty were displayed, showing the marked republican sentiments leavening the ever-moving masses. To avoid giving any pretext of inflaming popular passions, the regular troops, though close at hand in sass of necessity, were held in re- serve at fixed stations, the Civic Guards only showing them- selves to tha general public and lining the park in front of the King's palace. The city is in a state of excitement to- night, but the delegates are departing peaceably and good humour prevails. A few illuminations were to be seen at night.

The Rome correspondent of the Times telegraphs—That the cholera is spreading and growing more serious in the southern provinces of Italy there is evidence in the Impres- sion of the usual official bulletins from the worst localities; but that in the Venetian; and to some extent in other northern provinces, many cases which were in panic treateel as cholera were not. SOUTH AFRICA. CAPATOWN, JI7LY 28Th I (VIA PLYNIOUTH).—The financial proposals of th•-• IsTAtal Government have been published. It is estimated that the deficiency at the end of the year will be £233 191. The estimates for 1887 provide for an income of £682,450, and an expenditure of £756.494. Three new taxes will be proposed—a land tax, which is expected to yield £22.000, a house tax, £12,000, and an income tax, 1,17,400.

THE UNITED STATES. WASHINGTON, MONDAY.—General Augur, a prominent army officer on the retired list, was yesterday shot at by a negro whm he bad ordered away from the front of his resi- dence. The negro, on being spoken to, made an insulting reply, and was struck with a cane by the General, where- upon he drew a revolver and fired four shots, wounding the General in the legs and side, each bullet taking effect. None of the wounds are thought to he fetal. THE PRESIDENT OF URUGUAY WOUNDED. PARIS, WRDNESDAY.--A telegram from Monte Video states that as the President of Uraguay was entering the theatre yesterday evening he was approached by an indivi- dual, who, drawing a revolver, fired almest ooint-blank at the President's head, but only succeeded in inflicting a slight wound in the cheek. The would-be assassin was at once secured, and s.) maltreated by the infuriated crowd that he dial shortly afterwerds. SEIZURE OF BRITISH SCHOONERS. Sex Ftzetecteco, TIRIRSDAY.—The American revenue cutter Corwin has seized the British schooners Thornton, Onward, and Caroline for alleged violation of the sea fish- ing laws in Bebring's Sea. The schooners were taken to Toonolaska. The matter has been referred to the British consulate here. WAR PR R PAR ATI ON S IN THE EAST. CONSTANTINOPLE, WEDNESDAY NIGIIT.—The political in- terest here c,ntres upn the warlike movements now pro- ceeding in Servia and Bulgaria. Private advices from Sofia represent Prince Alexander as actively organising his forces and generally preparing for what is on all sides believed to be an early renewal bf the conflict with Servia. According to same odyices the consul of one of the Powers has expressed the opinion that war would break out within a very few weeks.

MORE RIOTING DT BELFAST. FATAL RESULTS. On Sunday there was a renewal of disturbances, with sad results, marksmen having congregated in the locality be- tween Shenkbill and Old Falls Road, and with a determine- tioddifficult to realise carried on a rifle duel in the still hours of early morning. The firing was continued for four hours. It commenced at one or two o'clock. The authori- ties were unable to get at the combetants. The crowds had at five o'clock to be dtspersed by the military after the Riot Act had been pool. Th 9 thoroughfares in which the firing to,* place are known as Ashmore, Conway, Cup, Northern., berland, and North Howard-streets. These run from the Protestant to the Catholic districts. They are inhabited by a labouring- class population. The commencement of the fight with r:fles is, as usual, enveloped inenystery. ludeed,in . no place out of Belfast is it so difficult to get at facts or to obtain impartial statements. But it Would appear that about two o'clock some eight or ten riflemen on each side began their cruel work. They posted themselves in empty houses, on mill roofs, in stacks of chimneys, in doorways, and at street corners. The parties were equally divided so far as can be ascertained. They were backed by immense crowde, carefully kept out of range, but prepared to render assistance in supplying ammunition and carrying away the injured. For four. hours the fusilade was kept up with the aid of a bright moonlight. What are the results are only partially known. The full extent of the mischief will never be discovered. The Protestants acknowledge that on their side a moo named Macfarlane was killed by a bullet which passed through the right lung. They had also two men injured, one named Smith, by a bullet in the hip. The other, Johnston, had his collar-bone and shoulder-blade smashed, also by a ride bullet. The Protestants claim to have either killed er wounded many Catholics, and to have seen the bodies carried away. The Catholics, on the other hand, deny havinghad a single casualty on their side. An inspection of scene of the battle shows that the Catholic fire was profuse and well directed. A public-house at the corner of Conwav-s!reet and facing the Falls Road is riddled with bullets, which passed through doors and windows, and were embedded in toe walls. It is remarkable that the in- mates should have escaped injury. On many other houses are undoubted signs of tha rifle tire. At the Catholic end the huller. marks are fewer in number, thus leading to. the belief that the Protestants were less active in firing than their opponents. Whenever the military came in sight the combatants shifted their ground, and it was not till five o'clock, after the Riot Act had been twice read, that the two crowds were dispersed and quiet restored. Farther evidence was forthcomine of the terribly unsafe condition of the town. The police had a strong force at Springfield to Pre- vent the threatened renewal of last week's battle. Four shots were fired at the force, and lodged in the wall behind them. Shots were also fired at the police at the corner of David-street. The house of a Catholic neblican in the Protestant district was looted, three arrests being made, and in other parts equally unpleasant circumstances occurred. The police did not, by special order, fire a shot, but there is reason to believe that the direction that they should use buckshot, and not bullet, has now been withdrawn. The inquest no :he body of John Edgewater, who was shot by the police was held on Saturday afternoon. The deceased, who was employed as a labourer for the Corpora-

5101, left his own house in Shankbill-road on Saturday, the 7th inst.. to visit an aunt, and was shot down in Shankhitl- road. The jury returned a unanimous verdict of " wilful murder against some member of the police force unknown to the jury." A desperate attack was made on Saturday night upon a train running between Portadown and Belfast. Shortly after the train had left the former station a number of large stones were thrown upon and into the carriages, and several shots were fired from above the embankment. One bullet passed through a first-class compartment occupied by Miss Minnie Palmer, the actress, a lady companion, and her maid, but unfortunately none, although greatly alarmed, were injured. The missile entered the open window on the one side and went out through the glass on the other, leav- ing a clean-cut hole. The outrage is attributed to local Orangemen, who are credited with the intention of injuring the persons travelling by the train to share in the Lady Day celebrations. While a Nationalist band was parading a Protestant dis- trict in Dungannon on Monday evening, a disturbance arose, in which a Protestant was seriously injured. One Nationalist was arrested with an open knife in his hand. A large force of police succeeded in separating the parties and preventing a serious riot, but further disturbances were feared. On Tuesday afternoon there was a slight renewal of the disturbances in Leeson-street, M'Donnell-street, and the thoroughfares adjoining Culingtree-road. Several charges were made, and the military succeeded in clearing the streets without the slightest difficulty. Every precaution has been taken by the authorities to prevent a renewal of riots in these localities. The crowds are not allowed to gather in the streets, but the worst feature of the guerilla warfare is that persons fire from their houses or over the wall at the rear, and thus escape detection. The authorities are of opinion that coostables'eannot for a long time return to duty on the Shankhill-road. as those who have ventured there in the day time have been beaten back, while is the dark they would certainly be murdered in cold blood. There are 50 injured persons in the Royal Hospital, and 200 have been treated externally. There are about a dozen In the Union Hospital. The number at the Mater Infir- morum Hospital cannot be ascertained, but among them are 50 policemen. One private practitioner has treated 80 cases, another 60—all on the Protestant aide. It is believed that many persons injured or killed on the Catholic side have been secretly removed. Two funerals took place on Tuesday amidst painful signs of passionate grief in the Orange district, the bodies interred being those of Samuel McFarlane, killed in the Conway- street battle, and Jackson, shot by a constable in Old Lodge-road. A fight occurred in the Cullingtev-road, this military havin to disperse the combatants ; and. some soli- tary cases of personal violence occurred in the Shankhill district, otherwise nothing calls for special remark. Several rioters have been arrested. The magistrates again closed the public-houses from five o'clock at night till ten in the morning. Several unsuccessful raids were made for arms. There was no disturbance on Wednesday, and for the first time since the commencement of August, a portion of the troops in Belfast garrison were allowed out of quarters oaf duty. There were, however, some 20 pickets of 50 men each and a large number of patrols on duty at night in the disturbed districts. The liquor sellers of the town Met on the same day to protest against the action of the magistrates in closing the public-houses, and it was decided to take legal proceedings to recover compensation. The inquest on Isaac Weir Jackson, who was shot on Saturday week during the time the police were firing out of M'Kenna's public-house, concluded soon after midnight On Thursday morning, and the jury • returned a verdict of "Wilful murder " against nine of the constabulary. The nine men against whom the verdict of wilful murder was returned have not yet been arrested, but remein under con- stabulary surveillance. The town is quiet to-day. On Thursday It was telegraphed that the most welcome indica- tions of the return ef peace are apparent on all sides. The resumption of work is general, and apprehensions of an out- break in establishments where party feeling or religious bi- gotry runs high are gradaally sulosiding. THE STATE OF ICEBRY.—A correspondent writes :—" A clergyman near Tralee, the Rev. Wm. Raymond, has been boycotted in the matter of saving his hay. A notice was posted forbidding labourers to mow the grass, in consequence of his having signed an anti-Home Rule petition. After the meadows had been saved in spite of the notice the bay was strewn about the field during the night. Several per- son's in a village of this clergyman's parish were also an- noyed for having signed the petition, and three farmers were summoned before the local National League on Sunday last to explain their conduct. They attended, and eonteas to having apologised for the rash act. The penalty of re- fusal, they allege, would have been ruin to them. The same night the Rector of Ardfort was attacked, and only escaped by his having left by the kitcken door, where he was Par- leying with the moonlighters before opening it, a second or two before the shot came through. He, too, had signed the petition, and his coachman had to apologise for the same offence to the lecal League."

THE POLITICAL SITUATION. Her Majesty held a Privy Council at Osborne on Monday afternoon, for the purpose of considering the terms of the Queen's Speech to be read in Parliament on Thursday. After the Council the Ministers had luncheon at Osborne, and left at 2.30. They embarked at Trinity Pier on board the ()lichees of Edinburgh steam packet, Lord Salisbury being with the party., and arrived at Portsmouth at 3-50. There was no demonstration, and the Ministerial party pro- ceeded to London by the train which left a few minutes later, and arrived in London at six o'clock. Lord Burghley (C) was on Monday nominated for North Noethansptonshire. Ihere being no other candidate his lord- ship was declared to be duly elected. Sydney Evershed (L) and Gerald Hardy (C) were nominated on Monday for the Burton Division of Stafford- shire. Mr. James Samuelson. of Birkenhead, was on Monday presented, in Glasgow, by the East Renfrewshire Liberal Committee, with a silver casket and an illuminated address, expreeeing their high appreciation of the ready. manner in which he accepted the invitation to become their candidate, and of the ability, intelligence, and courtesy displayed by him during his candidature. I believe, wrlt4s4 London correspondent, that amorw, the Scotch Radical members there is some idea of raising the question of Scotch Home Rule on the Address. The subject. is hardly ripe yet for Parliamentary action, but undoubtedly it is growing. The object of the Scotch Radical members is, however, not so much to force on the Scotch question as to assist the solution of the Irish one. Any scheme of Scotch Home Rule would be limited and moderate in character, and would certainly not exclude the Scotch members from the Imperial Parliament. Mr. Marriott, M.P., speaking at a Primrose League de- monstration, bele at Brocklesby Park, Lincolnshire, on Sat- urday, said with regard to Ireland, the Conservative party were determined to remove the system of tyranny practised by the National League and establish law and order. He did not know why the Irish were to be treated differently to English, Scotch, or Welsh. A committee of the Cabinet has been appointed to con- eider matters in regard to Ireland. This body held its first ' meeting on Saturday in the Cabinet Chambers, Downing. street. Mr. Matthews and Mr. Smith were the first to I arrive. Besides these right hon. gentlemen the committee consists of Lord Salisbury, Lord R. Churchill, and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach. The nomination for Leith Burghs took place on Satur- day. The candidates nominated were Mr. Munroe Forgo- son (Gladetonian Liberal). Mr. William Jacks (Unionist Liberal), Mr. McGregor (Unionist), and Mr. Henry Mun- ster, of Brighton, who has issued an address from which it is impossitile to gather whether he is a Liberal or a Con- servative. Mr. Labouehere, writing to the "Daily News," contends that the Liberals as a party have stood by Mr. Gladstone and pronounced against the dissentients. He says-4 Our course should be to call upon the Liberal electors throagh- out the country to formulate a political programme, and declare this to be the programme of the Liberal party, out- side whieh,there is ne salvation." A Halifax ventleman has received the following letter from Mr. J- Morley, M.P., in reply to queries which will tie understood from the letter itself :—" 95. Elm Park Gardens, South Kensington, S.W., August 9, 1886. Dear Sir,—Both the statements to which you refer are untrue. It is untrue that the bill for the Better Gevernment of Ireland was sprung upon the Ministry without prior consultation.' It is untrue that 'no member of the Cabinet, wive Mr. Gladstone, had any part in its production.' But pray do not suppose that either this or any other authentic contradiction will prevent the repetition of these foolish stories so long as they are convenient to the Paper Union- ists for electioneering purposes." The third Cabinet Council of the new Government wee held on Tuesday. at noon, at the Foreign °dice. It is understood that a draft of the forthcoming Queen's Speech was considered and approved. The Afghan frontier difficulty also claimed attention. With regard to Ireland the Government had decided to introduce next session a measure of local self-government which may subsequently be extended tie the rest of the Kinedern. For this measure Lord R. Churchill is mainly responsible, and, it is under- stood, it will be of such a character as to secure the suffrages of Lora Hartington and those who thick with him. Sir Richard Cross has now decided to take the title of Lord Cross, and Sir Frederick Stanley that of Lord Stanley. Mr. J. Harris Sanders, who contested the Hatboro' Divi- sion of Leicestershire at the list election, has been selected as the Liberal candidate for King's Lynn, to contest the seat vacated by Mr. Bourke. A "FATAL DEPAUTURE."—The Hon. Secretary of the Working-men's Protestant League 113.4 addressed a letter to Lord Salisbury expressing tha astonishment of "'°' com- mittee " that his Lordship should have given the office of Homo Secretary to Mr. Matthews, and also protesting stronaly against "this innovation upon our constitutional liberties, which inaugurates a new and fatal departure from genuine Conservatism."

THE CARDIFF RIOTS.—It is stated that Mr. Commis- sioner Bridge, who was sent to Cardiff to inquire into the late election riots in that town, in the report which he has now made exonerates the head constable and all the police officers, but considers that they acted without discretion, Whilst at the same time they were under great provocation.
