Superintendent Barker, in opening the cage, said that on Saturday night last about six o'clock, what was called an" Orange eland " arrived in Widnes from Garston, and proceeded to Fern- worth. They were armed with sticks and stones, and as they catne uack they shoutel and made a great noble, at the same time waving these sticks about defiantly ; and 1 as if challenging aevone to interfere with them. A fight occurred at Simm's Cross. and Constable Liptrot hearing screams, ran out of his house without uniform, but many people shouted out "Here's a policeman coming." He seized bold of the prisoner who was fighting, and told him be was a constable. At once the prisoner deliberately !struck him and rendered him unconscione, and he had not been able to attend his duties SinC3.—P.C. Liotrot deposed thet he was in his own house when he heard screams of murder, and he ran out. He saw a bandsman and another man dressed in ordinary costume and some other men ex- changing blows. fie apprehended the bandsman, and was taking him to hi a house. Severel men then set upon bim, struck him on the head with sticks' and he became uncon- scious, and tbe prisoner escaped. He received a large and serious wound on the head, and he was still under the doc- tor's care and unfit for duty. There was a great disturbance. He could not swear to the prisoner.—Jarims Fallon, labourer, Grenville-street, also stated that he came out of his house through hearing screams of murder, and he saw a number •

son, chief district inspector of mines, Mr. Martin, inspector of mines, and Mr. Norton, ttssistant in- spector, were present on behalf of the Home Office. Mr. Me:skin Peace, of Wigan, represented the pro- prietor of the colliery (Mr. John Speakman); and Mr. J. J. Hope represented the Leigh and Tyldesley Miners' Association. There were also present Messrs. T. B. Grace-Bough, Robert Isherwood, and Robert Woods (miners agent). The first witness called was Mr. John Speakman, who stated that he was owner of the colliery, and detailed the circum- stances attending the accident. He also described the method of -ventilation adopted at the colliery. from Which it appeared that the .quantity of air circulating in the workings equals 330 cubic feet per man, per minute. Gas had been reported in these workings before, but the air was always sufficient to carry it off. The inquest was again adjourned,

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. Parliament was opened by Commission at two o'clock on Thursday afterroon. The Speaker took the chair at a quar- ter to two, and immediately after prayers the swearing in of members, of whom about 250 have still to take their seats, was proceeded with. Shortly after two o'clock the House was summoned to the House of Lords to bear the Queen's Elpeech, and the Speaker, escorted by most of the members present, at once repaired to the Upper Chamber. On the return of the House the proceedings were, after the usual formalities, suspended until four o'clock. The following is the text of the Speech

Mr LORDS AND GENTLBMIN, I have summoned you to meet at this unusual season of the year for the transaction of indispensable businesa. The Session of the last Parliament was interrupted before the ordinary wirk of the year had been completed in order that the sense of my people might he taken on certain important proposals with regard to the Government of Ireland. The result of that appeal has been to confirm the conclusion to which the late Parliament has come. The provisional na- ture of the arrangement which was made by the last Par- liament for the public charge of the year rendered it inex- pedient to poftpone any further the consideration of the ce- eeseary financial legislation. LiIaNTLRIOIN OF TH_B Horn OF Commoss, The estimates which were submirted to the last Par- liament. and were only partially roted, will be laid before you. Mr LORDS AND GNISTLEMBN, At a period of the year usually assigned for the recess and after the prolonged and exceptional labours to which many of yo-a have been subject, I abstain from recommend ing now for your consideration any measures except those which are oerrential to the conduct of the public service. During the remaining portion of the financial year I am confident they will receive your prompt and careful atten- tion.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—TITURSDAY. DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. The House resumed at four o'clock, and several new peers were ietrodueed and sworn.—The Earl of ONSLOW moved and Lord DE Rres seconded the Address in reply to the Queen's Speech.—Earl GRANVILLE drew attention to the many omissions in that document, and asked for some de- claration from the Government on the Colonial and Indian questions. He appealed to Lord Salisbury to give a general and clear indication of his Irish policy, and not to leave the nation without information for six months —The Duke of ARGYLL avowed the delight with which he saw the rejection of the Home Rule Bill end Mr. Gladstone's defeat, for the Li- beral Government had been unmindful of the liberty of loyal subjects in Ireland. He hoped the Premier would net fall into Mr. Gladstone'e error by trying to make single- handed a new Constitution for the United Kingdom, ter that was a task beyond even him.—Lord CAT/MARTON earnestly trusted the Government would lose no opportunity of bring- leg about a perfect conciliation between England and Ire- land.—Lord SALISEURY, dealing with the questions of Earl Granville, said he could take no responsibility for the un- satisfactory state of affeirs in Burmah. The condition of that country was net the subject of any apprehension or alarm; more extended operations would be began at the close of the hot season, and be anticipated that all difficulties would speedily be removed. As to the Afghan frontier, it was not quite accurate to say that our Commis- sion had been withdrawn. The matters at issue between us and Russia, although of some considerable importance, were not large in respect of territory, and the negotiations could be as well conducted between London and St. Peters- burg. Going on to speak of Ireland, the Premier said the Government in power had been returned to maintain the Union, and it would he their duty to restore secial order and put down the organieed system of intimidation, either by existing law or, if need be, by other law asked from Parlia- ment. A Commission would be appointed to examine into the extent of that evil, and also to investigate the state- ments that non-payment of rent was due to absolute in- ability of the tenants, by reason of a fall in prices and other wises, to meet their engagements To works of improve- ments, such as railways, drainage, and harbours, they would give careful attention, but when he was asked for detail his only answer was that time, consideration, and inquiry were above all things necessary. Effective measures had been taken to suppress the disturbances in Belfast, and a Com- mission would determine on whom lay the responsibility for those excesses --The Address was agreed to, and their lordships adjourned until Monday week. ROUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAT. The House having adjourned after the reading of the Queen's Speech, the Speaker again took the chair at 4-15. PEERS AND PARLIAMENTARY ELECTIONS -- On the SPEAKER proposing the adoption of the usual sessional order prohibiting peers from interfering in Parliamentary elections, Mr. BRADLAUGH moved that the order should not be re-enacted, on the ground that it had been wilfully and persistently infringed, and mentioned the names of a number of Deers who broke the rule at the recent general election.—. Sir WILFRID LAWSON seconded the motion.— The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said he would propose that a committee be appointed to inquire into this subject. —Mr. GLADSTONE thought it would be wiser. to refer the qmuoetsi toi on nwteor et hpe rCe sosme dm he tet e eshoon Puidr ivvoi tahn and usea tad ot Nh, eartaimf etnhte. On a division the numbers were—for the renewal of the standing order, 2P4; against, 1213. THE BELFASC RIOTS, &C.—ln answer to Mr. Parnell, Lord It. CHURCHILL said it was the intention of the Gov- ernment to prorogue Parliament as soon as the financial business was concluded.—Ausvrering Me. Sexton, Sir M. HICKS-BEACH requested that notice might be given of a question bearing upon the withdrawal of the police at Bel- fest, and, in reference to an inquiry into the riots, said the intention was to strengthen the Commission appointed by the late Government, and to extend its scope, but not to create a Royal Commission. DEBATE ON THE ADDRES3. The Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne was then moved by Colonel KING-HARMAN, and seconded by Mr. MACLEAN. Mr. GLADSTONE said he wished to avoid controversial matters, and noted with satisfaction the evi- dence of the continuity in. the country's foreign policy. With regard to Ireland his views had not changed, nor had the condition of the country. The late Government had been much pressed to declare its policy, but he thought Ministers were entitled to a reasonable amount of time for ceneideration. It was satisfactory to find that the Speech made no allusion to repression, for to his mind the further they got away from repression the nearer they came to a sound policy. He urged the Government to declare their Irish policy while the opportunity was favourable, and not to let their deliberation be too prolonged.— Lord R. CHURCHILL, in reply, said that as Mr. Gladstone had taken the lead of the Nationalist patty, the GoYern- ment might assume that the Irish agitation would now be on constitutional 'lines. The noble Lord then went on to state the intentions of the Government as to Ireland in much the Same terms as were used by Lord Salisbury, and as to the state of crime and disaffection in the South- West of Ireland said the Government had deter- mined to send General Sir E. Buller into the dis- affected localities with power to organise arrangements for the restoration of order and the suppression ef the reign of terrer which had the-el been going on. If this should prove ineffectual, they would not hesitate to come to Parliament for such further powers as they might deem necessary. As to the land question, the Government would take their stand on tne Land Act of 1881, supplemented by the subsequent land legislation, iyith tne intention of carrying out the pro- visions of these enactments as fully as possible. They had, however, always entertained doubts as to the value of machinery for the apportionment of rents, and they were now of opinion that the time had arrived when they ought to have fall Aid satisfactory official information as to the working of the entire system. This being so, the Govern- ment had decided to appoint a Royal Commission, which in the coming autumn and winter would investigate the whole question.—Several members having also spoken, the debate Was adjourned on the motion of Mr. T. P. O'Connor. The House adjourned at 12 o'clock.
A SAD INCIDENT.
A sad incident has occurred in connection with the accident. The wife of Thomas Fairclough, one of the killed, died on Saturday night broken- hearted.
THE FUNERALS.

The last of the bodies was removed from the Wood End Pit on Monday morning, about half-past one. It was that of William Brown, who had been diligently searched for. The total number recovered is 38. Tbe remains of 10 of the killed were interred in the afternoon at the Leigh Cemetery, only a short dis- tance from the collieries. Some thousands of per- sons assembled, notwithstanding the heavy down- pour of rain, great sympathy with the bereaved families being felt. The names of the men interred were J. Hilton, James Hindley, Peter Ratcliffe, Wm. . Heaton, Henry Smith, Richard Mort and Wm. Mort (father and son), Thomas Hilton, Hiram Pemberton, W. Eekersley, J. Nuttall, R. Bowdon, James Brown, and the three Stirrups '(father and two sons). The bodies of the last three were conveyed direct from the collieries to the cemetery. In the other cases the funerals were from the respective homes of the bereaved. Without exception. the shutters of all the shops along the route were put up while the funeral corteges passed. The blinds of private houses were also drawn. Mr. J. Shuttleworth, a local preacher, conducted the burials in the Nonconfor- mist portion of the grounds, and the Revs. W. Smith, J. F. Lawton, and Father Cowley officiated at the I remainder. The Executive Council of the Lancashire Miners' Federation have passed a vote of condolence with the bereaved, and Mr. T. Ashton, secretary, was in- structed to request the , Home Secretary to send a legal gentleman to attend the inquiry.—Mr. Woods, of Wigan, was appointed to attend the inquiry on behalf of the Federation, with Mr. Isherwood, of Tyldesley. . Mr. Caleb Wright, M.P. for the division, has promised to subscribe OEIO for the widows and orphans. The Committee raising; subscriptions have signed a requisition to he Chairman . of the Local Board (Mr. James Thorp) for a towns meet- , ing. At the Leigh Court House, On ' Thursday, before Mr. J. B. Edge (district coroner) and a jury, the inquest on the bodies of the 38 miners who met their deaths in ' the accident at Woodend Colliery, on the 15th inst, was resumed. Mr. Joseph Dickir.-

At Westray, in the Orkneys, a shoal of 120 whales have been driven ashore and captured, and it is now be- lieved by the fishermen that herrings will be plentiful in the locality. The Board of Trade report on railway accidents in 1885 -shows that the number of persons killed was 957, and the number injured 3.467. Of the former 102 and of the latter 1.129 were passengers. The annual International Rifle Competition in connec- tion with Liverpool volunteers took place on Wednesday at Altcar. The trophy was won by Scotland with 829 points; England scoring 826, aud Ireland 802. A woman is in custody at Somerville, Massachusetts, charged with poisoning her eon. She is suspected of hav- ing murdered 100 persons by similar means during the last four years. The medical officer of Canterbury has reported to the saeitary authority that an epidemic of diphtheritic sore throat, which attacked 200 pereoes there, was caused by drinking contaminated milk. AN ENGLISH OFFICER MURDERED.—A party of Boers, who have arrived at Vry burg from the interior of Attica, report that Lieut. Bethell and a trooper of t e Bechttana police base been brutally murdered by Eaffirs while out shooting. A Mac MURDERER.—Bv order of the Home Secretary, James Mee, sentenced to oenal servitude for life for being an accessory in the murder of P.C. Lines in Birmingham eleven years aeo, was released on Tuesday. It is stated that Mee has gone raving mid, and will be removed to a lunatic asylum, FATAL Fterrr.—On Tuesday, John Armstreing and Dan WAlanan, Lillithgowshire, fought in a field. After forty- five minutes' fighting, It is alleged, el‘Alanan struck Arm- strong a blow under the chin, breaking the windpipe and felling him to the ground. Armstrong expired immediately. His assailant disappeared, and has not yet been traced by the police. "Sive, THINE "—Michael James Baker was on Friday committed to the Liverpool Sessions on a charge of stabbing Simon Byrne, because Byrne, hearing someone shout "stop thief," and seeing Baker running away, took hold of him and declined to let him go. Baker is also charged with stealing 10e from a drunken man, into whose pocket be was seen to put his hand. MR. GLADSTONE AND IRELAND —Mr. Gladstone, reply- ing to an inquiry from the Corporation of Cork as to whether be woald visit Cork to receive the honorary free- dom of the city recently conferred by the Corporation, has written in reply that he has no intention of visiting Ireland, but hopes to be able to make a short vide to the Continent In eight or ten days. BURNING I. MOTHER ALITE.—kt Selles, St. Dennis, France, a widow named Leboi, aged 60, was regarded by the people as a torcerese, though really of weak mind. Her sons endeavoured to procure her admission into an asylum, but failed, and to escape the duty of watching and supporting her, tied her to a stake and burnt her alive, sprinkling her with holy water. Religious motives are alleged. Seamus ILLNESS AMONG Cerren. Splenic apoplexy has btoken out in some herds of bollocks in Leicestershire, causing heavy losses through the death of animals. The disease has spread to a number of people through the car- cases being sold as human food. One man, who cut his fin- ger with a bene, died from the disease. A large number of families in Leicester ate the meat, and grayp results are ap- prehended. PAINFUL SCENE IN Cotrwr.—M Liverpool Police Court, on Tuesday, Benjamin Crierie was charged on remand with embezzling several sums of money of a considerable amount, the property of his employers, Messrs. Sharpies, Jones and Co.. provieien merchants. As the case was being opened the prisoner, who seemed to acutely feel his position, fell in the deck in a dead faint, and be was so long uncon- scious that the case had to be suspended pending his re- covery. EXCITING SCENE AT A FUNERAL.-0/1 Saturday. at Bol- ton, whilst proceeding to an interment, a pair of horses in the last vehicle took fright, dashed through the cemetery gates. and down a perpendicular embankment. The mour- ners jumped out, being severely injured, but the driver, George Smith, was thrown off the box, fracturing his skull and both legs. It was a miracle the whole party was not killed. Whea the excitement had subsided the funeral proceeded. ' IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE OP GREAT BRITAIN%—kt the usuel weekly meeting of the Liverpool Central Branch, on Sunday afternoon, Mr. M. WEvoy, who has just returned from a visit to Gwee-lore and other distressed parts of Ire- land, proposed the following resolution :--" We consider that Irish tenants who pay rent at peril of starvation to themselves and families are guilty of a serious crime, and merit no sympathy either from Irishmen at home or abroad." The resolution was carried unanimously. AN ALL-NIGHT STRUGGLE WITH A SALMON—The Hon. Major Hill had a great battle with a big salmon, in his fi-diery on the Wye. He hooked what appeared to be a very heavy fiah at 7-45 p.m., and had him on the whole night. Every angler will understand the feelines of the major when, after a twelve hours' stnigale, at 7-30 next morning the book came away. The fish- has been seen since—at least, it is presumed to he the same fish—at Bulith, and is estimated by good judges to weigh from 451bs to 501bs. FATAL SCYTHE ACCIDENT.—A sineulir accident oc- curred on Saturday, to a man named Dewsett, at Heding- barn. He was returning from work, carrying a scythe, and in getting over a gate caught his hand on the scythe and severed one of the principal. arteries. He walked some dise tance without meeting anyone, and then fell down in the road, saying to a labourer who happeued to pass at the time "Turn me over; lam dying." The man turned him ever, and then saw that his hand was bleeding very much. Assistance was procured but the unfortunate fellow ; died.

Barrett, statiQned at Bredon-on-tue-Hill, near Ashby-de-la-Z -web, was found on Monday snornitig in a brook, death being evi- dently the result of brutal violence. In the afternoon Jas. Banton was arrested at Derby on the charge of being con- cerned in the murder. A man named Gadsby has also been arrePted as an accessory after the fact. The officer's body was foetid 200 yards from his own house. The bead was frightfully smashed and other parts of the body badly bruised. Barratt leaves a widoT and teveral chil- dren.

FATAL FOOLHARDINESS.—On S:turdav evening, William Sutherland, a packer at one of the Nee:ton Nureeries, near Chester, with some other men in a public-house, bad an argument about swimming. A bet was pa,ele that,he could not swim across the river Dee and back. Deceased left the public-house at closing time, and proc,--ded to the river, near the Causeway. After divegtin,2: himself of his clothieg he jumped into the water and se-em to the opposite side. Af'er having swam some distance on the return journey he sank and never rose again. He was a good swimmer, and it is thought that he meat have been seized with cramp. CONFESSION OP MURDER BY A Boy.—A bon named Wm. Bell gave himself into custody at Sheffield on Monday night. alleging that several days ago he pushed another boy named Blackwell into the canal. At first his statement was not believed, but on the canal being dragged the body was recovered.—At an inquest held at Sheffield on Wednesday on the body of Blackwell, Bell stated that he and Blackwell were gathering coals on the bank of the canal, when they quarrelled about a basket, and while both were pulling at it he suddenly released his hold, and Blackwell fell into the water and was drowned. The jury returned an open verdict of " Found drowned." STRANGE CoNn-cCT or A PRISONER.—WhiIe undergoing at St. Augustine's Prison, Canterbury, sentences extending over a period of three months for brutal assaults upon twO soldiers, William Scamp has resorted to an extraordinary expedient. Be has " done " less than one month of his in- caiTeration, and, presumably for the purpose of avoiding further hard labour, put one of the fingers of his left hand in the cog-wheel machim ry of the treadmill. His intention was, doubtless, to sustain a mere trifling iejury, but to his dismay, he was unable to withdraw his hand, which was re- euced to a horrible state before the wheel could be stopped and the limb released. Amputation has had to be per- formed above the wrist. A CHILD CHAINED TO LOGS OF WOOD.—Fredk. Honeybourne, Bromley-by-Row, London, was charged on Friday with cruelly ill-using hie son,Wiiliam Honeybourne, aged eight vears.—Constable 59 K stated that at about two o'clock on Thursday morning he received instructions to go to the prisoner's house. In an upstairs room he found the little boy, with only a shirt on and a wrapper over his. shoulder, which the landlady had given him. Large logs of wood, attached by a short iron chain, were fastened round each leg. The little fellow was sitting on a chair, and the logs were haaging from him. The chains were fastened by a galvanised wire. Witness could not untwist the wira, and )tad to file it. The little by said his father had done it. Ho was only fed on bread and water, and the logs had been on his legs since the previous Tuesday morning. The lad was then examined by the provisional surgeon. When the prisoner was arrested he said, "I can repudiate the charge. It is illegall." There were marks on the child's body where be had been beaten with a cane. The lad was verr dirty.—Mr. Sanders remanded the prisoner. STRANGE ADVENTURES ON THE LIVERPOOL LANDING STAGIL—Tbe Greek gipsies, who have been lately encamped at the Zoological Gardens, Walton, have recently had some strange experiences in their attempt to get to the other side. of the Atlantic. The American line had contracted to take out 19, but when they got on hoard the tender on Thursday they were found to number 35 instead of 19. Tbe cornpanw refused to take more than they bad contracted for, and the whole community being put ashore, coolly improvised an encampment in a quiet coiner at the end of the Royal . Bridge, where they eat down and placidly smoked their ' pipes. For several hours the police were unsuccessful in getting them to " move on," hut at length, in the early hours of the morning, the chief of the party was prevailed upon.. to take his followers and his luggage back to the Zoological Gardens for the present. A cart was procured and the lu- gage put upon it, but at the top of the bridge the chief in- formed the carter, in answer to a pertinent inquiry, that he would have to look to the Greek Consul for satisfaction of his charges. The carter refused te proceed until the chief, with some persuasion from the police, paid the fare. HOW THE DISTURBAIVCE SPREAD.

Patrick Fox, who appeared to be about 18 years of age, was also charged at Widnes Court. on Thursday, with as- saulting John Platt, a labourer at the works of Messrs. Gas- kel I, Deacon. and Co., who lives at 11, Lacey-street.--Platt said he saw tke band at Farnworth railway station, and be walked down alongside it to the end of Lacey-street Whilst standing there the defendant gave him a violent blow on the face, and also struck him on the eve. A con- stab:e " flew to his assistance."—P.C. Cummins said he saw the defendant strike the complainant and got hold of him, but afterwards allowed him to depart.—The defendant denied that he was concerned in the disturbance, and called Mrs Lomas, the landlady of an adjoining beerhouse, who said he was in her house frcm half-past six to half-past ten. She was not in the room all the time, and he might have gone out without ker seeing him.—Patrick Quinn, a young man, said he lived at 23, Newtola-etreet, and worked at Messrs. Gaakell Deacon's works. He and the defendant were in the house of Mrs. Lomas from a quarter-past six to half-past ten. They did not go cut during all this time. When the band came past the defendant looked through the window.—P.C. Cummins, recalled, said he had the defen- dant in custody, and should have locked him up but for P.S. Robinson instructing him to take his name and address and let him gn.—Mr. Heald said the defence set up by the defendant made the case worse instead of better.—A fine of 10a and costs was imposed.

div.head: GREAT IRISH DEMZSTRXTIONS IN
div.p: GREAT IRISH DEMZSTRXTIONS IN
AMERICA.

VIOLENCE DENOUNCED BY MR. DAVITT. One of the most imposing demonstrations of Irish- men ever held in America took place in Ogden-grove, Chicago, on Saturday evening, and was attended by not fewer than 20,000 persons. Previous to the de- monstration a large number of Irishmen, representing the various Irish societies throughout the United States, proceeded to Mr. Davitt's hotel, and escorted him in triumph to the place of meeting, where he was received with the utmost enthusiasm.—Congresamau Finerty, who presided, said the Irish in America had been called Fenians, arch-conspirators, and the eternal enemies of the British Crown. me acknowledged that this was the ease, but the Irish were still a starving, beggared, and evic- ted race. If Ireland at any time felt herself in a position to resist the brutal British, the God of Battles would smile on them. If, as Lord Salisbury had • said, " Manacles and Manitoba" were the only remedies for Irish disaffection, he (the speaker) spoke no lying words when be said it would be the duty of the Irish in America te see that the people in Ireland were not left without the means of resistance. (Prolonged applause.) Congressman Finerty having resumed his seat, a long and fiery address from the United Irish Society to the people of America was read by Mr. Matthew P. Brady. The ad- dress set forth that every means would be resorted to to ac- eomplisk the deliverance of Ireland from British rule; that while they contemplated with satisfactien the results achieved by the Parliamentary party under Mr. Parnell, they were unalterably of opinion that no man had the right to bind, or could bind, the Irish nation to any adjustment as final by Act of Parliament which did not restore to Ire- land a native Parliament independent of the Crown. (Great applause.)—Mr. Devitt rose and went straight for the paint. It was, be said, natural that at a such a meeting the speakers should have breathed a spirit of revenge against the *Gantry which had driven them forth into exile, but those in Ireland had to choose between wasting their ener- gies on seeking revenge for past wrongs, or seeing their energies for use in the work of Irish independence. He, for one, bad put aside the policy of revenge. All the Irish leaders had done the same, and he would maintain that he was right. (Cheers.) They mast remember that fighting for Irish self-government looked very different is Ireland to what it did in America. It was an easy matter to set up an Irish Republic by patriotic speeches delivered 3,000 , miles away, but they could not do it on the hills and plains of Ireland. H.nce they had to accept the best measure it was possible to obtain. In conclusion, Mr. Devitt appealed to his hearers to con- tinue to sustain the Parliamentary party as generously anti as freely as they had done in the past. But he continued In impassioned tones, which, however, only elicited faint cheers, to warn them that neither he nor the Parliamentary party would allow the good people of America to teach them their duty or to show them how that duty could be done. At the close of his speech most of the audience jumped to their feet and wildly applauded Mr. Dewitt About the same time that Congressman Finerty held his demonstration in Ogden-grove, a rival demonstration, organ- ised by leading men more closely in union with Mr. Parnell and the constitutional policy, was held in the Driving Park. The chair was taken by a well-known Irish Catholic priest, the Rev. Father Toomey. and there were about 10,000 per- sons present. Mr. John Devoy, who followed, said the Irish National League in America did not want a man as presi- dent who kept one eye on Ireland and the other on political office in this counter. This was a reference to Congressman Finerty, and his aspirations to senatorial and even higher honours, and it was received with much applause. The Convention of American Irish delegates opened on Wednesday afternoon, amid a scene of much excitement. Mr. Patrick Egan. as the retiring president, delivered his address. He welcomed Messrs. Devitt, O'Brien, Redmond, and Deasy, and congratulated the Convention upon the progress which Mr. Parnell had made. Since the Boston Convention the treasurer of the league had for- warded over 320,000. dollars to Ireland. Victory was close at band, and be felt that there was enough dignity and sound sense in the Convention not to dash it away. He saw emblazoned on the walls of the hall mottoes. "We are for Trish liberty, peacefully if we can, otherwise if we must." That was the true national position which every American could appreciate, and which was the only position that England would respect.—Mr. Eean's remarks were mach cheered.—The Convention reassembled at eight o'clock en Wednesday night. It was proposed to cable a resolution to Mr. Gladstone—Mr. Sullivan opposcd on technical grounds, and Mr. Gannon supported him.—Mr. Sullivan was vigorously hissed, but his objection was sustained, and the matter dropped. Mr. Finerty. a leader of the Irish Nationalists, has made an explanation at Chicago of his policy. He considers Mr. Gladstenes proposals as totally unworthy of the dignity of the Irish national demand. 'They would reduce Ireland to the condition of a mere province. Mr. W. O'Brien, one of the " Parliamentary deputation," said the Irish party would seek by perfectly peaceful means to secure relief for the tenants who were being driven into hopeless bankruptcy. Mr. Redmond declared that Mr. Glads'one had consecrated the remainder of his life to the cause of Irish liberty.

RIDING ON SIIAFTS.—John Seddon was summoted at the Prescot l'etty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr. H. R. D'a Willis, on a charge of riding on the shafts of a wageon drawn by two horses. in Tarbock-road, Huyton, on the 6th inst.—He was fined 2s 6d and costs. OUTRMIE IN KERRY.—A daring outrage has been com- mitted by a band of armed and masked men, who ira broad daylight entered the house of Mr. Haggard, petty sessional clerk, at Milltown, county Kerry, and made a prolonged search for firearms. Only two old persons were in the house, and they threatened to shoot them if any alsrm were given. After seizing a cartridge-loading machine and some poe der, the men left, and visited alsother house, where they took possession of a double barrelled gun. Fourteen arrests were made, and the Milltown magistrates have cornmietvol six of the prisoners, who were clearly identified, for trial at the assizes. ATTEMPTED MURDER OP A GAM EMEEPER.—A. man man named Thomas Wright, labourer, of Crouton, was brought before Mr. W. L. Evans, at Prescot, on Monday, charged with attempting to murder Frederick Fryer. a game watcher on the preserves of the Earl of Sefton, at Tarbock, on Sunday morniag. From the evidence it appeared that Fryer, between four and five o'clock, observed twe men beat. ing the fields skirting Captain Willis's park, the prisoner, a notorious poacher, teing one of them ; and when they found themselves observed they separated, the prisoner going on to the highway. He carried a gun, and threatened the keeper several times that he would shoot him if he followed. He ran, and Fryer tried to overtake him, and when within thirty yards the prisoner turned round and delibeeately took aim and fired, literally riddling his victim, who, notwith- standing, rushed on ,the prisoner, and a desperate struggle ensued, in which the gun was broken, and the injured man fell exhausted from loss of blood. He was discovered about an hour afterwards by a farmer named Cartwright, who assisted him to the residence of the bead keeper, Edward Saint, and was attended by Dr. Brindle, of Prescot, where he found that sixty-tivt p,ilets were lodged over the front.of his body, legs, and left arm. He, was only able to extract half a dozen. Police Constable M‘Master apprehended the prisoner at Crouton on Sunday morning. He did net deny shooting the keeper. but alleged that it happeerd during the struggle for the gun. Prisoner was re- manded till Thursday, when he was again brought up bs.fore Mr. W. L. Evans. Superintendent Barker stzt!ed the in- jured man was unable to appear, and he accordingly asked for the prisoner to be remanded for another week. The ap- plication was granted. •

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, AUGUST 21, 1886.

THE Irish in America—the greater Ireland beyond the sea—are just now showing them- selves especially interested in the Home Rule Question, and the course to be taken in view of the defeat of the Home Rule advocates at the last election in this country. It is not unnatural that there should be much dis- appointment and some bitterness, both in the United States and in Ireland, at the failure to get a majority at the poll in faVour of Home Rule. We have seen, however, with great satisfaction how patiently the leaders of the Irish Pirliamentary party have accepted for the moment the situation as it stands, setting themselves to work, as they ought to do, to strengthen their stakes and lengthen their cords, so that when the United Kingdom is appealedec to lar ng tit a tma the may people pfloeuonfd Ireland a nb de ag i unitedn i n d shall be allowed to manage their own affairs in a Parliament of their own. But there is a large body of Irishmen in America who have for many years been in the habit of preaching force as the only remedy—their object being to compel England to do their bidding by setting Ireland absolutely free of English control. It is a wild notion, and impractic- able as it is wild, but it meets the tastes of those who preach the old, bad doctrine of revenge, and it serves the purposes of those who in the United States would thrive poli- tically by pandering to the worst passions of their fellow-countrymen. It is in this way ; that the party of violence has come into ' existence and attained considerable dimen- sions; and it is through continuous and determined agitation that there is an Irish question in the United States as in the United Kingdom. In both countries there are politicians of the baser sort who are ready to preach violence to any extent so long as it brings grist to the mill in the shape of , votes. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has shown himself in this country to be one of this class. Ulster," he said, " will fight, and Ulster will be right ;" but now that his words have been followed by blows he minds to keep the Irish Sea between himself and the fighting. He further shows how little he really cares for the Orangemen, how, in fact, he holds their ultra-Protestant views in con- tempt—by pushing aside a Protestant like Sir RICHARD CROSS and putting in his place, as Home Secretary, a Roman Catholic like Mr. HENRY MATTHEWS. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has his prototype in the United , States in the!person of Congressman FINERTY, who preaches violence to Irishmen less, it is believed, with the object of aiding Ireland than of serving his own ends as an American politician.
- Mr. FIN2RTY was the Chairman on Sunday evening at a great demonstration of Irishmen in Chicago, and he made what—coming from

a man in his position—must be regarded as a most violent speech. It referred to Irishmen in America as being. "the eternal enemies of the British Crown " ; and breathed from be- ginning to end a spirit of defiance and re- venge. Mr. MATTHEW BRADY read an 0:1- dress from the United Irish Society which was in a similar strain, for it asserted that no settlement of the Irish question would be final "which did not restore a native Parliament independent of the Crown." Mr. MICHAEL DAVITT was present, and was called upon to address the assembly after these ex- treme declarations. His position was an awkward one, for it is obvious that he could not countenance opinions of this kind, and at the same time strengthen the case in this country for Home Rule. He might, of course, have sat upon the fence, and, without jumP- ing down on either side, have said a good deal to influence the audience and fill the coffers of the Irish Parliamentary party. But he did nothing of the kind; he "went straight" as he seems generally to have done. He told them that the time had come when they in Ireland had to "choose be- tween wasting their energies on seeking re- venge for past wrongs, or saving their ener- gies.for use in the work of Irish independ- once. He, for one, had put aside the policYo.f revenge." This was speaking plainly; but it was more than that; it was speaking with courage and with wisdom. Mr. DAVITT, in the sentence we have quoted, puts in a nut- shell not only the case but the policy of Ire- land as affected by the fact that Mr. GLAD- STONE has brought the question of Home Rule within the sphere of practical politics. He did not hesitate to tell his hearers that he had no faith in an Irish Republic being set up by speeches made 3,000 miles away from Ireland; it was their duty to accept the best measures they could obtain; and he reminded them that notwithstanding the outcries of the Tories, and the action of Lord .HARTINGTON and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, "over a million Eng- lishmen had recorded their votes in favour of the principles of Home Rule." Mr. DAVITT concluded by stating that "neither he nor the Parliamentary party would allow the good people of America to teach them their duty, or to show them how that duty could be done." We are glad to see from this speech that the party of violence in the United States are to be told that their policy is an impossible policy, and that this is to be brought home to them even at the risk of alienating them. On the same evening that this the extreme section of Irish-Americans were demonstrating their strength, another section of Irishmen held a great meeting also in Chicago, at which resolutions were passed which "set forth that Irishmen in Ame- rica recognised the fact that the Irish leaders in Ireland were the proper persons to repre- sent the feelings, hopes, and aspirations of the Irish people in regard to their political present and future,and deploring the position of a certain class of Irishmen, who embar- rassed Mr. PARNELL :and his colleagues by foolish threats and suggestions." It will thus be seen that the battle of peaceful agita- tion which may be said to have been fought and won by Mr. PARNELL in this country it now raging in America, and that there Is every prospect of the men of violence being set aside and denounced. This done, the best men of all classes—the men of light and leading in England and America—will rally in ever-increasing numbers to a constitutional cause which is being supported by constitu- tional action, and by this means, before many years are over, we shall have Home , Rule in Ireland with a Parliament on College Green.

THE Liberals of the Newton Division have fought another battle, and they have again lost ; but they are not so badly beaten as to make their plight hopeless. If it could be foreseen that they would have no chance of winning, they would be unwise in ex- pending their energies to no purpose. But, having got witihin 400 of winning against such an antagonist as Sir RICHARD CROSS, it is their duty to try and try again. Lord BEACONSFIELD who could accept victory or defeat calmly and philosophically, said that it was the business of a minority to get them- selves converted into a majority; and acting on this principle the Liberal electors of the Newton Division must educate those who are not at present with them until they are per- suaded to take the new and the better way. Looking at the polling returns, we cannot but express surprise that, all things con- sidered, so many of the electors have re- corded their votes. Monday was a holiday for the working population of Earlestown ; many of them were away at Blackpool and other places, and it shows how highly they esteem the franchise that there were so few abstentions. A register is constantly being re- duced by removals and deaths; and there is a certain per centage of these even in a couple of months ; but we observe that the total number of voters polled was 7,417, that is 371 only less than at the General Election. The Conservative candidate, Mr. T. W. LEGH, polled z+o less than the total for Sir. RICHARD CROSS as the Conservative candi- date at the last election; and the Liberal can- didate, Mr. FRENCH, polled 13 z only less than his predecessor SiR GEORGE ERRINGTON. The majority of the Tories has therefore been re- duced by ro9—a result which is satisfactory as far as it goes. It must be remembered that Mr. FRENCH, unlike Mr. LEGH, came among the electors as a perfect stranger ; he had his Liberal principles only to recom- mend him, and we are glad to see that in so short a time he has made his views accept- able to so many of the electors. It may be thought that 707 is a large majority to wipe out ; but that it is relatively small will be seen when it is stated that if but one in twenty who have voted Tory were to vote Liberal there would be a majority for the Liberal candidate. There is as yet, unhap- pily, some division amongst Liberals on the Home Rule question; but this is not likely to be permanent. Already there are some signs of a t)etter feeling, and it is to be hoped that those who are responsible for the management of party affairs will take care that nothing is done to make it difficult for all who are now outside the fold to get back again. The Home Rule difficulty, like other difficulties, will disappear; and then—the Liberal party once more united—the Libe- rals of Newton may enter upon a contest with some confidence that zeal, energy, and good organisation will secure them a victory.

W.IDNEs C.E.T.S.—Under the auspices of this society, the Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson, curate, delivered a lecture, entitled "Rambles in Scotland," on Thursday night. A good audience assembled in the National Schoolroom, and the Rev. J. R. Jones, 8.A., presided. A WIDNES PATENT.—A. patent has been taken out by Messrs. E. W. Parnell and J. Simpson for improvements in the treatment of ores containing sulphide of antimony, for the purpose of cbtainiug such sulphide in a concentrated form, with any gold and silver that may be present." ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—James Burns, a young man who resides in Oxford-street, Lugsdale-road, met with a serious accident at the copper works of Messrs. Bolton and Sons, yesterday. He was caught between the buffers of two rail- way waggons, and sustained such severe internal injuries that his recovery is doubtful. He now lies at the Accident Hospital under the care of Dr. O'Neil, and his assistant, Dr. Saul. DEATH OF MR. CHADWICK, OF DITTON.—On Monday the funeral took place at Ditton of William Chadwick, son of Mr. William Chadwick, Rose-mount, Ditten. Deceased was in vigorous health a week from that date, but was taken ill with diphtheria on the Tuesday, and died on the Friday evening. Dr. MacLennan attended him, but although un- able to preserve his life,khappily prevented the disease from spreading further. INSPECTION OF POLICE AT RUNCORN.—The annual inspec- tion of tne Runcorn Police Force was made on Tuesday by the Hon. Captain C. E. Legge. There were on parade Su- perintendent Hollingsworth. Inspector Millington, 4 ser- geants, and 23 constables. The inspecting o.licer examine 4 tne books, and the cells, and the uniform and the appoint- ments of the men and found everything in a satisfactory condition. The men were put through drill by Sergeant Booth. Colonel Hamersley, chief constable, was Present. SALVATION ARMY FESTIVAL AT WIDNES.—The Widnes branch of the Salvation Army celebrated its fourth anni- versary by a series of meetings held on Saturday, Sunday, and Monday, which were attended with considerable suc- cess. On the evening of the latter day about 100 persons sat down to a tea provided in the Drill Hall, and subse- quently there was a "free and easy" meeting held at the same place. Captain Winfield and Lieutenant Howe were in command, and officers from other districts took part in the proceedings. A RUNAWAY WIFE AT WIDNES.—At the conclusion of the ordinary basinesa at the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thurs- day aftsrnoon, a woman of respectable appearance, named Elizabeth Pennington, applied to the Bench for an order compelling her husband to support her. She stated that she had left her husband in London and had walked to Widnes. Her husband had told her to leave him, and had promised that he would send money for hr support. He had only sent her lls, and she wished the magistrates to cempel him.-.--The magistrates said that as the woman had left her husband of her own free will it was evidently not a case of desertion, and they could not interfere. They ad.

vised her to return to her husband. , RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—The usual fortnightly meeting of this body was held on Tues- day, in the Board-room, at the Workhouse, Dutton. The chair was occupied by Lieut-Colonel Ashton, and there were also present the Revs. J. J. Lockwood, and J. W. N. Tanner; Messrs. Aaron, Stokes, T. Hadfield, Brandreth, Weir, Whitlow, Mclntyre, Knowles, Lewis, Hall, Dansey (Local Government Board Inspector), and H. Linaker (clerk).—The Local Government Board wrote urging the Authority to take all necessary precautions against cholera, and Mrs. Allison, of Frodsham, forwarded a complaint of a nuisance existing opposite her shop; the manhole in the sewer was, the letter stated, very offensive.—The Sanitary Inspector (Mr. Farrington) submitted his usual report, which concluded the business of the meeting. . RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.-7-TllB half-yearlv report of this company states that the revenue account shows a balance of £673 4s lid, including £163 us 10d brought from the previous half year. Out of this sum the directors recommend a dividend of 4 per cent per annum. This would leave a balance of £73 4s lid to be carried fonvard. There is, the report states, an accumulation of sand several feet deep in the well, which was found to be interfering with the action of the pumps. The directors had thought it advisable to consult Mr. Hawkelev, the en- ' glneer, of London, as to the best means of removing it and continuing the water supply to the customers at the same time. Operations with this purpose have begun, and would be continued until the sand had been got out in as economical a manner as the difficulty would admit. ROUNDERS MATCIL—LIVERPOOL v. SEMI'S CROSS, WID- NES.—This match was played on the ground of the former club, on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by 17 runs. Scores:— LIVERPOOL.

Total A COUNTY COURT FOR • WIDI•TES.—An order in Council for the establishment of a County Court at Widnes has been received by Mr. Tyrer, registrar of the St. Helens County Court. As three months notice of each sitting of the court is necessary, his Honour Judge Thompson will be unable to try any cases until 1887. Mr. W. T. Husband, to whose labours the public of Widnes are much indebted for the privilege that has been conceded, is aiding Mr. Tyrer in the selection of suitable offices for the transaction of official business, in order that the first sitting of the court may, if possible, he held in January next. Some years ago the magistrates promised the use of the Police Court for the trial of County Court cases, and it may be taken for granted that they are still willing to make this concession. To tradesmen and others who have found it necessary to seek the aid of the County Court at St. Helens, the new arrangement will be much more convenient and less ex- pensive. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A RUNCIORN MAN.—The district coroner (Mr. F. Price) held an inquest on Thursday, at Salford, concerning the death of Joseph Shorrocks, 43 years of age, who resided at Bilton House, Canal Bank, Runcorn. The deceased was captain of a flat belonging to the Man- chester and Liverpool Carrying Company. On Tuesday evening the flat of which Shorrocks had charge was being loaded with goods from a warehouse adjoining the river Irwell in Stanley-street, t alford, a teagle being used for that purpose. The deceased was packing the goods in the hold as they were sent fiorn an upper storey of the warehouse by the teaele, when he was struck on the head with a large case. He was knocked backwards over another case and severely injured. He was taken to the Salford Royal Hos- pital and Dispensary, and it was found that he had sustained a fracture of the spine. He died from his injuries on Wed- nesday morning. A verdict of "Accidental death" was

returned. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—On Tues lay afternoon this Board held a fortnightly meeting in the 13,ard-room, at Dutton Workhouse, Lieut.-Col. Ashton presided, and there were present Mr. ‘Vcir (vice-chairman), the Revs. J. Tanner and J. J. Lockwood, Messrs. Aaron, Mclntyre, Stokes, HadfieH, Speakman, Knowles, Whitlow, Fisher, Brandreth, Farrell, Hall, Whittaker, Lewis, 'Forster, Smith. Dansey (inspector of the Local Government Board), and IL Line ker (clerk) —The Local Government Board .wrote ad- verting to a letter of the Guardians informing theta of the proposal to anow the Workhouse Master's son, aged sixteen, to reside at the Workhouse, a certain sum per week being -repaid for his maintenance. The Board objected to this, and requested that arrangements should be made for the son to reside elsewhere. It was stat.d that the request had been complied with.—The Clerk read a circular letter from the ,Walsall Uoion with reference to the law of set'hrment, en- closirg copy of a memorial adopted by that Unism. No action was t,.lten on the matter.—The report of the Relief -Supervision Committee was received and adopted.—The Cle;i't reported -tbe receipt of a county rate precept for £1,500 odd, as compared with .£1,319 odd the previous pre- ,cept.—Mr. Dansey said that the Local Government Board had had a letter saving that it was proposed to erect a bath • In the girls' wash-house. instead of where was proposed some ftime ago. It was not stated what size the bath was to be, and no plans or sketch had been submitted. It was also not 'stated what the cost would be.—Mr. Speakman said that the bath was one got for the purpose some time ago, and it was now on the Premises. It was thought the Cost altogether would be about .o.—The subject dropped, and the meeting then concluded. FUNERAL OF THE LATH MR. HUNTER, 031' WIDNES. The interment of the late Mr. D. W. 'Hunter, formerly head master at Warrington-road Board School, Widnes, took place at FernwOrtti Parish Church, on Saturday afternoon, in the presence of many hundreds of spectators. Long , before the arri'val of the mournful procession the sacred edifice was crowded with scholars and sorrowing friends, while many hundreds were assembled in the burial ground. The body was borne by Messrs H. W. Cookson, E. M. Davies. St. E. Oakden, Hi Yates, J. Grant, and W. ,Celland. The chief ,i:ourners present were Mrs Hunter (mother), Misses Hunter (sinters), Mr. and Mrs Miles, of stoke New- ington (twee and,aant), and Mr. IL' Kitchen, of St. Bees. Representatives of the societies with which the deceased had been connected ,formed part of the nrocession, and In- cluded the Rev. R. G. Hughes, Drs. Hunter and J. Mac- Lennan, Mr. and Mrs 1. C. Crawford, Messrs. H. W. Dea- con, D. Forster, .r. W. Waring, R. Fogg, W. S. Callender, E. H. Brown, .J. W. Davies, A. G. Davie, F. Davies, T. A.. Eunuch]. H. V.dentine, W. Hill, W. Smith, J. Williams. John G. if, and J. freacv, and Mrs Sbowan and Miss Oak- den. The following head teachers, assistants, and pupil , teachers at the various Board schools were present :—Misses Sampeen, Strong, Pomeroy, Hartles,- Jones, Dodsworth, Clark, Stout, Johnson, Tattoo, Branch, Pilling, Maddison, Wyllie, Ellis, Davies, Hurst, Longsbaw, Morgan, Burril, Bailey, Poulson, Whiteside, and Mather. and Messrs. T. Showan, 5. Snoddy, Devonald, J. P. Streets, T. Kongilien E. Bailey, and E. Neild. The service in the cburcla was performed by the Rev. George Bend, M.A. vicar, and at the grave side by the Rev. S. A. Spoonekr, M.A.. Numerous beautiful wreaths were placed on the Om by the teachers and scholars of the various schoole, and were sent by Misses and Mr. E. T. Gourley, Mrs Dunn. Mr. and Mrs J. B. Imi- aon, airs W. Pritchard, Mr. and Mrs J. C. Crawford, Mr. and Mrs Taylor, Miss Turton, and Miss Branch. An appro- priate address was delivered by the Rev. George Bond to the large assembly. Mr. Hunter who bad only reached his 29th year, was highly respected as a teacher and a towel.. Man.

I WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK —At Widnes Petty 7 Sessions, on Thursday, Mr. G. H. Denby, dlerk to the School I Board, prosecuted the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—Thornas Nloore, Adam Cook, John Westhead, Charles McKenna, Patrick Daley, Robt. Hoey, and Thos. McAuley. The usual penalty of 5s was imposed in each else. ASSAULTS AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Petty Session.. on Thursday, Archibald Sullivan was fined 20e and costs for assaulting a married woman named Ann Golding, living in Water-street. The defendant did not appear.--Jane ' Paley, who did not appears was dealt with in a like manner for assaulting Margaret Fay, a married woman.--For as- saulting Jane Jackson, Ellen Mason was fined 2s 6d and costs. WIDNES THEATRE ROYAL. . A special Session of the Widnes Police Court, was held on Thursday, by Messrs. W. N. Heald, F. H. Gossage, T. S. Timmie, and H. Gaskell, junr., for ths purpose of hearing an application by Mr. Geo. Mellon, for a renewal of the license to the Theatre Royal. The magistrates granted the application, and the usual sureties for the • proper conducting of the theatre were entered into. UNJUST SCALES AT DITTO:T. —John Barlow pleaded guilty, at Widnes Petty Sessions, to having on the 14th inst. a pair of flour scales in his possession which were 'l4 drachms out of balance against the purchaser. The de- fendant, who is a grocer at Hough Green, was fined 203 and costs. Honor Cleeton, of Ditton, had been guilty of an exactly similar offence, and she was fined 203 and costs. Superintendent Barker proved the cases. ATTEMPTED BURGLARY AT WIDNES —At Widnes Police , Court, on Wednesday, a man who gave the name of James Jackson was remanded on a charge of attempting to break into the shop of Mr. Brookes, tailor and clothier. Waterloo- I road. It appeared that the poisoner was seen about the 1. premises about three o'clock on Wednesday morning, and a boy working at the works in Ash-row heard the smashing of ghost- The prisoner was apprehended by PC Laing near the spot, and he had an instrument in his posseesion which had evidently been used to remove a pane oi glass in one of the rear windows. No goods were stolen. THEPT OF BRASS AT RUNCORN.—At Widnes Police Court on Saturday, before Mr. H. Gaskell, jun., an elderly man named James Keating was charged with having stolen 16ibs. weight of brass, value 103 Bd, the property of the Alkali Company. On the morning of the 2nd inst., Joseph Collier, employed as a watchman by the company, met the prisoner with the brase in his possession in Anne-street East. Suspecting that the brass had been stolen. Collier seized it and took it to the works, where he found his surmise to be , correct. The prisoner was arrested at St Helens on Fri- day, and was now committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. 1 HOUSEBREAKING AT WIDNES.--JOhll Tooney and Mary Ann Pomfret, of no occupation, were brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, charged on suspicion with having broken into the dwelling-house, 24,Widnes-road, and stolen a vest, two handkerchiefs, and two pairs of boots, the propertv of John Brady. The house was secured on the night ef the 16th inst, and next morning at five o'clock the back door was open, and the scullery window broken. The articles named had been stolen. Jones, a lodging- house keeper, Lugsdale-road, deposed that the vest had been worn by Tooney at his house, and a companion of his had I worn the shoes. The prisoners were remanded for a 1 week. I SUSPECTED THIEF AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police I Court, on Thursday, before Captain Hezlehurst and Mr. I James Handley, an elderly man named George Percival. of 1 Canal-street, was charged with attempting to steal a number of copper coins from the till of the Grapes Inn, Halton-road. —On Wednesday the prisoner was served with a pint of beer at the bar, where he was left alone for a few minutes. On Mrs. Ormesber returning, she saw the prisoner behind the bar with the till drawer open, and some coppers in his hand. He dropped the coppers back into the drawer, and when apprehended and searchecra few minutes later he had only a halfpenny in his pocket.—The prisoner, wl.o is em- ployed at Messrs. Ockleston's tanyard, was given a very good character, and as there was a doubt in the case he was discharged. CRUELTY TO HORSES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, Wm. Rowlands, contractor, Widnes. was summoned for cruelly ill-treating two horses by allow- ing them to be worked whilst in an unfit state, and his son Wm. Rowlands, jun., was charged with working tbe same.— P.S. Coutts said at 9 45 on Tuesday morning, the 10th inst , he visited the Liver Alkali Works, Ditto-road, where he saw a dark-brown horse and a bay horse belonging to Mr. Rowlands, and driven by young Rowlands, drawing a rail- way waggon. Seeing that the horses were in poor condition and appeared to be in p sin, he examined the animal'. He found a wound underneath the collar and one on the left shoulder on the bay horse. There was also one large raw wound the size of a five shilling piece on that animal. On the dark-brown horse he fouud five raw wounds on the left shoulder under the collar, four on the right shoulder, each the size of a florin, and large wounds in other parts of the body. They were all raw wounds, with the harness pressing upon them. At the sergeant's request Mr. Rowlands sent the animals to the stable in Widnes.—P.C. Worthington corroborated.—For the defence, Mr. John F. Dixon, veterinary surgeon, Warrington, was &lee, and stated that he examined thaorse on the 10th. He found a few super- ficial wounds on the dark horse but they did not render it unfit to work. He did not find any wound on the bay horse, and it was not suffering any pain whatever.—ln reply to Superintendent Barker, the witness said the wounds were not raw, but healed over.—Mr. Heald (chair- man of the Bench), said the defendant had been in court be- fore on a similar charge, and had also been earned, and the meseistrates considered this to be a gross case. A penalty of £5 and costs, or two months bard labour in default, would be imposed. If he came there again the Bench would most decidedly send him to gaol for the full term without the option of a fine. He ought to be ashamed of himself.— The costs amounted to £1 3s 6d. Rowlands the younger did not appear. HA.YNES'S, for Ladies' and Gentlemen's newest styles.— Advt. Sin R. Cnoss's PEERAGE.—It is now announced that Sir Richard Cross has changed the title he will take on elevation to the House of Lords from Vis- count Warrington to Lord Cross of Broughton-in- Furness. THE LABOURERS' ALLOTMENTS QUESTION.—It is stated that Mr. R. C. Naylor, Hooton Hall, Cheshire, has set apart a considerable tract of land near the village of Sutton, Cheshire, as allotment gardens for his cottagers and labourers. Major Mousley, the agent, having fixed the rent at a moderate figure, nearly fifty garden allotments are now under culti- vation. As a further inducement to obtain effective cultivation, Mr. Naylor has offeied prizes for the best cultivated plots. The scheme, it is said, works admirably. GENERAL WOLFE ANGLERS' SOCIETY, WARRING- TON.—The subscribers of this society, to the num- ber of 40, journeyed to Frodsham on Saturday last in charge of the genial host of the above hostelry. Their object.was to engage in war against the finny tribes, and many, were the chubby fish perched at the heels of the victors, who received not only the. bodies of the slain, but also numerous prizes which were competed .for. Everthing passed off most satisfactorily, and all were apparently well satisfied with the expedition. Mr. Brundrett and the com- mittee beg to thank those kind friends who con- tributed to the various prizes. The winners were: —lst prize, tea service, C. Basketer ; 2nd, copper kettle, Jr Higham ; 3rd, Metal tea pot, J. Allison; 4th, pair of lustres, J. Bradshaw; and. 18 other prizes. THE VOTING AT THE GENERAL ELECTION.---The following figures relative to the voting at the General Election are not without their lesson as to the real feeling of the country with regard to the great question submitted for decision :—Votes given to Ministerial candidates, 1,220,826; votes given to Liberal Unionists, 330,805; votes given to Conservative candidates 978,6464 absentees, calcu- lated by deducting total number of votes from the number of electors for each electoral district con- tested (this must of course include duplicates and deaths), 908,245; number of electors on register where MinisterialiKs were returned unopposed, 900,587; number of electors on register where Liberal Unionists were returned, 259,492; nuMber of electors on register where Conservatives were re- turned, 783,287. ELECTION EXPENSES.--:-The expenses of Sir George Errington, the unsuccessful Liberal candidate for the Newton Division at the last general election, are returned as follows :—Returning officer's ex- penses, £lB2 Os; agents, £l3l ; polling agents, clerks, and messengers, £ll5 14s 104; hire of rooms, printing, postage, advertising, stationery, and sundries, 0E477 (is lid; candidate's expenses, £6B 6s 9d- total, £974 17s 6d. The election accounts of Mr. F. R. Twemlow, the Conservative candidate for the Crewe Division of Chester, have .also been issued. The sum total is £913 Os 541, made up as follows :—Returning officer's charges, £l9O 18s .Sid ; candidate's personal expenses, £7O is 6d ; printing, £95 4s 3d; postage, £34; advertising, £lB 3s 6d.; sub-agents, £300; messengers, £2l is; committee- rooms, £3B 6s 8d; clerks, £79 Os 6d ; bill-posting, £24 19s 84. The item for election agent is nil. The expenses of Mr... W. S. B. McLaren, the successful Liberal candidate for the same division, ha e also been issued. They are :—Half of the returning lofficer's fee, £l9O 18s: candidate's personal expenses, £57 3s 10d; election agent, £105; sub-agents, £240; total, £B9B 14s -4d.

FATAL ALPINE ACCMENT:—On Wednesday a party of tourists, including two Englishmen, made the ascent of the Matterhorn. While on the summit they were overtaken by 4 heavy ,snowstorm and the descent became impossible. After some hours had been passed, a guide, at the risk of his life, descended for help. Twenty guides at once set off, and in face of • tremendous difficulties reached the natty, which had passed thirty hours. on the mountain. Ode of the Englishmen, named Mr. ButCkll*tdt,is dead, and the other not ,expected to live, while all the members of the party are more or less frost bitten. The rescuers were work- ing continuously for 30 hours in the snow before reaching the imprisoned party.

THE EXAMINER, 9 9 SATURDAY AUGUST 21 188 G- THE ALLFGED LAND-GRABBING BY I WARRINGTON. A WIDNES IRISHMAN. A crowded meeting of the members of the Wid- nes T. P. O'Connor Branch of the Irish National League of Great Britain was held on Sunday after- noon, Dr. O'Keeffe, president, occupying the chair. —Eleven new members, were enrolled, and several members had their cards renewed.—The case of Mr. Thomas Drury, who had been charged by the Boyle (Ireland) Organising Committee with land-grabbing and evicting, came up for consideration. The President, who had been in communication with several persons in the aistrict where the land- grabbing and evicting were said to have taken place, read letters from the Rev. Father White, C.C., Kilnamana, and from the alleged evicted tenants. Father White said "The whole of the statements made are absolutely false," and the tenants said "It is an unfounded and concocted statement."—A son of one of the tenants, who re- sides in Widnes, was present, and he stated posi- tively that there was no truth whatever in the state- ment made before the Boyle Organizing Committee. —After hearing such conclusive evidence, the meet- ing unanimously adopted the following resolution, on the motion of Messrs. Laughlin and M. Ford:— "That we, the members of the Widnes branch of the 1.N.L., G.G., be to offer to our treasurer, Mr. T. Drury, out hearty sympathy under the unfounded and scandalous charges of land-grabbing and evict- ing brought against him by some unscrupulous per- sons in Ireland, and we be to tender him our re- newed confidence."
