A DEAR PURCHASE FOR HELSBY GROCERS.- DIPORFANT couNry couar AC CION. _

An action which excited much interest, and occupied His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes five hours, was tried at Runcorn County Court, on Thursday. John Wiseman, corn miller and flour merchant, Chester, sued Sarah Davies, fat- mer and grocer. Elelsby, for £ll 23 for flour, bran, 4;c., sold to her by William Rowe Adamson, who had obtained the goods from the plaintiff under false pretences. 101 r. Stewart (instructed by Messrs. Bridgeman, Weaver, and Jones, of Chester) appeared for the plaintiff, and the de- fendant was represented by Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Messrs. Linaker and Linaker, of Runcorn.) This was a test case, which covered fourteen or fifteen others, against grocers and farmers. Sic., including Lawrence Booth (Nethertan), and James Dixon, Thomas Atherton, Thomas Wright, Joseph Garner, Daniel Dunbabin, Joseph Jeffe, R. Foster, D. Savage, V. Wheelhouse, Ann Wright, J. Rawson, and Samuel Williams, all of Helsby, near Run- corn. The case for the plaintiff was that Adamson, who is eighteen years of age, and whose mother is the proprietoress of what is called the Horns Mill, Helsbv, went to Mr. Wiseman's establishment and represented that he was re- quested by his uncle, Samuel Rowe, to purchase various articles. In consequence of this statement Mr. Wise- man allowed the youth to have a large quan- tity of wheat and other miller's produce. Hay- ing obtained possession, Adamson went round the neighbourhood of Helsby and sold the stuff to various people, including the defendant. Subsequently Mr. Wise- man discovered that Adamson's statement was false, and as a result of a criminal prosecution at Chester City Sessions the youth was sentenced to three months' hard labour.— Mr. Stewart argued that under these circumstances Mr. Wiseman was entitled to recovensfrom the persons to whom the youth bad sold the cereals.—Mr. Mulholland sub- mitted that no case had been made out, and com- mented strongly upon the fact that Rowe had not been called, and that plaintiff's case rested entirely upon the evidence of a convicted thief. He argued that as the trans- action had taken place with Adamson, who had been paid, the plaintiff had no remedy against the defendant.—After a long argument between counsel, his Honour held that the intention of Mr. Wiseman was to deal with Rowe, and that as there was never any contract with Rowe the goods did not pass. He gave a verdict for the plaintiff for £9 is 6d, and costs on the full amount claimed, the difference being in the price that Adamson bad charged and what the plain- tiff would have charged had he sold the goods direct. Leave was given to appeal.—This decision ruled the other cases, in which nearly £4O was claimed which had beea paid to Adamson, with the exception of £3.

WASTING WATER AT WIDNES. A WARNING. Before Mr. W. N. Heald and Mr. T. S. Timis, at Wid- nes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Louis Most, a pork but- cher in Widnes-road. was charged with wasting the water supplied by the Widnes Local Board on the 29th July. He plcaded gnilty.—Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk to the Local Board, prosecuted for that body, and stated that for many years there had been a considerable waste of water in the town- ship. In order to minimise the waste a special inspector had been employed to repair small leakages, and in great leakages prompt measures bad always been taken. This measure had, however,enot stopped the constant waste of water, and the Local Board had obtained some waste water detectors, which were meters fixed in several parts of the township. Through these meters any leakage could be easily traced ; and an improper use of water had been discovered in many instances. Before taking any steps against the offenders the Board sent round a warning, and the defendant bad received one. On the 26th July the defendant had the water tap at his establishment running a:1 night for the purpose of washing the intestines of pigs or sheep. At first the defendaat denied the allega- tion, but when it was proved to him he admitted the offence. The Board felt compelled to bring the case before the court in consequence of the large amoun,/ of waste in the township. He had made a calculation an discovered that the waste amounted to 61 gallons per head per day, which equalled 66,075,000 gallons per year, and the value of that volume of water to the Beard was £l,4oo.—Tham4s Barrow, the inspector, having been examined,—The Board inflicted a fine of 203, and costs 83, or 14 days' hard labour. They wished the public to clearly understand that the magistrates would not permit this waste of water, and that in future the maximum penalty allowed by law, £5, would be enforced.

A RUNCORN BARBER'S MAD DO.—COWS AT- TACKED WITH HYDROPHOBIA. About a month ago the collie dog belonging to Mr. Bow- yer, barber, Church-street, Runcorn, made its escape from the house. At four o'clock the sulssequent morning the animal turned up at Park Side Farm, Aston, kept by Messrs. Percival Bros, and was seen chasing and biling a number of COWS in the fields. There were over a hundred caws upon the farm. Mr. Percival shot the dry, which was afterwards identified by Mr. Bowyer as his own. On Friday last, a cow was taken ill on the farm, and the veterinary surgeon who was called in stated that the animal was suffering from hydrophobia. The cow was therefore killed. On Tuesday two other cows were attacked in a similar manner, and were slaughtered. The loss to Messrs. Percival is very great,and we believe theg have placed the matter iin the hands of 'a solicitor.

THE QUEEN. —On Wednesday morning er Majesty passed through Warrington on her way to visit the Edinburgh Exhibition. SUDDEN DEATH.—Annie Carty, aged eight weeks, daughter of Ellen Carty, of Keen-street, was found dead in bed at eiglit, o'clock on Tuesday morning. r PRIMITIVE METHODISM.—The anniversary of the Primitive Methodist (Legh-street) Sunday Schools is to be celebrated on the 29th inst. THE REVISION.—The annual revision courts are now about to be held. The political agents are busy with the registers, and the following figures represent the number of objections and claims made by the Liberals :-492 objections, 262 claims, and 200 lodger claims. CRICKET: LA.TCHFORD 2ND V. TIMPERLEY 2ND. —Played at Latchford on Saturday last, and resulted lin a victory for the home team by 30 runs. The patient batting of W. Collier ought not to pass with- out special mention. Going in first, he carried his bat through for an invaluable score of 34, without giving a chance, and was loudly cheered on his re- turn to the pavilion. Score :—Latchford, 79; Tim- perley, 49, ANTIQUARIANS AT WINWICK.—On Saturday after- noon upwards of forty members of the Lancashire and Cheshire Antiquarian Society visited Winwick and inspected the various places of interest in the village and neighbourhood, including the ancien' parish Church and St. Oswald's Well. Mr. J. E Worsley, of IVinwick, ably acted as conduct/r. Afterwards they partook of an excellent tea at the Swan Inn, provided by Mr. and Mrs. Cooper host and hostess. A MYSTERIOUS AFFAlR.—Between nine and ten o'clock on Monday evening a man was observed to throw himself into the Mersey, from the bridge spanning the river at the end of Bridge-street lead- ing to Latchford, a hat was found near by, and given into the possession of the police. It appears that several persons saw someone jump into the water, but fio clue has as yet been obtained as to the identity of the person. It is believed that the man was carried a distance down the river and then succeeded in getting to land. OUTBREAK OF PLEimo-PNEumoNIA.—The Chief Constable of Cheshire (Colonel Hamersley) an- nounces that pleuro-pneumonia has broken out in the township of Appleton, Cheshire. One animal was affected. It was immediately slaughtered .and buried in quicklime, and the police hay received instructions to carefully isolate the cattle which have been in contact with the diseased animal. In his weekly statement, the Chief Constable further announces that 23 animals had died from swine fever, and that the disease had appeared on eight fresh farms in the townships of Arclid, Dunham Massey, bole, Little Leigh, Malpas, Odd Rode, and Sutton, near Runcorn. FIRE AT THE DOG AND P.A.RTRIDGE.—A fire broke out on Tuesday 'afternoon, in a stable connected with the Dog and Partridge public-house in Man- chester-road. A mounted messenger gave informa- tion at the borough fire brigade station, and the brigade, under the direction of Superintendent Turner, proceeded with all possible speed to the place. The flames had got a hold when they ar- rived, and it was not until after an hour's hard work that they were subdued. The landlord of the house, Mr. T. F. Nevins, sustained rather a serious accident. When pouring water on the burning material he fell from a ladder upon which he was standing, and broke his arm. His back was also injured. The damage estimated to have been caused by the out- break amounts to about £5O, and, it is said, is covered by insurance. It is not known how the fire originated, but it is supposed that a lighted match had been dropped on the straw by tramps. DISTRICT HIGHWAY BOARD.—A general meeting of members of the Warrington and District High- way Board was held at the Surveyor's Office in Sankey-street on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. R. Houghton presided, and there were also present Messrs. James Wright, Edward Marsh, W. Royston, J. Harrison, James Houghton, John Grounds; T. E. Withington, and J. Hartley (ex-officios) ; H. B. White (clerk), and J. Thompson (surveyor).—The Clerk read the surveyor's report of the repairs and improvements effected in various townships in the Board's district. Several encroachments • had been dealt with, and in the township of Poulton the road at Padgate had been improved and was undergoing macadam. With reference to the macadamising of the pavement of Winwick-road, it was reported that the Board were at liberty to proceed with the work.—A number of payments were reported as having been made to the treasurer since the last meeting. There was a balance left in the bank of .£1,146 lOs 11d. Only three townships had paid the call due on the 4th inst, and it was decided to write to the overseers of the remaining townships, re- questing that the calls should be paid.—A number of accounts that had been examined by the Finance Committee were passed for payment.—lt was re- ported, in reference to an application that was in June last made to the county authorities asking that three roads might be declared to be main roads; that a reply had been received saying that the matter would be attended to.—This was all the business.

A 31verzatous DISA2PEA.U&NOE.—Abont a fort- night ago some alarm was occasioned by the disappearance of a married woman named Alice Cropper and her twit chil- dren, who left their home in St. Helens, during the absence of the husband and father. The police were in- formed of the " mysterious " disappearance, and inquiries were instituted, but no information as to their whereabouts could be obtained. Mrs. Cropper, with her children, unex- pectedly returned to her home on Tuesday, and stated that she had been on a "visit" to Southport, alleging as a reason for doing so that she had had some words with her husband.

MAYORAL AT HOME.—On Thursday the Mayor and Mrs. Harrison will hold an "At Home" at the Town Hall. Should the weather be fine there will , be tennis on the lawn at the rear of the Hall. BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLE.—Yesterday, at the Borough Court, a travelling shoemaker, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horse- market-street, on the previous afternoon, and fur- ther with assaulting P.C. Ford at the same time. It appeared that the prisoner was using bad lan- guage and creating a disturbance, and on being asked to desist struck and kicked the officer in a brutal manner. P.C.:Johnson came to his assistance, and the prisoner was locked up. The Mayor ob- served that the prisoner had committed a dangerous and outrageous assault, and he must be committed to prison for two months, with hard labour. THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For week ending Saturday, Aug. 14th, 1886.—The mean temperature was 59.8 Fahr., and therefore 3.3 deg.- warmer than the preceding week. The Maxi- mum temperature 70 Fahrenheit. was recorded on the 14th inst., and the minimum temperature. 50 Fahrenheit, on the 11th inst. The rainfall measured 5.9 inches. The general direction of the wind was N.W. During the week, which was the 33rd of the current year, 33 births and 16 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 17 per 1,000, against 16.2, the average rq the previous four weeks, and against 14.8 the cor- respondiiig week of last year. The deaths included I from diarrhcea, 1 from phthisis, 1 from syphilis, 4from brain disease, 2 from cancer, and 1 from old age. One case of typlioid fever was reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—JNo. H. GORNALL. Medical Officer of Health. CLAIM FOR MEDICAL ATTENDANCE. At War- rington County Court; on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, Dr. James Willett, practis- ing at Stockton Heath, claimed £l6 12s from John Done, brickmaker, Hatton, for medicine and attend- ance. Mr. H. J. Longton appeared for the plaiptiff, and Mr. 'Percy Davies for the defendant.—Mr. Longton said the claim was for medicine and at- tendance on the defendant from September Ist to the 24th November, 1884, during which period the doctor attended the defendant nearly every day.

It appeared from a letter which Mr. Davies had sent , him, the defence was that Done was a member of the Rechabites' Club, and was not, therefore, liable for the claim, but Mr. Willett had never been doctor for the Rechabites' Club. The Rechabites offered the doctor £lO in settlement of the affair, but he refused to accept it.—The plaintiff then gave evi- dence in support of Mr. Longton's statement.—ln answer to Mr. Davies, plaintiff said he did not know who paid the accounts of the patients of the Recha- bites' Club from 1881 until 1884. He sent in his accounts to the persons he attended. The letter now produced was in his handwriting. The letter was addressed by the plaintiff to the District Secre- tary of the Club of the Rechabites. In it the plain- tiff said he should be glad "if you can tell me what course the Society of Rechabites intend to pitrsue in reference to the various accounts which are yet owing to me on behalf of their members located in Hatton. The various items and accounts of each person have been forwarded to the society in suc- cession as aforetime, when the accounts were duly settled. My arrangements with the society were that. I should send in the bills within six weeks !after the illness of each member, when they wonld be settled, but these accounts have stood over nearly 12 months; and I should feel obliged by your writing to say if you think the society will shortly settle them, or what I am to trio in the mat- ter. I could not conveniently look over the matter much longer."—His Honour: That cannot affect I the question. If he was the medical officer of the club and was directed) to attend a patient that would be another thing, but when a member of a club obtains the services of a medical man on his own pereonalresponsibility, so long as the doctor is not medical officer of the club, it cannot affect the question of liability.—Mr. Davies said the defendant was a member of the Rechabites' Club in 1884, and in September of that year he became very ill. He sent for Dr. Willett, and informed him that he was a member of that club, and the doctor handed him a certificate addressed to the Society, stating that defendant was unable to follow his employment. The defendant took the certificate to the Society and became entitled to sick pay, and he received it on about 14 or 15 other certificates also handed to him by Dr. Willet. No application was made by Dr. Willett to him for payment of his account, but he did apply to the District Secretary and apolo- gised for the account being so hea`vy ; explaining that it was owing to the long distance from his surgery to Done's house. Mr: Davies submitted that the plaintiff must have trusted the Society; and not the de,fendant, or he •would not have sent in his account to the Society.—His Honor said all the facts went to show that the plaintiff was not the accredited officer of the society, but seeing that they were willing to pay the accounts, he used to send in the bills to them. Sometimes the Society paid, and at other times they did not. This was orie of the cases in which they did not pay, and the plaintiff therefore fell back on the original party, namely, the defendant. He thought the Society ought to appoint a Medical Officer, because the pre- sent state of things were misleading to the mem- bers.—Mr. Davies said the head society had taken up the matter, inasmuch as they sent some one over to offer £lO to settle the account. He bad been informed that no dottor had been appointed by the rules, and that a gentleman from the head office had come over prepared to settle with the plaintiff.—His Honor gave judgment for the plain- tiff, defendant to pay 4s. a month. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, TIIITIZSDA.Y. There was a full muster of the House of Commons to-day on its re-assembling for the despatch of pub- lic business. Crowds outside and inside, though the day was gloomy, with occasional . showers of rain. Mr. Gladstone came down in good time, looking better than ever, and evidently in high spirits. It is curious to note that even in his pre- sent situation he has lost nothing of his popularity. After his fall in 1874 his passing in and out of Pal- ace-yard was a matter unnoted. Even so recently as last year his removal from office was contempo- rary, with a great falling off in the applause of the populace. But to-day, as a fortnight ago, the great crowd at the gate of Palace-yard enthusiasti- cally 'cheered him, overpowering a fragmentary hostile demonstration. The difference in demeanour between Mr. Gladstone and Lord Randolph Churchill was strangely marked. Lord Randolph has put on a manner of almost overawing solemnity. His quips and quirks his swift movement about the bench which characterised his sitting below the gangway have all been abandoned. He now sits in the place of leader as silent as the late Mr. Dis- raeli' with one arm folded across ' his chest, whilst with the other he curls his still mutinous mous- tache. Mr. Gladstone, on the contrary, is as lively as Lord Randolph used to be, talks to everybody near him, particularly Lord Hartington, and is as buoyant as if he had achieved a great victory in- stead of having suffered a crushing defeat. The Queen's Speech is one of the shortest on re- cord, and has created varying emotions. It is popular with the Conservatives. It is accepted as inevitable by fair-minded Liberals, and it has mad- dened the Pamellites. If we consider the circum- stances ef the case, it must, be admitted that little' more could have been expected in the Speech. The Government have determined to make the sittings which open to-day a seasion of themselves, that is to say when the estimates are complete Parliament wi'.l be prorogued, not adjourned. The Queen's Speech, of course, has reference only to the area of the session, whether limited or extended, and since the Government have no intention of dealing with the Irish question this side of Christmas, they were not bound to include mention of the subject in their programme. Whether it would have been wiser as a matter of tactics, to have introduced some concili- atory reference to the inevitable task which Mr. Gladstone was obliged to lay down before comple- tion is another question. Of course Lord Salisbury has his own party to consider first, and he has pleased them by the construction of the Speech. That Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill will have to deal'with the Home Rule question few people with any knowledge of affairs can doubt. For myself I believe that not later than next session they will bring in a scheme distinguishable from Mr. Gladstone's only in some unimportant details. But it would be too embarrassing to take up such a position without some decent interval of time, and this will be afforded by the recess. In the mean- time, since something has to be done, there are to be .Coramissions of Enquiry into the land question in Ireland and into the condition of public works. This is a very feeble expedient of which we are likely to hear some plain words in the course of the debate which opened to-day. There Ms been enquiries and Commissions enough about Ireland, including that memorable one a Mr. W. H. Smith's. What the Government hope is that these Commissions will be taken as an earnest of their intention to deal with the Irish question, and perhaps it may. .But it would have been simpler and more straightfor- ward to have given an assurance of intention to deal with the matter next session.

Queen's confidential political agent. Through she learns all about the inner life of politics-and. through him,she usually communicates with states-. men and,politicians. At the last Ministerial crisis, as happetied at the two preceding it, the newspaper reader could not fail to observe how suddenly the name of Lord Rowton began to appear in para- graphs relating to Ministerial and ex-Ministerial movements. Lord Rowton has in charge the pre- paration of the Life of Lord Beaconsfield with. which I believe he is very little advanced. Be could write, and possibly is writing„ another book which would open the eyes of posterity as to the secret movements of politics in this late Victorian era.

div.head: LoCAL BOWLING.
div.p: LoCAL BOWLING.

- T. LEE AND W. WEBSTER FOR £4.—The green at- tached to the Dog and Dart Inn, Grappenhall, was the scene of a lively contest on Saturday afternoon, the above players, both of Warrington, contesting a game of bowls, 51 ui, for £2 a-side. There was a good number present, and the green was in'fair cim- dition. Throughout the contest, the spectators took advantage of Mr. Kirkland's illness, as they con- tinually kept walking on the green and interfering with the players, both of whom contested the game in an ambitious manner, and it eventually resulted in T. Lee winning by a single point. The scores were: —Lee, 51; Webster, 50. J. BROMILOW AND J. GItEAVE FOR £so.—One of the most important .matches that has taken place in this neighbourhood for some time took place on Tuesday on the Bank Quay Subsgiption Bowling Green, Warrington, the contestan :tebeing J. Bromi- low, of Westhoughton, near Wigan, and Jos. Gleave, jun., of Warrington, who had signed articles to play a game of bowls, 101 up, for £25 aside, neither man to change bowls during the progress of the game. Although the match was not advertised, the green was surrounded by a large number of specta- tors, among whom were several professionals of this popular summer game. Mr. Mellor deserves great credit for the excellent condition the green was in, and his well known demeanour kept the onlookers, with one exception, from showing any partiality to the detriment of either player. At the commence- ment of the game Bromilow was made favourite, odds of 6to 4 being laid on him. He scored the first end, and .continued in front until 20 was reached, when Gleave went to 26 to Bromilow's 22. The latter now began to play much better, and passed his opponent, totalling 39 to 33, 43 to 36, 46 to 40, and -at half game was five points in front, the scores being: Bromilow, 51; Gleave, 46. After a short interial the game was resumed, and again Bromilow -scored the 'first end. At 58; 60, and 62 he was 10 in front, when Weave made a run of four and two singles. This was Gleave's nearest ap- proach to his opponent throughout the remainder of the game, as Bromilow now scored four singles, and totalled 67 to 58, 76 to 61, 80 to 64,86 to 66, 93 to 67, and eventually ran out an easy winner by 28 points. The scores at the finish were: Bromilow, 101; Gleave, 73. Bromilo w played well througn- out the game, whilst Gleave, when in possession of the jack, made some very bad leads, and it is owing to this cause that he suffered so decisive a beating. J. SHAW AND R. LYTHGOE FOR £4o.—On Thurs- day afternoon, on the green attached to the Norton Arms Hotel, Halton, .T: Shaw, of Warrington, and R. Lythgoe, of Earlestpwn, opposed each other for the second time within the past fortnight; the stake at issue being £2O aside. On the previous occasion Lythgoe proved victoribus by eight points; but Shaw's party thought he owed his defeat to the heavy rain that prevailed during a portion of the game. In this case the weather was all that could be desired, and Shaw won by 14 points. There was a good attendance, and previous to the game starting betting was brisk at guineas to pounds on Lythgoe. This player scored the first end, and the pair peeled at 8. Shaw then went to the front, and totalled 36 to Lythgoe 22, when the latter made a run of 12, and at half-game was five points behind, the scores be- ing:—Shaw, 51; Lythgoe, 46. During the second portion Shaw continued to keep the lead, though the play of neither was first-class, and at the finish of the game the scores were :—Shaw, 101; Lythgoe, 87. Mr. R. Barlow, of Lostock, was referee and stakeholder.

The story about Lady Dorothy Nevill ani Mr. Gladstone, which has been delighting the re-assem- bled House of Commons to-day, probably wants a little illumination for persons not acquainted with the heroine. A lady's age Is a dieult topic for discussion. But it may be delicately hinted that neither Mr. Gladstone. nor Mr. Disraeli, nor Lord Palmerston was the earliest acquaintance amongst Prime Ministers of this lively politician. She is a a strong partisan, and her Sunday luncheons are understood to have considerable influence upon public events. Prince Albert Victor is still in the neighbourhood, Bridge House, Bewsey-road, Warrington, August but next week sets out for Balmoral, and will thence 18th, 1886 proceed to Copenhagen, whither his father and mother are bent after their cause of. German baths. The Prince of Wales has left England under some- thing of a cloud, as far as society is concerned. The season was finished up, as usual, at Cowes; where ' Mrs. Mackay, the eminently rich American, shone with her customary splendour. She gave a grand ball to the yachting people anchored in the Solent, and the Piince of Wales, shocking to relate, danced every dance with the pretty American girls whom Mrs. Mackay assembles on these occasions. If that had been all it would have been enough, but on the following night another American lady gm a ball when H.R.H. showed 'similar preferences. This is indeed sufficient to cast a•cloud over the closing i hours of the most brilliant season. The position of Mr. Montagu Corry, known in these later days as Lord Rowton, is a very peculiar one.. div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE,
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. 141ozsmar —Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and
Alderman Webster,

Dnunriarxtss.—NVilliam Smith, charge-1 with being -drunk and disorderly at the police station on Saturday evening, was dismissed on promising to leave the town at once.—John Baker was charged with being drunk in Butter- market-street on Saturday. He was fined 2s 61. including costs.—James Coyne, for being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street. was fined 5s and costs.—Margaret Jones was charged with being druuk and disorderly hi Market-street. She was dismissed on promising not to offend again.— John Peers, a you•b, charged with being drunk in Buttermarket- street, was ordered to pay a fine of 5s and cests.—Mary Jones, summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Silver. square, was fined 54, including costs —Bridget Lally, Maria Shields, Mary Baldwin, and Winifred Conway were charged with biz drunk and disorderly on Pinners-brow, and were each sent to prison for 14 days. A DESERTER.—WiIIiam Randolph was charged with being i a deserter from the Royal Welsh Fusiliers, stationed at I VVrexhana. He admitted the offence, and said that he de- serted a week ago. He was remanded to Strangeways to I await an escort. AN OBSTINATE MARKET' PORTFTL.— James Leslie wai summoned by Inspector Place for refusing to give up his badge as a market porter on the 11th inst. He had been dismissed for misconduct and obstinately refused to give up possession of the badge. He was fined 3s 6d, including costs, and the badge was given up. BREACH OF TWA Praca.—Mary Coyne and Annie Daley were, for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Scotland-road on the 11th Inst., ordered to find two sureties in £5 each for six months, and pay costs. UNREGISTERED LODGING Horsas.—John Jeffries, whose wife appeared, was charged with keeping lodgers without having his house registered, on the Bth inst. There were extenuating circumstances, and the Bench did not impose a penalty.—Bridget O'Brien was summoned for a similar of- fence. She-was ordered to pay costs. WIFE Assanur.—William Hopwood was charged on re- mand from Saturday with assaulting his :wife Catherine.— Complainant said that she had been married to prisoner for twelve months, and he had been abusing her the whole of that time. He never gave her more than 7s a week.—P.C. Monoghan said that when he apprehended prisoner he threatened that he would kill her.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for two months, with hard labour. WEDNESDAY—Before Alderman Pickmere.

DrCNIZENtiF39.-Philip Mnrray was charged with being drunk and diecrcierly in Bridge-street on the previous day. He was Oned 53 and costs. 101 6d in all. Thomas Hnsbin, for being drdtk and disorderly on the day previous, was fined 5s and costs. _ _
fn-i;ey-.Liefore the Mayor (Ald•rman Harrison), Ciotain Rpynolds, Messrs. John White, Robert Garnett, and Chas. White.

DAMAGE TO PROPERTY.—CIifford Kinsey, a youth, was summoned for doing damage to the window of a hottse in Salisbury-street, to the amount of is 6d, the property of William Gibson. Chief Constable Hunt said he had re- ceived constant reports of damage to unoccupied houses in that neighbourbood.—l he Bench imposed a fine of lOs and coats —Mary Ann Tarpoy and John Lee were summoned far doing damage tp windows of a house, occupied by Mrs Mary Morris, and were ordered to pay the damage, 63 6d, and the costs.

THRBATS.—Margaret Kelly, was summoned for using threats to her husband, Rhoda Kelly, on the 16th inst. Complainant alleged that he was afraid of his life, as his wife had threatened to cut his throat with a razor or kill him with a poker.—Defendant acknowledged the offt•nce, and said she had no excuse to offer.—She was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for three months. AssAuf.:2.—Ann Davies was summoned for assaulting Ellen Regan on the 14th inst., and was bound over to keep the peace for three months.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY—Before Messrs. S. Rierr and J. Tinsley.

DRUNKENNESS. &c.—Peter Travis was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly on the 10th inst, and Joseph charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a lurry and two horses, was fined 7s 61 and costa.—William Buckley was fined 5s and costs for being drunk en the high- way at Penketh while in charge of a h7sree and cart, on the 7th lost, and for being asleep on his lorry at Great Sankey on the 4th inst was fined 2s 6d and costs.—Thomas Kelsall was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly on the highway at Great Sankey on the sth inst.-2 John Perrin was fined Sc and costs for being drunk and disorderly at Rixton on the 11th inst. BRFACH OF THE PEACE.—SiE men named Randall, Broad- hurst, Mellor, Bellian, Webster, and Russell were charged with committing a breach of the peace at Great Sankey en the Bth inst. The allegation was that defendants were sing- ing, cursing, and shouting, thus making a great noise. Ran- dall an 4 Webster were ordered to pay costs and the others were dismissed, Mr. Rigby warning them that one o'clock in the morning was not a suitable time to sing cones in the street. It transpired that defendants or some of them, had been "keeping up" a wedding.—John Maloney and Walter Moesley were ordered to be bound over for committing a breach of the peace in Winwick-road. A SLEEPY Cawrzn.—John Naylor was fined is and costs for being asleep while in a cart of which he had charge, on the 6th inst.
LY3IIII PE rI Y SESSIONS. FnlDAY.—Before Mesars. J. B. Dewhurst (in the chair), H. Stanton. T. P. Norris, and B. Allen.

Semen FLVER.—Patrick Cullen was charged with remov- ing a pig into an area that had been declared affected with swine fever, and Thomas Ford, his employer, was charged with ceasing the animal to be removed. The offence was committed on the 23rd July. Cullen was dismissed, and a fine of 10a and 183 81 costs was imposed upon For I.—John Mills was charged with removing. and Daniel Pe, civil with causing to be removed, a pig into an affected area on the 7th inst. Mills was dismissed, and Percival. who pleaded that he did net know the district into which he caused the pig to be taken waeaffected with the disease, was ordered to pay the costs. The police stated that swine fever was be- coming very prevalent in the country. HAWKING WITHOUT A LICHNSIL—Joseph Battersbv, described as a hawker from Warrington, was fined 21 61 and costs for hawking without leaving a license, at Lymm, on the 27th Ult. DBUNKENNESS.—James Harrison, labourer, and Nephi Drinkwater, fustian cutter, were each fined 5s and costs for drunkenness at Lymm. MAINTENANCH.—Robert Burgess, Altrincham, was charged by his wife, Eliza, with not complying with a magistrates' order to pay 7s a week towards her maintenance. The arrears alleged to ba due up to the 16th inst. amounted to £2B 4s. Complainant and defendant made chargee of mis- conduct against each other. The Bench ordered the defen dant to comply with the order,or go te prison for a month.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. G. L. Davies. MISCELLANEOUS.—Maria O'Neil was summoned for using threatening language towards Mary Ann Brannon, of Water- street ; and there Was a cross-summons charging Brannon with assaulting O'Neil. The Bench dismissed both cases Margaret Frame, a young woman, was fined lOs and costs, 9s 6d, for using profane language in Mersey-street on the 7th inst.—John Burke, Christopher Rough, Bridget Mc- Mullen, an old woman, and Mary Helena Kelly were each &mil for drunkenness. DAMAGE.—John Yarvvood, George Taylor. and Jos Taylor, Taylor, young men, were charged with wilfully committing damage upon the property of El;za Ann Kirk- man, by breaking a wooden fence, doing damage to the ex- tent of 10s. The defendants pleaded guilty.—lt appeared that the fence enclosed the house formerly occapied by Mr. Craig in Irwell-lane, and the defendants were caught in the act by one of the tenants. A fine of 103 and costs was im- posed upon each defendant.

WIDNES POL'CE COURT. Mane—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junr. DRUNXIINNESS AND BEGGlNG.—Matthew Taylor, Hugh McMullen' hn Jo Burns, and John Cooney were fined 5s and costs, and John Doyle, Edward Neven, and Mary- Hulse, lOs and costs, for I)eirm drunk. and U. Gaskell, janr. Golding was hound over to keep the n iace, and a warrant was ssued, for the apprehen- sion of Sullivan, who did not appear.

YouNG GlMBLBlls.—Jarnes Edge, Michael Ford, Thomas Rogers aod James Byron, boys, were charged with gamb- ling by playing cards on Sunday, the 10:h inst.—P.C. 245 saw the boys playing cards in Back Walmsiey-street, He saw money !los several times —All the defendants stontiv denied playing for money.—They were ordered to psy each or seven days.

DEUNIXIMESS.—WiIIiam Llftns, John Mnlhearne, and John Golding were summoned for being drunk and disor- derly in Earle-street, Earlestown, en the 7th inst; each was fined 5s and costs.—Jarnes Downs was summoned for being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on the 7th inst, and was fined 5s and costs.—Patrick Waldron, for drunkenness in James-street, Golhorne. on the 6th inst, was fined 10s and costs.—William Travis, Golbnrne, for a similar offence committed in Wood-street, Golbornet. was fined 5s and costs.—Catherine Walsh was summoned for being drank and disorderly in Queen-street, Golberne, on the 10th inst. and was fined 55 and costs.—Juhn Schofield, Haydock, was I fined 5s and costs for being drunk in Black Brook-road on let inst.—A similar fine was imposed on John Jones hr being drunk and disorderly in Penny-lane, Haydock, on the let inst. BRIACH or TIM PHACll.—Mary Unsworth and Ann Whittle were summoned for committing a breach ef the peace at Newton, on the 31st nit, and were ordered to be bound over to keep the peace.—Mary Downs, for commit- ting a breach of the peace In Viaciabt-street, Earlestown, on the 31st tilt, was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace. Crammer ON FIRE —James William Leyland was sum- moned for having the chimney of his dwelling-house on fire at Wargrave en the 3rd iast, and was fined 3s 6d, in- eluding costs.

PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS. Tuispe.Y.—Before Mr. H. R. D'a /3n.mcs OV THI PRACE.—Samuel Jones and Thomas Jones, Whiston, were summoned for committing a breach .of the peace on the Bth lost, and were ordered to be bound over to keep the peace.—William Jones and Richard Lyon, labourers, Huyton, pleaded guilty to a similar charge com- mitted at Huyton Quarry. on 3rd kilt. 'hey were ordered to be bound over.—Ann File, for committing a breach of the peace in Glover's-court, Prescet, on the 7th inst. was ordered to be bound over.-Isaac Jones and Thomas Cavanagh, of Huyton, were also ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for a similar offence. DRIINIENNESS.—WiIIiam Cartwright was charged with drunkenness at linyton, on the 2nd lest, and was fined 5s and cnsts.—Andrew Dobson, for being drunk at Prescot, on the 17th July, and also on the 14th August, was fined 10a and costs in each case.—Patrick Kelly was fined 5s and casts for being druask in charge of a horse and trap at Tar- bock.

Eccleston, 20s and costs; Thomas Anders, Eccleston, .10s and costs; Joseph Lamb, Windle, 7s 6d and vista ; Walter Greaves, Eccles- ton, 7s 61 and costs; Elizabeth Lawrenson, one months' imprisonment; Catherine Houghton, Sutton, 5s and costs; Henry Johnson, Sutton, 5s and costs ; Catherine Clarke, Parr, 5s and costs; Thomas Hughes, Parr, 5s and costs; Francis Hughes, Eccleston, 5s and costs; Mary Clayton, Parr. 5s and costs. OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—.QnSan Clayton, Parr, ARS sum- moned for using obscene language on the 7th inst, and was fined 2a 61 and costs. PITCH AND Toss.—Timothy Connor, Windle, was sum- moned for playing at pitch and toss on theAtib inst, an& ' was fined 2s 6d and costs. RIDING ASLEEP IN HIS CART....-Pater BenyOn, Parr, was summoned for being asleep in his cart on the 6th just, and was fined 23 6d and costs. Bianaoli ov THE PEACE.—Frank Needham, Parr, was sum- moned for committing a breach of the peace, and was or- dered to be bound over to keep the peace—Joseph Leachey, Parr, James Riley, Parr, and James Samrnon, Windle, were similarly dealt with for like offences. SLEEPY.—A tramp named William Murphy, was charged with sleeping in a hay shed belonging to Mr. John Smith, farmer, Newton-road, Parr, which contained a large quantity of bay, had in his possession some matches, a pipe, knife, dre., but no money. The prisoner, who stated that be had tramped from Manchester that day, was sent to prison for seven days, Mr. Hall remarking that be had endangered the safety of the property by his conduct,--Robert Hall, a young sailor, of no fixed residence, was charged with sleeping in the St. Hel‘ns Chemical Works.—The prisoner, who admitted the charge, handed up to the Bench a written character.—The magistrates discharged the prisoner in con- sideration of the excellent character which he held, and on promising to leave the town immediately. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. B. BirMll.

BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Patrick White, 42, Fenton-street, and Joseph Woods, 18, Duke-street, were ordered to be bound over for committing a breach of the pease on the previous day. CONGREGATIONAL Canitert.—On Wednesday evening the members of the above congtegation presented Mr. A. J. Shaw with a handsome leather portmanteau, as an expres- sion of their regard, and in appreciation of his services prior to his departure for the United States. Mr. Trueedale and Mr. John Beesley, supported by the Bev. James Johnston, presented the gift to Mr. Shaw, who made suitable acknow- ledgment. Mr. Shaw sails on Tuesday next from Liverpool, in the "City of Berlin," for Now York, en route for Detroit, Michigan. A BAD CHARACTIL—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Mr. H. R. D's Willis, John Gilligan. a col- lier living at Prescot, was charged under a warrant with as- saulting John McEgan.—The prosecutor said he did not wish to press the case against the prisoner on account of the latter's wife and children.—Superintendent Barker said the prisoner had been 33 or 34 times previously convicted and was one of the worst characters in the town. The prosecutor had been badly assaulted, and at his request a warrant was issued for the apprehension ot the prisoner. The Bench ordered prisoner to be bound over to keep the peace for three months. ALLEGED ihtLiNyrorL WOMMING. —At the Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr. Willis, Patrick Conlan, an elderly man, was charged with unlawfully wounding his wife Margaret with a knife on the 13th inst. P.C. Walker , said from information he received he apprehended the pri- soner. Mrs. Conlan suffered from a large wound, three inches in length and cutting to the bone, on her right hand. 1 He charged the prisoner with causing the injuries, and he replied "I am innocent." Superintendent Barker said the prisoner's wife refused to give evidence, and he could not carry the case any farther. She had stated that her hus- band talc a knife from her and struck ker with it, but sbe had since said that the knife slipped through her hand and cut her. The Bench hoped it would be a warning to the prisoner, and said be was very lucky he had not been sent to gaol. As his wife would not give any evidence he would be discharged PRHSCOT SCHOOL BOARD.--The monthly meeting was held on Monday, Mr W L Evans, J P., presiding. There were also present Messrs W Goldsworth, Henry Fogg, and H Cross (clerk). The Clerk again submitted the report of the Government Inspector on his annual inspection of the schools, and after the consideration of that part relating to the Infants' Se,hool, it was resolved that all the children under five years of age at present in the Infante' School be allowed to remain on the terms under which they were ad- mitted, but that no other children under five years of age be admitted on those terms without the special permission of the Board.—lt was ordered that the appointment of Miss Alice Noonan as monitress in the Infants' School be ap- proved, and that she be paid at the rate of 2s per week from the 7th June last.—The Clerk read a letter from Miss Alice Elizabeth Sayer, certificated assistant mistress in the Girls' School, asking for an increase of salary, and after consideration it was moved by Mr Goldswortb, seconded by Mr. Fogg, and carried, that the salary be increased to £55 per annum from the 16th olt.—The consideration of the staff in the Girls' School was the next business, and it was moved by Mr Goldsworth that the services of Miss Eliza- , both Doke be retained as assistant mistress in the Girls' , .Sohool until the 22nd October next, and that her salary be . increased to the rate of £3O per annum from the 7th ult.— Mr Fyg seconded the motion, which was passed.—This was , the principal business.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Presco-t -BOard of Guar- dians was held at the Workhonee, Whiston, en Thursday, when there were present Mr. John Lowe (chairman), Rev. T. Chambers, Messrs. W. Birchall, W. Gerrard, T. Heald, W. Middlehurst, J. Whalley, J. Matthews, J. Fisher, W. Tyrer, C: B. Johnson, J. Ranson. J. Leitherbarrow, E. Syd2r, J. Kenwright, J. W. Waring, J. Jacksen, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). RELIEF RETURNS.—The Workhouse Master repoi ted there were 471 inmates of the house this week, against 470 last week, and 421 in the corresponding week of hat year; 58 vagrants bed been relieved, against 29 le the corresponding week of last yia”. THE MILE 6IIPPLY.—At a meeting of the Visiting Com- mittee, on the 19th inst., the question of the milk supply was considered, and it was ultimately decided that the con- tract with the present contractor (Mr. Ward) be determined on the 6,.,12 September, and that advertisements for tenders to supply milk to the Workhouse of the same standard and quality 38 b?fore be issued. This reeolution gave rise to a tenKthy discussion, but the minutes were passed by ten votes to 9. VACCINATION.—The Local Government Board wrote on the sth instant, stating that with reference to the explana- tion of Mr. Pendleton, vaccination officer for the Huyton district, relative to neglect of duty reported by the Board's inepecter, lr. R-iyle, they postponed consideration of the explanation until they had before them the return of vacci- nation due from him. The Board approved of the appoint- went of Mr. D. J. O'Neill as assistant deputy for Farnwortb aid Lower Widoes districts on the distinct understanding that the deputy vaccinator's services would be .employed only In the unavoidable absence of the public vaccinator.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, AUGUST 21, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, AUGUST 21, 1886.

THE AssisTANT Gunman 702 Eccizarow AND KNOWSLBT.—Writing on the 13th inst., the Local Govern- ment Board informed the Guardians that they had ad- dressed communications to Mr. T. Parkinson, assistant overseer for the townships of Ecclesten and Knowsley in reference to the report made by the district auditor after his audit of Mr. Parkinson's accounts for the half-year ended at Lady Day last, hut they had obtained no reply. Under the circumstances they requested to be informed if Mr. Parkinson still held the office of assistant overseer and whether they had reason to believe that Mr. Parkinson had received the several communications addressed to him.—Mr Burchall moved that Mr. Parkinson be called before the Board to give an explanation why he had not replied, and also to explain why so much rate had not been collected in the townehip.—Mr. Fisher seconded the motion.—The Clerk said the uncollected rate amounted to £2,777.—The motion was carried. WIDNES VACCINAMON KrAnoN. The Local Govern- ment Board wrote that at the recent inspection by Mr. Royle, he was informed that the public vaccinator of Farn- worth and Lower Widnes district was not using the room provided by the Guardians as a station at Widnes, but a room approached by a staircase, down which a woman and her child had fallen. They wished to knew if that was the room now in use as a vaccination station at Widnes.— The Clerk observed that negotiations were in progress for obtaining, if possible, Lacey-street Wesleyan schoolroom, for use as a pnblic vaccination station, and also for use as a meeting-room for the Relief Committee for the Widnes dis- trict. The amount asked for it was £2O per aunum.—On the motion of the Rev. T. Chambers, it was decided to ac- cept the room on those terms. DR. HIFFIRNAN.—The Clerk said be had received:slater from Dr. Rogers. of Basinbill Asylum, with reference to Dr. Hiffernan, formerly a surgeon in St. Helens. It appeared the relatives were anxious to remove him Lo Ireland. 'The Guardians were unable to remove him, and ,he suggested he should write to Dr. Rogers to that effect. The suggestion was adopted. POOR Law CONYBRIINCS.-011 the motion of the Rev. T. Chambers, the chairman (Mr. Lowe), the Rev. T. Finegan, Mr. Tyrer, and the clerk (Mt. B. H. Hartley) were appointed representatives of the Union at the forthcoming Poor Law Conference at Liverpool. ESTIMA.TBS.—The Clerk submitted an estimate of the probable amount of expenditure in the relief of the poor and other charges by the Guardians for the half-year ending 25th March next. The total was £23,400, and 10 per cent added for contingencies, £2,340, made a tot al of £25,740. The actual amount spent in the same period last year was £22,149. He remarked that the amount given in relief was steadily increasing, while lunacy generally was also on the increase.—The estimate was approved. This was the principal business.

WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB. ANNUAL ATHLETIC FESTIVAL. The third annual athletic festival promoted by War- rington Football Club, which was held last Saturday, afternoon on the ground of the club, off Wilderspool- causeway, was a favoured event in every respect. The entries for the varions contests were numerous, and an unusually large proportion of those who had entered turned out, the weather was every thing that could be desired, and the concourse of spectators was very great, probably numbering between three and four thousands. A popular variation on previous pro. grammes was made by the intro4uction of a football contest, which there can by no doubt was an irresisti- ble attraction to a great many people. The prizes offered by the committee were of a handsome charac- ter, and had, together with the judicious selection of a day on which to hold the sports, doubtless not a little to do with the satisfactory nature of the entries. Although there were no unavoidable delays in push- ing on the proceedings the sports were not finished till dusk, but notwithstaniing this the interest taken In them was so great that the attendance was large , till the finish. Tao whole of the arrangements were ' successfully carried through by the following officials I —Handicapper, referee, and timekeeper, Mr. T. R. Sutton (0 Athletic News") ; judges, Messrs. John Evans, J. Critchley, and W. Dillon; referee for foot- ball contest, Mr. G. W. 'Vickers, Salford - starter, Mr. J. E. Warren; clerk of the course, Mr. T. Pemberton; stewards Messrs. H. Boardman, D. T. Smith, W. Dumbell, S. Whittaker, James Winstanley, P. , Whittle, J. Bramhall, James Looker, C. Hamblet, and G. Smith; Mr. .1. E. Warren, hon. sec. The band of the 9th LR.V. was presentiluring the afternoon, and , rendered an excellent selection of music. The follow- ing are the results :- 200 YARDS HANDICAP FOR MEMBERS OF TEE WARRING- TON F.C.—lst prize, silver cup, value £2; 2nd prize, writing desk, value £1; 3rd prize. cigar case, value IN.—First heat: 1 J Thomason, 7 yards; 2 J Buxton, 5 yards. Second heat: 1 It Gilbert, 11 yards; 2 11 Ashton, 12 yards. Third heat : 1 C Unsworth, 10 wards ; 2 F Acton, 10 yards. Final heat: 1 C Unsworth ; 2 il' Acton; 3 E Gilbert. Time 22 3-5 secs. The final of this race was hotly contested, and was won by about balf a yard, a similar distance intervening between second and third. 120 YARDS FLAT Racy HANDICAP.—First prize, marble timepiece, value £5; second, silver cruet, value £2; third, field glasses. value £l. There were seven heats in this con- test, the first in each running in the final. First heat: 1 F Broadbent (Lees), ei yards start; 2 J Barrow (Chester). 4. The scratch man, IN, Raynor, of Manchester, was mak- ing a promising attempt to win this heat, when he unluckily fell after accomplishing threeoquarters of the distance. Time, 123.5 secs. Second heat: 1 T LaWe (Widnes),si; 2 W J Williams (Crewe), 54 ; 3 H Barlow (Liverpool), 2. Time, 12 3-5 secs. Third heat: 1 J R Brockbank (Carnforth), 8; 2 J Thomasson (Warrington), 9. Time.l2 3 5 secs. Fourth heat: 1 D A Harding (Whines), 5; 2 T Jackson (Barrow), 9. Time, 12 3-5 secs. Fifth beat: 1 T Little (New Brighten), fei ; 2 J Ellison (Earlestown), 6. Time, 12 2.5 secs. Sixth beat: 1 E T Lever (St. Helens), 5; 2 T Booth (Warrington). st. Time, 12 3-5 secs. Seventh beat: 1 J McLaughlin (St. Helens), 2; 2 J Kean (Liverpool), 5. Time, 12 2-5 secs. Final heat: 1 McLaughlin, 2 Brockbank, 3 Broadbent. In the final McLaughlin rar splendidly, and es won amid cheers by about half a yard. Tin k?, 12 1-5 secs. 440 YARDS FLAT R&CR.-ISt prize, silv r gong in oak frame, value £4; 2nd, case of carvers, value 30s; 3rd, dressing case, 15s. Firsf beat : 1, B Parkinson (Manches- ter), six yards start, and J D Johnson (Chestfire Tally Ho), 12 (dead beat); 3, E ItrEvoy (Warrington), 18. Time, 53 3-5 secs. Second heat : 1, S Morrie (Widnes), 2 yards, and R P McMahon (Widnee), 24 (dead heat); 3, J Law- rence (Liverpool), 27. Time, 53 2-ssees. Final heat : 1, Johnson; 2, McMahon ; 3, Parkinson. This was a good race, and was won by two yards, about half a yard separating second and third. Time, 53eecs. ONE MILE FLAT RACE HANDICAP ISt prize, marble timepiece; 2nd, pair of bronze horses ; 3rd, telescope. Out of twenty-two entries there were no fewer than nine- teen competitors turned out for this race. The result was 1, T Locker (Warrington), 85 yards ; 2, J Kelly (Widnes), 105 yards; 3, J Wright (Widnes 1, 50 yards. Locker was evidently bent upon winning this race if possible, and ran in a splendid fashion from the beginning, and steadily forged to the front. In the last lap he put on a spurt which carried him a considerable distance in ailvance of any com- petitor, and he came in an easy winner, .receiving a popular reward in the shape of a hearty round of applause. Time 4 mine. 28 secs. - FOOTBALL OONTEST.—The item in the programme which seemed to suite the most general interest was the football contest, for which the first prize consisted of seven silver tea services of tills aggregate value of ET ; and the second prize seven gold breast pins, of the aggregate value of £3 10 The entries comprised F Turner's, H Ashtoree, and J. Whittle's Warrington teams, the Warrington Rangers, Valentine's Swinton team, Salford Athletics, and Highfield. There were seven players in each team, and the time allowed for each contest was twenty minutes, 10 minutes each way, with the exception of the final which was a quarter of an hour each way. Valentine's Swinton v. F. Turner's Team: The first teams to take the field were Valentine's Swinton team and F. Turner's Warrington team. It was son seen that Valentine and his half dozen comrades were well able to maintain the high reputation of their club, for although the Warring- toe team contained such adepts at the game as Barnes, Jolley, F Turner, &c.. the ball was quickly carried into the home quarter. The Varrington players, however, as usual, made a torigh defence, but in the end ewinton had a minor placed to their credit, and soon afterwards a try, which resulted in a goal. In the second half Turner and his comrades showed decidedly bettor form, and ultimately secured a minor point, and Jolley also scoeed a try from a maul. No goal, however, resulted. During the last few minutes a very strong game was played by Warrington, and they were somewhat un- lucky in that it did not result in some further points being put to their credit. This contest ended as follows :—Swin- ton, 9 points: F Turner's team, 5 points. —Warrington Ranger's team v. J. Whittle's team: This was is Berne re- spects the most interesting contest, as the Rangers showed an unmistakeable supremacy over their opponents,especially in the passing game. The Rangers soon scored a minor point, and within a minute or two after an easy goal. On behalf of the opposing team, Whittle, as usual, played well, and Walsh defended the goal in a praiseworthy man- ner But the Raneers were not to be denied, and the contest closed with 11 points to their credit, as against 1 secured by Whittle's team.—H. Ashton's„ team v. Salford Athletic team : At the outset Ashton and his followers severely pressed the Salfor4 men, and the latter were not lAng in conceding a touchdown. The Athletics then, however, began to bestir themselves, and some hot play ensued dangerously near the Warrington posts, and ultimately a try, fron) which a goal resulted, was eecured by the visitors. On a change of ends the home team had the game pretty much in their own hands, and Buxton by a clever ran soon secured A try which was not turnrd into a goal. Theball had barely been re- started when Ashton by a determined effort won another try for Warrington which was this time transformed into a a goal by Anderton. The gaBm_e_en:s%cedinateonfolvl.owirei.gAhfishetiodn:s Itenamth.e23poin Swinton and Highfield teams were the first to turn secondtns u:t round out,Sa l High field having had the benefit of a bve in:the first round. Valentine's men quickly manifested their superiority, and in a few minutes three minors were placed to their credit, and later en a try, which did not end in a goal. Another try was soon awarded Swinton. but at this point the Highfield players took exception to the ruling of the umpire, that did

not leave the ground as they at first seemed inclined to do. On resuming Swinton secured two more tries, and the game ended thus, Swinton 25 points, Highfield nil.—Ashfon's Team v. Rangers: These were the teams which next en- tered the field, and Gee Iteneem made good slimed ageriist their formidatfie o. ponents. It was not lIN after some tough play that Ashton's men managed to gain a minor point, but after that scoring went on more rapidly, Buxton securing two tries and Ashton one, and in the end the game stood— Ashton's team 15, Rangers 2. Although, as might be ex- pected, the Hangers were not able to bold their own against their powerful antagonists, their play was again much ad- mired, ..nd pat ticularly their tackling and passing.—Final : Valentine's Swinton team and Ashton's team next came together in the final, and some good play was witnessed. Valentine's men again showed first-rate form and were not long in securing a try, which was not converted into a goal. Other points followed, although the Warrington team played a strong defensive game, and at times, by spirited efforts, endangered their adversaries' goal. The outcome of the game was that Swinton won by 16 points to 3, and conse- quent', were declared the winners of the first prize, Ashton's team taking second honours. Lamm-Cum STRIPLICHASIL—Teams of four, first three only to count, distance *bent two miles; three prices for winning team, aggregate value £8; three prizes for second team, aggregate value t 3; and a gold medal for the actual winner, value £2. In this contest members of the Salford Harriers, Liverpool Gymoasium, Warrington Harriers, Liverpool All Sainte, Liverpool Sefton Harriers, and Che- shire Tallo Ho took part. In each lap of this rase there were three hurdles and a water jump te clear, and the latter was the cause ef much amusement, as more than one runner tumbled bodily into the water. Farrell, for Salford,Massey, for Warrington, and Stewart, for Liverpool Gymnasium, came in in the order named, the running of Farrell ta par- ticular being much admired. The result of the race was as follows :-1, Salford Harriers, 10 points; 2, Warriegton Harriers, 15 points; 3, Liverpool Gymnasium, 26 points; 4, Tally Ho, 31. Liverpool All Saints were disqualified, as they did not finish.

Mrs. Francomb afterwards distributed the prizes to the successful competitors. Mr, J. Carrcaravr proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mrs. Francomb for so kindly distribrtting the prizes, and also for her presence at the sports, (Ap- plause.) Mr. J. E. Wanninv seconded the proposition, and expressed the hope that that lady would often grace the football matches by her presence. (Applause.) The resolution having been carried by acclamation, Councillor FRkNOOMB returned thanks, and said be could assure those present that Mrs. Francomb had taken as lively intereet in the football sports as he had done himself. He °mild only hope that although they had had a most successful season, the next would 'be more so. (Applause.) The proceedings in connection with this very suc- cessful athletic gathering then terminated,

AVERY IMPORTANT CONSIDERA.TION. A most important omaslderatlon for all at this stetson ef the year is how best te rid the system of the diseases induced by the trials of winter. In many cases it seems as though the seeds of consumption had been planted in the system by the trying weather we have gone through. In other cases various forms of Liver or Kidney Complaints are developed ; the lassitude becomes nervous weakness; the sleep is uneasy, and trriubied by unpleasant dreams; and ne patient, instead *of waking refreshed, gets sip with a feeling of weight and ,anguor, and every action seems a burden. NEWTON DIVISION ELECTION. LIBERAL MEETINGS On arriving at Earlestown from Liverpool on Fri- day morning, Mr. French, the Liberal candidate, at once proceeded to Penketh, and addressed a meeting of the electors of that part. Later in the afternoon he journeyed to .Bispham, where A second meeting was held. From there he drove to Billinge, near St. Helens, and addressed a large and enthusiastic as- eembly in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom. Mr. Challoner presided. At half-past eight he arrived at Rainford, and held the principal meeting. of the even • ing in the National Schools. Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P., presided, and he was supported by the Rev. James Johnson and Meagre. H. Martin and J. B. Leach. During the course of an address the candidate ap- pealed to the electors to support the Liberal measure of justice to Ireland, thereby encouraging Mr. Glad- stone in his noble efforts for the pacification of that country. On the questions of land and mine royal- ties the electors might rest assured that Mr. Legh, if elected, would loot( well after his interests as a landowner, and stated that, if returned, he (Mr. French) would use his best efforts for the welfare of the miners, the farmers, and the electors at large. Resolutions of confidence in the Liberal candidate were passed at all the meetings. BLACKBROOK. The first meeting of the series was held at eleven o'elook In the forenoon in the Colliery Schools,. Blackbrook, Hay- dock. There was a fair attendance, and Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P.,.presided. Addresses were delivered by the chairman, the eandidate ( Mr. French, Q.C. ), Mr. F. 'F. Kennedy (Liver- pool), Mr. Taylor, and others, and a vote of confidence in the candidate WAS passed. Mr. French and his party next drove to

courNs GREEN, Where an open-air meeting was held on the road side, near the Pear Tree lan. In addition to an address by the candi- date, Messrs. Pilkington, Kennedy, and G. W. Rawlins (Rainhill), also spoke.

div.head: GOLBORN E.
div.p: GOLBORN E.

ALLBGBD BREACH ON THI Plum—At the Newton Petty Sessioas on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton and W. F. Gooch, Patrick Hannon and John William Wilks were summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in High-street, Golborne, on the Oth inst. The °sees were dismissed.

PITCH AND Toss.—Before Messrs. R. Houghton and W. F. Gooeh, at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, James Edwardson, Joseph Aspinall, and Ralph Heyes were sum- moned for playing at pitch and tees on a. public footpath in a field at Gol borne on the let inst. P.C. Ratcliffe proved the case. The defendants, who sail they were only "pick- ing mushrooms," were each fined 2s eld and costa. EXTRLORDINLRY CONDUCT ON TEN RAnwaY.--John An- derton, an elderly man, was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Mr. R. Houghton and Mr. W. F. Gooch, for trespassing on the London and North-Western Railwav, so as to enslanger his life, on the 6th ult.—Mr. Ferrand, who pros•cuted, asked the Bench to inflict the full penalty of 40* and costs.—lt appeared that about half-past eight en the 16th ult. the defendant was seen walking along the line. He broke open the door if a platelayer's but, and took a number of fog signals, one of which he placed on the line. Shortly afterwards a London express train came up. the fog signal exploded, and caused the driver to slacken speed. Evidence to this effect was given by James Taylor, farmer, John Burchall, platelayer, and Railway-Detective Gunning.—The defendant, who strongly denied the charge, and said a " mistake in the man" had been made, was fined 20s and costa.

Cur Malta TIMMS'S° ON • RIILWAY.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton and W. F. Giech, Patrick Waldren (11), Mary Waldren (12), Martin Davies (10). Ralph Hibbert (11), and Michael Hand- ley (13), all of Golborne, were charged with unlawfully trespassing in the London and North-Western Railway, at Golborne, on June 20, and they were further charged with wilfully and maliciously setting fire to a stack of wood situated near the railway, also at Golborne.—All except Hibbert pleaded gailsy.—Mr. Ferrand, of the solicitors' department, Lime-street, Liverpool, said these and other children bad been playing in the Golborne goods yard for several months, using it as a playground. On the day in question (Sunday) a pointsman named Byrom discovered defendants playing in the goods station yard, and subse; quently he discovered they had set fire to a stack of "sleepers." The children took tallow from the waggons and placed it on the "sleepers" to make them burn np. Witness and another man extinguished the fire with buckets of water.—The Bench alluded to the seriousness of the charge, but undertook to inflict only a small fineion the understanding that their parents would give defendants a good flogging when they got homo.—The parents consented, and a fine of 5s and costs was imposed ia each case.--The defendant Handley, along with Wm. Holden (11), Richard Glover (11), and Thomas Joyce (8), were then charged with trespassing on the railway at Golhorne. by playing in the goods yard on the 26th Jaly.—Each defendant was fined 2,3 6d, including costs.--Robert Harvey (15), Christopher Collins (14), Mary Waldren (12), Ernest Heyes (11), and James Davies (8) were also fined 23 61 and costs each for a similar offence.

div.head: SOUTH WALES.
div.p: SOUTH WALES.

ANOTHER COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—A Newcastle telegram reports that a serious accident occurred on Wednesday morning at Cos Lodge Colliery, Gosforth, by which about 20 men were injured. The " back-shift" men were going in, riding on tabs drawn by the engine, but one of the sheaves through which the rope connected with the tubs passed had broken, end was hanging from the roof of the As the engine was going at a considerable speed, many of the men were bidly crushed about the head and shoulders, and sustained suci4 serious ittlaries that they had to be conveyed home in carts. The pit is now laid idle.

EARLESTOWN GOOD TEMPLA.II9. —The usual weekly session was held on M9nday evening last in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, Earleitown, Brother J. McDonald, W.C.T.; presiding. There was a very fair attendance of members. After opening, one candidate was initiated. Circulers of district lodge session for Saturday next, and temperance fete at Liverpool Exhibition on 28th August, were read,and arrangements made for visiting them After business had hen gone through a very pleasant and profitable evening was spent, by songs given by Brother J. McD)nald, Sister Whittv, Sister E. Clarke; recitations by Brother John Warburton, Sister C. Barnard, Sistet C. Day, and readings were given by Brothers William Harding and John Warbur• ton. Lodge closed at 9-45.

div.head: BURTONWOOD.
div.p: BURTONWOOD.

Continuing his journey. Mr. French, Q.O „proceeded to the National Schoolroom. Burtonwood. weere. at one oleiock an enthusiastic meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. F. A. R. Neill (Bold). . _

div.head: CLOCK FACE.
div.p: CLOCK FACE.

This part of the division was next visited; and a very eneeessful meeting was held in a tent, erected fer the pur- pose, in one of the fields near the railway station. As this was the first occasion upon which a Liberal candidate for Parliamentary honon-s had been seen in the district 7 the visit of Mr. French, Q.C., excited some interest. He re- ceived a most enthusiastic welcome. ' The chair was occu, pied by Mr. F. A. R. Neill (Bold), and the various- speakers- including the eandidate, were warmly applauded. The usual resolutions were passed amid applause.

• ST. HELENS. At four o'clock a meeting of Liberal workers and.friends, fairly well attended, was held in the Public Hall, Hardsha.w- street, St. Helens. Mr. Sinclair. J.P.. occupied the chair, and among those present were Mr. H. S. Hall, Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P. Messrs. G. W. Rawlins, H. Martin, H. L. Rthy, Councillor Forster, ke. The Chairman said they were again met to fight the good cause ,whiah he hoped' I they would always be willing to fight whenever an. oppor- tunity presented itself. (Applause), They should let ne opportunity of convincing their neighbours pass until they bad been enabled to return a Liberal member both for the borough and for the Newton division of the county. ( Ap- plause.) They were quite sure that their principles were right, and they must prevail.—Mr. French, QC., who was received with hearty applause, said in the last two elections the Liberal party had been thoroughly well whipped, but they were not a bit discouraged, and they were determined to peg away and fight the battle out for all time until, by the very right of their cause, they should be able to corn, mend success. (Applause.)—Mr. Henry Martin proposed "That Mr. French is a fit and proper person to represent the Newton Division in . the House of Commons." He thought Mr. French was the best man they could send to tha House of Commons. (Applause.)—Mr. J. J. Dutton seconded the resolution, and remarked that he felt be would be doing right in working and voting for Mr. French.—The resolution was carried with acclamation, and Mr. French responded.—Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P., proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman. He was only sorry that they tiad not been able to give him sufficient support to have put him where he ought to be. (Applause.)—Mr. H. S. Hall. J.P., 'seconded the vote of thanks, which was carried, and the chairman responded.—The meeting then concluded.

div.head: MOSS BANK.
div.p: MOSS BANK.

An open air meeting was held near Moss Bank School, about six o'clock in the evening. Mr. A. Sinclair, J.P., Presided, and was supported by Messrs. W. C. Eccles, C. Pilkington, J.P., Cf. W. Rawlins, H. S. Hall, J.P., J. Forster, H. L. Riley, T. Roberts, and R. Unsworth.—The Chairman said the Liberals were convinced that they would be able to carry the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire, and they meant to go on until they did. (Applause.) If all the Liberals of the division woald cone forward and pat their shoulders to the wheel they would be able to carry the divi.- sion, and he hoped they would do so. (Applause.)—Mr. French. Q C.. next addressed the meeting, asd said the question was whether they would free themselves from the landowners—from the Gerards, the Leghs, and the Crosses —whether they would assert their own position, and have a member who would really represent the interests of the people: (Applause.) For twenty years that part of Lanca- shire had been represented by Tories, and the time bad come to woke a change—.r. M. J. Lennon moved a‘rote of eonfl; deuce in the candidate, and Mr. Weldon seconded.—The resolution, on being put to the meeting., was carried unani. mously.

div.head: DENTONS GREEN.
div.p: DENTONS GREEN.

Later in the evening a meeting was held at Dentons- green, Mr. W. C. Eccles in the chair. The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said it gave him very great plea. sure in introducing so good and worthy a Libaral candidate, as he felt they held in Mr. French.—Mr. French, in ad.- dressing the meeting, said the Liberals represented the,cause of progress and liberty ; they, were in favour of legisla- tion for doing justice to Ireland, and the question they would have to settle wet whether they would have land- lordism, Legh, and Toryism, or Liberalism and union and justice to Ireland. (Applause.)—Mr. C. Pflkington moved a vote of confidence in the candidate, and the resolution was seconded by Mr. J. Gregsen, and was Unanimously adopted.

div.head: RAINHILL.
div.p: RAINHILL.

The last meeting was held at Rainhill in the National Schoolroom, which was crowded with an enthusiastio audi- ence, and the reception given to the candidate was of an exceptionally cordial character. Mr. G. W. Rawlins pre- sided, and supporting the candidate were Messrs. J. D. John— son, F. F. Kenneth', H. D. Maitland, T. Hamner. E., Tom- kinson, the Rev. J. Barton, ecc.—The Chairman, in opening the proceedings, said that in Mr. Legh they bad a candi• date who admitted he knew nothing of political affairs, but Mr. French tboroughly understood an would ably represent the great interests of that important constituency—Mr. French, who was received with ringing cheers,,said that Sir Richard Cross had introduced Mr. Legh not as a strong Tory candidate. but as the nominee of the landlord interest;: he was introduced upon the assumptibn that the Gerard% the Le.ghs, and other great landowners in the division still had the right to nominate their representative,. and bring forward any man they liked for the constituencvond their verdict must be ratified. ("Shame.")--;4lr. Maitland pro- posed, and Mr.J. D. Jahneon seconded, a resolution in sup— port of the candid its, which was unanimously carried, amid, great enthusiasm; and a vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings. THE POLLING.

The whole of the lilaTrlheestopwrinn,caipnadi arrangements in connection therewith were of a simi- , lar character to those reported about a month ago. The Liberals had secured rooms in Bridge- street for the purposes of committee rooms, and among the workers on behalf of the Liberal candidate, were Messrs. B. Harrison (chairman. of the Earlestoen pertion of the "300 ") L. T. Foulkes, A.. J. Rawlinson, P. Davies, G. Sturgess, Stevens, Jrc. Their political opponents had again secured a plaza in Cross-lane for the same object. The poll— ing started at eight o'clock,. when a fair number of persons had gathered round the palling station and the committee. rooms of the two parties. The polling was fairly brisk during the morning, but the busiest part of the day was in the forenoon and about noon. 11:p to twelve o'clock about 1,100 voters had entered the polling station, bat from, that time the voting was much slower. Very few vehicles were in use, and these were nearly all seed by the Consezvatives. The Conservatives asserted that they secured a larger num- ber of suites thanon the last occasiod, while the Liberals were somewhat doubtful as to their ability to muster as strongly. Towards eight o'clock, when the poll was cloaed, the streets were rendered almost impassable, and the rival partisans cheered or groAned to their hearts' content. During , the day the two csndidates drove about the division, and they were received with mingled cheers and hoeting. About half-past four o'cleck in the afternoon Sir Richard Cress drove up to the Earlestorvn polling booth and entered to re- , Sir Gilbert cord his last vote, presumably for Mr. Logh. As at the last election, the voting for the Warrington i polling district took place in Cairo-street School-room, the rsebceoirndged their votes during the morning may be of a quiet and formal character. voters on the register nrimbered LI Ice L 270, inclusive, and number two for those on the rexister from L 271 to 141$8, also inclusive. The presiding officer at number one polling starion was Mr. Michael Jackson, solioion, Wigan, and the poll clerk Mr. Charles Fairtiterst, Wigan, the personation agent for Mr. Legit being Mr, Thomas Etiggs Cross, and for Mr. French Mr. Herbert Messiter. At number two polling station the presiding officer was Mr. J. Houghton, Wigan, and the poll clerk Mr. 11-R. Griffiths ; and the per- sonation agent for Mr. Legh Mr. Ralph Johnson, and for Mr. French Mr. Samuel Dun bobbin, of Warrington. Two houses on the opposite side of th, street were used as the Liberal and Conservative committee-rooms. The voters on the register for the Ashton township num- barest 1,523, and the Local Board Offices. Bryn-street, were utilised for voting purposes. The regiater fer Haybock con- tained the nanins of 875 vofers, and these polled at the Col- liery Schools ; the Golborne electors (744) recorded their opinion as to whom was the most "fit and proper person" at the St. Thomas's Church Schools; the Billinge contin- gent (601) voted at the Church Schools, Billinge; the 353' voters in Raiohill were required to', vote at the National Schools.
