National Schools. The polling at St. Helene was conducted in a quiet manner. .No public interest appeared to be mani— fested in the voting, which took place at the Cowley (Mid, die)Schools, College-street. Opposite the schsoleach party had secured committee rooms, and for the Liberals Mr H S Hall,J.P., Mr Wilfrid Leash, Mr Joshua Slats (Portico). Mr David itimmer, and Mr Patrick Byrne were specially active. Among other gentlemen in the division who exerted them- selves on behalf of Mr French were Mr Urpuhart, Newton; MessrsTbomas Roberts and Whitefield, St. Helena; Mr Mit- chell, Golberne ; Messrs. F. A. R. Neill and Parker, Sankey; Mr G W Rawlins, Rainhill; Mr Saville, Rixton ;. Mr Wm. Roberts, Warrington; Mr Pilkington, Haydeck ;, Mr Chid- loner, Billinge; Mr Thomas lioterte, Ashton;. Mr Wylde, Batiniord.

Blectieneering literature was, to qttote a common expres- sion, rendered conspicuous by its entire absence. Beyond the addresses of the respective candidates, the only placards to denote that an election was at hand were, "'Vote for Legh, the Unionist, and set for French, the Separatist" ; "Vote for French, the real Unionist candidate, and not for the Tory and coercion, leading to dis-union";. and "Vote for It.agh, the Conservative-Unionist candidate." The Con- servatives, in addition, bad a number of cards printed, with a blue blackground, cornered by the Union dick, and bear- ing the words "Legh and Unity." One incident of the election excited a great deal of inter- set and comment. A statement was circulated that the nomination papers of Mr. Legb, the Conservative candidate, were illegal, and that if an oi.jection had been:taken to them it would have proved fatal to Mr. Lsgh's candidature. This statement occesioaei some alarm in the Tory ranks, with the result that the retarning officer, Mr. J. Hughes (under sheriff 4 was communicated with. In his reply Mr. Hughes said no objection was taken to the nomination papers of Mr Legh at:the time they were handed in, and be consequently took them as being valid. The Conservatives circulated this reply in the form of a handbill, and mentioned that the assertion in question had been made by Mr. Wm. Urqnhart, ehairmen, and Mr. W. D. Burdis, vice- ebairtnan of Mr. French's election committee. On Monday, the day of polling, a handbill, of which the following is a copy, was issued :—" The indersigned,,who are not respectively chairman and vice-chairman of. Freach's Election Committee, as stated by Mr. T. H. Pear- son, hereby declare that what they have stated is perfectly correct:. ]it. That there was an irregularity in both Mr. T. W. Legh's nomination papers, via., that the candidate's name was omitted from one of the spaces provlded for. its insertion. 2nd. That this irregularity might have been fatal to his nomination as a candidate for this division had an objection been made. 3rd. That this irregularity can be verified on reference te the original document,s, which were inspeeted by the solicitors or agents to the respective can- didates at the time. .4th. That Mr. French, the Liberal s candidate, instructed his agent not to take advantage of this irregularity, nor to take any legal point of any kind, but chose to contest the division, and thereby proved himself to be a fit and proper person to represent an electorate of honourable men in Parliament. They also challenge Mr. J. Hughes to produce the original nomination papers.— WM. Uk4UHAIIT, W. D. BIIIIDIS.—Newton-le•Willowe, August Mb, 1886." DECLARATION OF THE RESULT.

After the polling the whole of the boxes were conveyed with all possible speed to the Town Hall, Newton, where they were counted under the directions of the returning officer, Mr. Hughes. While this was being done, a large crowd gathered in the vicinity and patiently awaited the official declaration. At eleven o'clock some hundreds had congregated, and shortly after that hour, Mr. Huglees, from one of the windows, declared that the result was ,as

div.head: Mr. Legh (C) 4,062 Mr. French (L)
div.p: Mr. Legh (C) 4,062 Mr. French (L)

Majority for Mr. Legh 707 The sknnouncement was received with prolonged cheers, groans, and hisses. The local Conservatives' in anticipation of victory, had stored a quantity of fireworks in the neigh- bourhood of the committee rooms, opposite the Town Hall, and these were immediately discharged when it became known that Mr. Legh had been returned. Shortly after the declaration, Mr. LEcar, M.P., Appeared at the window, and addressed the crowd. His remarks were entirely inaudible to every one in the sheet below, the crowd keeping up a continual fire of groans, hisses, and cheers. Mr. Legb said: Gentlemeo,—Tbis time we have achieved a most satisfactory victory. It has not been a con- test between man and man, or one class against another. class, but it has been a contest of principles, and you have ratified the judgment which you passed a short time ago. It has been my good fortnne to be returned as your repre- sentative in succession to Sir Richard Cross, and I cannot. find words to express sufficiently the honour I feel and my thankfulness. All my best energies will be devoted to your interests, and it shall be my aim and object to serve you to the beet of my ability, and I trust I may never give you reason to regret the confidence which you have placed in me. With regard to the contest that has just terminated, I am • glad to be able to testify to a general absence of per- sonalities, and my opponent and myself met as friends, ,we font as friends, and we part, I hope, as friends still, and we have, I think, conducted ourselves as gentlemen. (Cheers.) Mr. French, Q.C., was received with loud cheers, mingled with groans. He said : Gentlemen, the Liberal party has been again beaten, but we mean to fight at the next election and whatever may happen we shall not be discouraged, but we will continue to fight until the Liberal party finally win this constituency. My opponent and I have fought on friendly terms. He has done very well, and I coneratniate him upon his success, but I hope to beat him next time. (Loud cheers.), _

The crowd then gradually dispersed._ THE NEW MEMBER. Mr. Thomas Wodehonse Legh, of Lyme Park, Dieley, near Stockport, Cheshire, is the eldest son of Mr. William' ;min Legit, of Lyme Park (who WAS for many years M.P. successively for South Lancashire and East Cheshire) by his marriage with Emily Jane, daughter of the late Ven. Charles Wodehouse Archdeacon of Norwich, and was born in 1857. • Mr. Legi; entered the diplomatic service in 1880. Hewes appointed a third secretary in 1832, and was until quite recently employed at the British Embassy at. Paris. He married in 1880, Evelyn, daughter of the late Mr. W. Bromley Davenport, M.P. Mr. Legh, who noiv enters Par- liament for the drat time, is the Exst new member returned to St. Stepheu'e since the recent general election. His re- turn on the present occasion makes no difference in the political balance of parties. It has been calculated that the Liberals lost fully fifty votes in consequence of the Eaelestown Railway Waggon Works three days' excursion to• London having been fixed for last Saturday. About 400 people took tickets extending to Monday night, and although urgent appeals were issaed to them to return in time to vote, the loss indicated is re- garded as a.very moderate estimate. Out of a total poll of 7,417, only about a score of voting papers are stated to have been spoiled. Many more are said to have been irregularly marked, (Jut where the intention of the voter was dia. ce,nible the vote was allowed to the muta.,ll satisfaction of , all partiea.

The weather being ehowery the children assembled la the chapel for tea; after which they spent a very enjoyable evening in the field kindly lent by Mr. aichardson. Aboat 100 prizes were given away for racing, &c. In the course of the even- ing the paety collected round a table. an which was spread a very handsome china tea set, which was than presented by the Rev. div.p: MARRIAGE OF A WIDNES SOLICITOR. A marriage which excited much interest in Widnes and neighbourhood, and attracted a large number of spectators, was solemnised at Farnworth Parish Church on Tuesday morning. The bridegroom was Mr. John Wright Knowles, of Myddleton, Winwick, near Warrington, who practices as a solicitor at Widnes, and the bride was Miss Annie Johnson, second daughter of the late Mr. Thomas Johnson, of Heath House, Bold. Long before the time fixed for thr ceremony to take place, eleven o'clock, a good conaTegation occupied the sacred edifice, and the wedding guests were viewed with eager and friendly ' interest as they arrived and took their places near the chancel. Their names arc Mr. and Mrs. Cooke (St. Helens), Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Johnson, Mr. and Mrs. Longton, Miss Longton, Mr. and Mrs. Lowe, Mr. James Cook, Mr. awd Mrs. Fairhurst (Warring. ton), Mr, and Mrs. William Johnson, Miss Fairhurst, Miss Lowe Longton, Mr. D. McKechnie (St. Helens), Miss Kate Johnson, Mis John Johnson, and Mr. and Mrs. T. Glover (Runcorn). The bride walked up the centre aisle leaning upon the arm of her brother, Mr. William Henry Johnson, and accompanied by her sisters, Miss Johnson, Miss Maggie and Miss Maude Johnson, the bridesmaids. The bride was attired in a beautiful dress .of ivory satin dushass, with pearl front drapery. and her head was adorned with a wreath of myrtle and orange blossoms, while her features were screened with a long white tulle veil. In her hand, the wrist of which was adorned with a gold bracelet, set with diamonds; the gift of the bridegroom, she carried a large bouquet of choice exotics. Miss Johnson, a bridesmaid, wore a dress of coral satin, trimmed with lace, while Miss Maggie and Miss Maude were attired in pink delaine, trimmed with lace. Rich wore a hat trimmed with cream lace and roses, and carried baskets of pink roses and stephanotis. The bride• groom had presented each with a gold bracelet. The service was full choral, the vocal harmony being dis coursed by the choir, under the leadership of Mr. Watts, and Mr. James Glover presided at the organ. The impressive ceremony was performed by the Rev. Geo. Bond, M A., vicar, and as the wedding party proceeded to the vestry to fulfil the formality of sign- ing the register, the organ played Mendelsohn's Wed- ding March. Rice was showered upon the happy couple as they left the church. Breakfast was served • at Heath Housea and in the afternoon Mr. and Mrs. , Knowles departed for London, where they intend to , spend the honeymoon. The presents were numerous and costly.

CHALLENGING i Docrou TO A DIIBL.—An extraordinary ease came before the Deputy Stipendiary of Liverpool, on Saturday. Franz Hoeffner was charged with threatening Dr. Burton, one of the honorary surgeons of the Women's Hospital Institutiol, who figured in a singular case at the recent assizes. The woman had been in the hospital, where a serious operation had been performed on her, and she had been discharged cured. Prisoner afterwards wrote to Dr. Burten, charging him with perpetrating outrages on women without hinting to their husbands what he was going to do. He described the doctor as a fiend who sacrificed the happi- ness of ' hundreds to an insane idea originating with Satan. Prisoner concluded by challenging Dr. Burton to a duel. Be did not wish to shoot him unawares, as he deserved. Prisoner admitted writing the letter, and said the doctor had ruined his wife, and life was not worth living. He was re- manded.

SOUTHPORT AND CHESHIRE LINES EXTENSION RAIL. WAY.—The report of the directors for the half-year ending June 30th, 1886, save :—The gross receipts are £5,986 12s as compared with £,232 Is 5d for the six months ending June 30th, 1885, showing an increase of £757 lOs 7d. The cold weather which lasted until late in the spring, and the counter attractions of the Liverpool Exhibition, combined with the depressed state of trade, largely diminished the number of visitors to Southport, and in consequence the traffic receipts have proportionately suffeed. £lB,OOO has been borrowed on mortgaie bonds at 4± per cent per annum, and has been chiefly applied towards paying off the Cheshire Lines Committee's bill for works, bearing interest at 5 per cent, per annum. In the past half-year several out- • standing obligations under the company's Acts of Parlia- ment have been satisfactorily settled, and every effort is being made to close the capital account. ROYAL VISIT TO EDINBURGH. Os Wednesday her Majesty paid her promised visit to the Exhibition at Edin- burgh, and received a most enthusiastic welcome during her progress from Holyrood Palace through the main thorough- fares of the city. Her Majesty was accompanied by Princess Beatrice and Prince Henry of Battenberg. lhe Duke and Duchess of Connaught arrived at the palace shortly before her Majesty. On their arrival at Edinburgh at eight o'clock the Royal visitors were met by the Lord Prevost. At the Exhibition the Qeeen was received by the Nlarquis of Lothian, the President of the Executive Com- mittee, the representatives of the Scratch municipalities, and a numerous gathering of the nobility and gentry. An ad- dress to the Queen WAS presented on her arrival at the Ex- hibition. In reply her Majesty expressed her deep sense of the loyalty and attachment ever manifested towards her by her Scottish subjects. Aker being conducted through the various departments of the Exhibition, the Queen returned to Holyrood. The railway companies carried into the city vast numbers of visitors. In the evening the city was brit.

liantly illuminated. ATTACK ON IRISH HARVESTMEN.—At Spalding Petty SeBSiADS on Tuesday four labourers named Samuel Brough- ton, David Broughton, Green, and ehurchin, aged from 18 to 25, were brought up in custody charged With inflicting grievious bodily harm upon Thomas Dukin, aged 50, har- vestman, from Sligo. It was stated that the complainant was lying in a critical condition at the Union Infirmal-y. His statement was handed in. He said that he had visited I:teping St. Nicholas annually for 30 years. On Sunday afternoon he and three fellow-countrymen were walking quietly along the road when the prisoners attacked them, commencinr, by knocking him down with a heavy blow en the head. His mates ran away. He crawled to a hay stack and hid himself. The prisoners came back and found him, and commenced kicking him about the head, face, and body until he became insensible. When diocovored Dukin was found to have several ribs broken, and he was other- wise injured on the face and body. Prisoners made no ne- wer to the charge, and it was decided to remand them for a week to see if the complainant was likely to be able to give evidence. Bail was asked for but refused. div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF

. GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Greening, Gibson, Jolley, Voisey, Woods, Heaton, Isherwood, Harrison, Balharry, W. Houghton John Houghton, Blackhurst, Clarke, Eckersley, 11:bbert, Humphreys, Wright, Granger, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk.) THE HOUSE COMMITTEE. This committee recommended the payment of an account from Mr. H. B. White for £3 108. The Clerk explained that this account would probably be the expenses of prose- cutions.—On the motion of Mr. VOISEY, seconded by Mr. CLARE, the minutes were confirmed. SCHOOLS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee stated that the superin- tendent had submitted a correspondence with the Local Government Board, received from the Clerk, in which it appeared the auditor had reported an omission and an error as follows—(I) folios of the relief lists omitted ; (2) error in the total days for the half-year. The books being now laid before the cignmittee duly amended the superintendent was instructed to check similar)sntries therein, until his assistant had had more experience of the work. The audi- tor having also complained of an order for 1131bs. of cheese when 1701bs. were already in stock, the duperintendent ex- plained that he found cheese to be more satisfying to the inmates, and to be more profitably out and distributed after it has been kept in stock. The committee, while entirely concurring with the auditor'e objection to the purchase of too large a stock of cheese, think the eXplanativa satisfac- tory.—The superintendent's report was read. The children were reported well, their health being exceedingly good.'-=' On the motion of the CHAIRMAI . seconded by Mr. Woons, the minutes were confirmed. SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE. This committee reported that school fees had been allowed in 120 cases. 87 of which were old and 34 new cases.—Mr. lianalsox moved, and MI. JOLLEY seconded, the adoption of the report.—ln reply to a question, Mr. HAR-' nrsow said he thought tiais was a vary large number of cases.—The CLERK said there was unquestionably an in- crease in the nun:o)er of the Wes. As far as fustian cutting was concerned, he thought they woeld feel the pressure during the eesuing winter.—Confirmed. THE WARRINGTON VACCINATION OFFICER. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, to- gether with an accompanying communication which the Local Government Board had recesved from Mr. George Holford, vaccination officer for the Warrington district, and the Guardians were asked if in their opinion the other duties of Mr. Holford would interfere with the regular and efficient performance of the work of a vaccination officer.— The letter of Mr. Elolford to the Local Government Board, which had been sent in reply to a communication asking him to either resign his employment as commercial traveller or the duties of vaccination officer. Mr. Holford explained that he was not a commercial traveller in the ordinary sense of the word; and the was out ef his district only two days in the week, and only for a few hours on each of these days. It also mentioned that he had now almost worked off all the arrears, and a letter from Dr. Gornall, medical officer, testified that Mr. Holford was performing his duties in a satisfactory manner.—Mr. BLACKHURsT thought that if the district was attended th in a preper manner they should not interfere with Mr. Holford on account of his other duties.—Mr. HARRISON said if Mr. Belford's description of his duties wad accurate they should hardly come to an ad- verse decision.—Mr. WOODS said he in a was position to say Mr. Hqlford's description of his duties was perfectly correct. —Mr. JOLLEY said they should also take into consideration the letter of Dr. Gornall.—lt was decided that the Clerk should write to the Local Government Board saying that the Guardians were disposed to advise them in this instance to continue Mr. Holford in his office, and that they hoped he would give no further occasion for their displeasure. DL SACK'S APPOINTMENT. A letter was read from the Local Government Board with regard to the recent appointment of Dr. Jack as a medical officer of the Unidn, and inquiring when Dr. Jack would take up his residence in the district to which he was ap- pointed. Having communicated with Dr. Jack, he (the clerk) bad received a letter from him stating that he had had a little difficulty in obtaining a suitable house in the district.—lt was agreed, on the motion of Mr. JOLLEY, sec- onded by Mr. VOIsItY, that Dr. Jack should be requested to remove into his district within three menthe. THE ALTERATION OE AN accourr. The Clerk read a letter from the Lecel Government Board adverting to his letter of the Bth ult, respecting an erasure and alteration made in an account for erg-cies sup- plied and work done by Mr. John Hedgcock, and transmit- ting to the Guardians an accompanying copy•of a commu- nication which the Board had received on the subject from Mr. G. Mackey, the master of the Workhouse.—The letter from Mr. Mackey to the Local Government Board, referred to above, stated that his explanation about the erasure in date of invoice was that he had an old inmate in his office named George Webster, who, seeing that the invoice bad not been tarnished until the week it was entered, altered the date, but as he was a very old man, and at times scarcely responsible, and since dead, be (Mr. Mackey) took all the blame sooner than say anything of hies, because he he knew he meant weli—Mr, Haasox said he did not think it was the first time in which bills had been altered and the Local Government Board had taken objection.—Mr. BLaczarrasr : I hope it will be the last.—Mr. firarroet said that in his experience it was a favourite practice of a late clerk in order to prevent the trouble of writing to the Local Government Board. He bad no doubt their present clerk had done that sort of thing. (Laughter.)—The CLERK: If you will exeuge me I will repudiate that soft impeachment. (Laughter.)—Mr. flawrorr: You will know they did it before your appointment. --- The CLERK: I don't know about if. Continuing, the Clerk said it was quite true that in the days Mr. Heaton referred to the auditors were not so strict as they are to-day, but he would be sorry to think that any of his predecessors did anything so wrong as that would be viewed in these days. He cer- tainly had no recollection of anyone making erasures in bills. —Mr. GRKENING was of the same opinion as the clerk.— Mr. HARRISON thought they would have to receive Mr. Heaton's statement cum gran. *ado. (Laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN said he did not see bow they could directly con- tradict Mr. Heaton, but he wished they eould.—After little farther conversation it was agreed that the following reply, drawn up by the clerk, should be seat to the .Local Government Board, viz. :—" The Guardians have sonsidered your letter of the 14th instant. They regret that when the auditor in January, and again in April last desired explana- tion of the eraanres and alterations of invoice it was With. , held from him. Until the admission entered ow the mi- nutes of the House Committee in July the auardians were also uninformed of what was then stated. Iu these circum- stances they feel themselves unable to assist your honour- able Board beyond giving you the original entry as it ap- peared on the minutes verbatim et literatim as follows s— " The Local Government Board's letter dated 25th June, 1886, was read. The master saiel seeing the account had not been rendered by Mr. HedgeoCk in time, made the alte- ration so as to save as he thought any trouble, but the work .had been done, and the money was due to Mr. Hedgcock." Mr. Mackey's statement that Webster was a very old man is quite correct. He was 78,and was certified by the Workhouse medical officer to have died of old age item to point out also that Webeter died on Dec. 25th, so that bad the Guardians known the circumstances in January they would have been in no better position to assist you than they are new. As regatds the appeal (against surcharge of account) by Mr. Brown, I am to remind your honourable Board that payment was directed by the whole Board then present, and that it was not aura long after such payment had been made that the above admission was made and entered on the commit- tee's minutes. The exercise of your equitable powers here- in is therefore solicited." THE WORKHOIrsit MASTER'S CHILDREN. In accordance with a request made at the p.evions meet- ing, the CLERK read a statement as to the maintenance of the workhouse master's (Mr. Mackey's) children, after which Mr. GIBSoN moved, and Mr. EltromaT seconded, that the re- port should be sent to the master, with a request that he should furnish the Board with a statement in accordance with it.

TEE GRAPPENHALL ELECTION PETITION. In answer to Mr. Harrison, the CLERK said he bad heard nothing of the result of this petition from the Local Govern- ment Board. In answer to Mr. Voisev, he said that if the two votes in question were declared invalid it would then be Mr. Woods' turn to appeal.—Mr. EIAHRISON They might carry it to the House of Lords. (Laughter.) PRESTWICH ASYLUM. The Caen:max mentioned that the Clerk, Mr. Jolley, and himself had since their last meeting visited Prestwich luna- tic asylum. They found everything in apple•pie order, and the only thing that struck hint was that there should be a public road through the middle of the institution. He won- dered how they managed to keep the lunatic., inside, and he was not surprised to see from the papers that since their visit a lunatic had escaped from the place. It was a very large institution, and the doctor who took them round said it was the second largest in the kingdom. There were about 2000 inmates at the time of their visit. The relid cases were then proceeded with.

div.head: M. VALLANCEY.
div.p: M. VALLANCEY.
FREETRADERS AND RAILWAY RITES.

Sir,—lf I were asked to point out a man who is superior to the vagaries and prejudices of other men, I could not but point to a real sincere and convinced Freetrader. Such a man, in matters of trade and commerce of coarse, is troubled with no qualms and pestered with no doubts. He is the follower of immutable principle, and he decines problems which perplex and embarrass other people as the tailor decides the measurement of a piece of cloth—he uses his principles as the tailor uses his yard wand, and that which bears the test he accepts, and that which does not he rejects. Yet, so infirm is human nature even at its beet, that the Freetrader is not always without his lapses ; he at times descends as it were from his high pedestal and acts as inconsistently with his principles as if he were only an ordinary individual. With regard to rail- way rates, for instance, it is not, uncommon to heir an avowed Freetrader abuse the foreigner, or rather—for he never descends so low as to abuse the foreigner—abuse his own countrymen for allowing foreigners to send their goods into England at a cheaper rate than they allow Englishmen to send their goods out of the country. Now, sir, the office of pointing out when a good man makes a slip, is a somewhat odicees one, but really this is rank heresy. Freetrade doctrine lays it down as an inexorable law that the foreigner's goods which come to England must be paid for by the English goods which go to the foreign& and in no other way. Therefore the cheaper the foreign commodity is got into the• English mar- ket the be•ter.it is for Englishmen, because the more of it is to be got for a given quantity of English commodity. The very best thing that could happen from the Freetrade point 'of view would be the entire annihilation of all cost of car- riage of foreign goods sent to England, because the less we would have to give for them. It is not at all material from the same point of view how heavy the cost of carriage on Enelish goods sent to the foreigner may be, because it is the foreigner that will have V, pay the whole cost. If, for example a certain commodity is worth one pound when sent from an English factory on its journey to France, and the cost of transit thither adds another pound to the price, the Frenchmen will have to give two pounds' worth of silk or wine, or something else in exchoge. Now if that two pounds' worth of silk or wine, or whatever else it might be, could be conveyed to England entirely free of cost we might enjoy it here at an expense of only two pounds; whereas if the cost of carriage were at the same rate as that of the outgoing material the price in England would be doubled, and we would have to pay four poends. It le, therefore, a perfectly obvious deduction from the Free- trade doctrine that imports are paid for with exports, when it is said that preferential rates of railway companies to im- ports are a benefit to tile community. That people who are proud to be called Freetraders should think otherwise only goes to show, as I have said, how difficult it is for even the best of men to always take as their guide the fixed star of principle instead of the of popular prejudice which is constantly misleading inferior personages. HODGE.

div.head: CANCER IN THE TONGUE.
div.p: CANCER IN THE TONGUE.

Sir,—Havirg seen your issue of the 6th of May, 1886, Yefiich contains a letter by the Rev. J. H. Guy, describing my case of cure from cancer in the tongue, will you kindly allow me just a short space in your valuable paper to add a line or two by way of testifying that it is a thorough genuine case ? I have the greatest satisfaction in express- ing—indeed I deem it my bounden duty to express—my high approval of Dr. Turnbull's skilful treatment, also of his most gentle and humane demeanour towards me. He seems in hearty sympathy with his work, and too much cannot he said for his medical ability.. Previous to hearing of Dr. Deunie Turnbull, of No. 1, I;Voodside, Sunderland, I had been under the care of two medical men practising in this neighbourhood. Both of therm treated my tongue with- out lotting me know what the disease was from which I wee suffering. Each of them applied severe caustics to the disease, and notwithstanding all the burning process, which I endured moat patiently, my poor tongue rapidly got much worse. Indeed, my tongue was so badly swollen and frightfully hard that it was with great diffi- culty I could swallow any kind of food. There was also a constant discharge of nasty corruption flowing from the , ulcers in the tongue, which troubled me greatly, and, as for talking. it pained me so much that I was obliged to keep myself as quiet as possible. At this stage my doctors told roe it was necessary that the diseased portion must be cut out; and no doubt more than one half of my tongue would have gone had I submitted to such a fearful opera- tion. Happily for me, just at this time, when I feared all hope of saying my tongue was gone, a friend advised me to try what Dr. Turnbull could do for me before yielding to the Imife. On the 7th day of September, 1885, f made my way to consult Dr. Turnbull. As soon as Dr. Turnbull looked at my tongue he told me it was a fearful cancer that I was suffering from. I asked him if it could be cured- He said he would not like to promise me a perfect cnre. Neverthelers, be said lie would do his best far me if f deceled to place myself under hiscare. After inquiring about the charge for treatment, I found my circumstances would not permit of me entering ripen i ;, however, I took courage and fully explained my circumstances to the doctor; and, after Winking over my affairs for a while, he (the doctor) most kindly undertook my sad case, saying at the ; same lime that be would do his utmost for me, provided I faithfully carried out all his inetructions.l tenet not forget to add here, though I was under treatment nearly five months, , I Only lest about two days' work, and my work, being a plumber, ie pretty laborious at all times. Such a statement 55 this, of my own personal experience, I think is fully cal- cnlated to set forth the great value of Dr. Turnbull's method

Zetter to the gditor. THE SUTTON CHURCH DIFFERENCES. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me in your paper to contra- dict a statement just come to my knowledge, and other reports totally without foundation. The Vicar of Sutton has never received £lOO per year, nor a pound from the curate's fund, nor any other fund to pay his curates, whose stipends have always been £150; his present curate's £2OO. It is also decidedly untrue, and as absurd as false, that the vicar tried to mortgage his living; `• only an idiot could spread such a report." It is just as incorrect that he bor- rowed money for his late demands. All his want!, and very many pressing wants in his parishes, have been sup• plied by his mother's money, his fellowship in King's Col- lege, Cambridge, and his livings; his present one so exaggerated by our parish reporter, who has published so many wilful mistakes. Some deep motives mast have prompted such untruthful reports; of course it was quite plain to all ; the motive, and satisfactory results of those misrepresentations, insinuations, and untruths published by our Sutton reporter last October. Had my position allowed me, for the old vicar's sake, his family's, and some others, I certainly should have had proper proof to every report then circulated. Some of those reports "even had they been true," no gentleman would have allowed any one to circulate for his benefit. One of the vicar's old parishioners expressed the wish of many to contradict publicly those reports. The vicar was wiser to take no notice of them; deceit and untruth were sure to work their own ruin, but truth will stand firm to the end. I regret to say it had to be acknowledged to many lately that underhand deceit and untruth have crept into parish and church within the last year or two, and great excitement, which pleases the most part for a time, but soon tire of it, and feel a want of something, as was expressed by one lately. A lady some time ago left her own parish church because it was too quiet, and took seats in another more lively, although she said it was far, very far, from her idea of what the house of God should be. Does that lady go there to pray? or only to say she goes to church? I know it is so with many in this parish; better follow my example, no go at all.— I am, sir. Sutton Vicarage, St. Helens.

div.head: WILLIAM E. EARL.
div.p: WILLIAM E. EARL.
COMPULSORY VACCINATION.

Sir,—l oh-Serve, in your issue for Saturday week, the re- port of the vaccination debate, at a recent meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians. I also observe a letter signed " Justice," which letter refers in somewhat harsh terms—to say the least—to certain persons at Earlestown who object to incur the ghastly risks implied by inflicting the operation called vaccination upon their helpless children ; These persons claim their parental and God given right to use their own discretion as to the treatment of their children with reference to vaccination, and very properly so too. As I have the honour of being the individual who squeezed the now notorious "Evesham letter," on the subject of vaccina- tion prosecutions, out of the Local Government Board, will you kindly permit me to make a few observations as to vac- cination? And first, I would ask your correspondent, "Jus- tice,' what it is he is so desirous to force, by the terrors of an unconstitutional and abominable law, upon the accept- ance of these Earlestown parents? He himself does not know what! What is vaccination? Let me tell those of your readers who have not as yet given the subject any conside- ration what it is! It is the forcing of poisonous matter in- to the blood and system of the individual submitted to the operation! What the result of this operation may be no medical man can possibly tell ! The matter thus empleyed is entirely corrupt end loathsome; but lest the people, up- on whom it is forced by an abominable law, should be dis- gusted and alarmed by its true name, it is called " pure lymph." Now there are three sorts of this filthy abomina- tion. First, there is "humanized lymph," originated God knows how! but declared by the immortal quack, Jenner, to have been obtained from the gseasy-heeled diseased horse. This " lymph " has been used in the human subject for some eighty years. collecting in its course from arm to arm, the germs of various dreadful diseases, etuch as syphvlie, cancer and consumption; this " lymph " has beer con- demned for some length of time. Secondly there is "vario- lone lymph." This particular kind has been obtained by inoculation of the cow with small-pox matter. This "lymph" has been very extensively used all over the kingdom, and has been the means of inoculating vast numbers of the peo- ple with nothing less than small-pox. Then there is the brand new much-vanntad "pure calf - lymph." This "lymph," which is supplied by the Government authori- ties, was originally obtained -- so I have been recently informed by the Local Governinet Board—from a case of spontaneous cow-pox which was discovered at a farm in the village of Safor4t, near Bordeaux. But are not the ox and the cow a vast theatre of pestilences and diseases ? Cattle plague. rimierpest, and steppe•murrain, are words of terrible import. Foot-and-mouth disease is not a pleasant thought in connection with vaccination. Moreover, the "immortal Jenner " declared that vaccination from spon- taneous cow-pox was of no usa as a protection against small-pox. Under these satisfactory circumstances I advise the Earl estown objectors to vaccination to stick to their colours," and to persevere in their refusal of vaccination at all costs. I advise your correspondent. "Justice," to procure and study the parliamentary return No. 433, published in 1877, entitled "Vaccination mortality," which shows that some twenty-six thousand children are fatally injured every year by diseases induced or excited by vaccination. He may also find from the Regis- trar General's reports for the past three years, that during at period 179 deaths were caused by vaccination. The report of the medical officer of the Local Government Board or 1884, on vaccination, shows that 55 children died from

the effects of the operation during that year. This report also shows that of 1,243 persona who died in London alone, from small-pox, during the year, 727 were vaccinated. Sta- tistics and facts—yes, facts, Mr. Editor—have abundantly proved vaccination to be an utter delusion, and a very dan- gerous experiment. The law will have to be repealed at no distant date.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, • RENCH HENSLEY. Ivy Bank, Broadway, Worces ers It e, August, 1336.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The nominatien for King's Lynn has been fixed for the 24th inst, and the polling for the day following. CRICKET. The Aunt/alian innings against Wvatts' eleven closed for 236. Wyatts, in second innings, ma4e 55 without losing a wicket. The polling at Leith, on Friday, took place with very little excitement. The counting of the votes commences this (SaturdayYmorning at nine o'clock. FATAL WRESTLING MATCH.—On Friday morning, at Leigh, Edward Mather was remanded on a charge of caus- ing the death of James Oran, at Lowton. The young men left a beerhouse at closing time on Wednesday night, and went down the lane and wrestled for two shillings. , Oran was thrown heavdy, re ceiving injury to his back and died on Thursday night. BLACKPOOL ELECTION—The poll in connection with Blackpool Division election opened on Friday morning. The Conservatives assert that the voting for Sir M. White Ridley far exceeds their expectations, and that the Conser- vative majority will be very large. It is said that a con- siderable proportion of the voters on the register, [ principally Liberals, will abstain from exercising their franchise. The result will be made known about noon to- day. COLLISION AT SE4.-9. double collision occurred off the Yorkshire coast during a dense fog on Thursday night. The steamship Cato, of Shields. ran down a vessel on her way from Hull to the Tyne, but all of the crew were saved. Shortly afterwards the steamship Lebanon from the Tyne to Huelva, ran into the Cato, injuring her so severely that she in her turn foundered. Both the crews on board were fortunately saved, and landed at Sunderland on Friday afternoon. A TowN HALL oN FlRE.—Carlisle Town Hall narrowly escape 4 being burned down late on Thursday night. A fire broke out in the clock tower, causing great excitement. The fire engines were soon on the spor, and the flames, which had broken through the tower and bad shot six or seven feet into the air, were subdued before extensive dam- age was done. Near midnight the fire again broke out, but was extinguished in a short time. A special watch was kept until this morning. THE QUEEN IN EDINBURGH.—The Queen, accompanied by the Duke and Duchess of Connaught, visited the Royal Blind Asyluii/ and School at Craigmillan, Edinburgh. yester- day forenoon; and was greeted with great enthusiasm. She afterwards witnessed some exhibitions of manipulative skill by the blind worlxpeople. and she was presented with a boaquet by a little blind girl. The Queen, after express- ing her interest and satisfaction at all she saw and beard at the Blind Asylum, re-entered her carriage and drove WO the city to visit St. Giles's Cathedral. In passing up High- street, the centre of the old town of Edinburgh, she was cheered by many thousands of the working classes who re- side in and about it.

div.p: IRISH CONVENTION IN AMERICA.

At the meeting on Thursday in Chicago of the Conven- tion of the Irish National League, Mr. Fitzgerald was elec- ted permanent chairman. Resolutions were afterwards passed approving the course pursued by Mr. Parnell and his Parliamentary associates in the House of Commons, and thanking Mr. Gladstone for his great efforts on behalf of self-government for Ireland._ _ _

div.head: CONDITION OF BELFAST.
div.p: CONDITION OF BELFAST.

At Belfast, on Thursday, the nine memhers of the Royal Irish Constabulary against whom a warrant had been issued by the Council on Wednesday. for the wilful murder of a man named Jackson, who was shot in the street. were taken into custody and lodged in gaol. A Belfast correspondent telegraphed on Friday morning: The peace of the town is still maintained, everything being per- fectly quiet. The strength of the military and police is still maintained without reduction, but some relaxation is allowed to the men.
It is reported that irritation prevails in Belfast ameng Protestants at Lord Rinclolph Churchill's defence of the constabulary. His impressions, they allege, are based upon constabulary reports.

div.head: AMERICAN ANARCHISTS.
div.p: THE AMERICAN ANARCHISTS.
CHICAGO, FRIDAY.—Seven of the Anarchists conn sd with the bomb conspiracy have been sentenced to death, and another has been sentenced to fifteen years' penal ser- vitude.
LOSS OF A TEA-LADEN STEAMER.

ODESSA, FRlDAY.—lntelligence received here reports that the British steamer Aberdeen, with 5,500 tons of tea, bound from Hankow. for London, foundered when leaving the China Sea. The fate of her crew is not known.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.---FRin&y.

The Speaker took the chair shortly before four, there being a very full attendance on both sides of the House. LEASEHOLDERS.—Mr. NOLAN gave notice that on an early day he should move that it was desirable to give leaseholders facilities for purchasing the fee simple of their noldinP.:s.

PnocEnunE.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, In reply to Mr. Morris, said it would be desirabie early next session to proceed with the consideration of the reforms in procedure of the House, but he could give no definite promise on the subject, as it might embarrass the Govern- ment.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT.—RepIving to Sir W. Lawson. the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHFWER said he could not pledge himself to contents of the Local Government Bill to be brought in next session. No doubt ic would deal with the licensing question. _ _

THE BUSINESS or THE SESSION.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, replying to Mr. Labouchere, said it was de- sired to confine the business of the present session to finan- cial matters, and it would he inconvenient to mix it up with bills of private members. Under those circumstances no- tice of opposition on the part of the Government would be given to all such hills and notices. That step was taken in view of the convenience of all pinata members and nothing else.

TIIE BELFAST RIOTS, &C.-Sir M. BEAC' H' reply.ing to Mr. Sexton, was not able to give the names of the two new Commissioners to inquire into the Belfast riots. The in- quiry would extend to the or:g.in of the riots, and the con- duct of magistrates.—Mr. BIGGAR moved a new writ for Sligo in room of Mr. Sexton, who had been returned for that place and West Belfast; but the Speaker declined to put questions, as a petition had been presented against the return of the hon. member for West Belfast. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.

The adjourned debate on the Addres was resumed by Mr. T P O'CoNNon,who, referring to the Belfast riots, contended that the speeches of the Chancellor of the Exchequer in Ulster were the real origin of those lamentable proceedin:rs. It was said that the proposed inouiry into these riots would include an inquiry into the action of the National Lague, but if that was so an inquiry into the transaction of the Primrose League ought in fairness to be made. He believed that the Royal Commission to inquire into the development of Oe natural resources of Ireland would lead to no practical good.—Sir W. HARCOURT contended that the speech of the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer was wanting in definiteness and precision, and he tack particular objection to the declaration of the noble lord that the question of the restoration of social order was to he kept distinct and treated by itself. That was the prin- ciple of Lords Eldon, Castlereagh, and Sidmouth. It was the fundamental policy of the Tory par. y, hut to that the party with which he was associated was totally opposed, and the Government might rest assured that until they satisfied the national sentiment in Ireland all offsets to res- tore social order would fail. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 21, 188(1
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 21, 188(1

FAILURE AT ST. HELENS.—On Monday, at the Liver- I pool Bankruptcy Court, Mr. Registrar Bet ringer granted al receiving order against John Mather, of 50, Liverpool-road, St. Helens, fishdealer. The order was made upon the pe- ' tition of the debtor himself, for whom Mr. J. Massey ap- peared. The public examination was fixed for August 30, at eleven o'clock, at the Liverpool County Court. LOCAL BUILDERS FINED.—At the Town Hall, oni Monday, before Dr. E. P. Twyford and Mr. A. Sinclair, I Messrs. Hugh Roberts and Griff Jones, builders, residing in Lewrenson-terrace, Boundary-road, were summoned at the instance of the St. Helens Corporation for an offence under the by-laws, viz., "commencing to erect buildings without giving notice to the borough surveyor," and they were fur-1 I ther charged with erecting buildings without giving the re- quired notice. The defendants were unrepresented. while 1 Mr. J. O. Swift prosecuted on behalf of the Corporation. ! Mr. Swift stated that the by-laws required notice to be given to the surveyor, and plans to be submitted of new buildings before their erection was commenced. In April last Mr. assistant-surveyor, was in Gladstone-street, and saw defendants erecting six houses for which no notice or plans had been received. A short time afterwards one of the de- fendants called at the borough surveyor's office and said they were going to send in plans, which came in on the nth April, and wereapproved. Some time afterwards the defen- dant, sent notice of their intention to erect other houses, and altogether fourteen houses were commenced, but plans were only rticeived for twelve houses.—Mr. Bell, assistant surveyor, and Mr. G. J. C. Broom, borough surveyor, gave evidence to the foregoing effect, and the Bench inflicted a ins of 40s and costs in one case, Mr. Swift withdrawing one of the charges. A HORSE TRANSACTION.—At the St. Helens County Court, on Saturday, an adjourned case, in which Elijah Mowe, of St. Helens, sued Henry Ireland, of Huyton, for £25 damages for breach of warranty and misrepresentation of the qualities of a horse, was resumed before Judge Thompson and a jury. Mr. T. Swift, barrister (instructed by Messrs. J. 0. and W. Swift). represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Stewart, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. Gorst, of Liverpool), appeared for the defendant. The ex- amination of plaintiff's witnesses was continued, after which Mr. Stewart said the question to be decided was whether there was a warranty, and if there was a warranty*, had there been a breach of it.—Mr. Swift afterwards ad- dressed the jury, and urged that Mr. Ireland's warranty had been broken, and therefore Mr. Mowe was entitled to the damages which he sought to recover at their hands. There could be no doubt that at the time the horse was sold to Mr Moen it was fit for nothing at all, and in getting £25 for it Mr. Ireland had deceived Mr. Mowe, who was entitled to recover.—His Honour said a commendation of goods did not amount to a warranty. The case did not rest upon whether these was a warranty or whether there was simply a commendation of the horse. The plaintiff said that what the defendant said to him was a misrepresentation, wilfully, and knowingly made, and if a bargain was made in conse- quence of that misrepresentation, then the purchaser was at liberty to recover damages which resulted from, him being misled, owing to the misrepresentation.—The jury retired to consider their verdict, and afte'r a few minutes absence eeturned, and declared that they found tor the plaintiff, for the full amonnt of the claire.—His Honour then gave judg- ment for the plaintiff for £25, costs being allowed. SINGULAR CLAIM AGAINST A SON-DT-LAW.—At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge. a Mrs. Fillingham brought an action against her son-in-law, a young man named Barton, under somewhat singular circumstances. Mr. Peters, of Widnes, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. 0. Swift for the de- fendant. From the statement of Mr. Peters, it appeared that a great part of the claim related to expenses incurred by the plaintiff during the sickness of defendent's wife (plain- tiff's daughter), and her subsequent burial. Defendant mar- ried plaintiff's daughter about a year ago, and a short tune ago, in consequence of Mrs. Barton's illness, they went to live with Mrs. Fillingham. Mrs. Barton was confined on the 16th May and died on the 30th May, and the claim related to the expenses then incurred.—Mrs. Fillingham then gave evidence, and said she had lent sums of money to the de- fendant, and she defrayed the expenses of the funeral and the medical charges. Prior to her illness and death her daughter (defendant's wife) had been a mem- ber of the Salvation Army, and the defendant in- vited the members of the 'army to the funeral. In reply to Mr. Swift, plaintiff said she did not tell defendant that it was her daughter's wish the army should be invited. The claim included items for lodging, washing, money lent, and miscellaneous expenses. For the defence, Mr. Swift said his client was willing to do what anybody considered fair and just. The plaintiff had keet no proper account and nothing was said about the matter until eight or nine weeks after the funeral. Nothing was ever said about pay- ing either for the lodging of himself or baby, but the de- fendant had offered a sum of £5 in cash, on condition that the furniture he had removed to plaintiff's house was re- turned. After a somewhat lengthy hearing, His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff tar -£5, ordered defendant's furniture to be returned by the plaintiff, and each party to bear their own costs.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. MILES DICKINSON.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. MILES DICKINSON.

The many friends associated with the Primitive Metho- dist connexion, and other denominations, resident in St. Helens and Earlestown, will be pleased to hear of an inter- esting presentation to the Rev. Miles Dickinson, of St. Helens, and formerly of Earlestown. After 42 years of ministerial life, the Rev. Miles Dickinson has been super- annuated, and t},e Liverpool District meeting, held at Birkenhead in May last, decided to honour the event by a fitting testimony to the efficient services rendered by that reverend gentleman. The presentation took place on Fri- day last at Liverpool in tile presence of a large number of ministers and other friends. After devotional exercises, Mr John Jones, of Chester, took the chair, and referred in eulogistic terms to Mr. Dickinson's life and labour.—The Rev. J. Travis (president), then presented to the Rev. Miles Dickinson a splendidly illuminated ad- dress enclosed in a massive gilt frame. Addresses were also given by the Revs. J. Mould, W. Gra- ham, J. Jackson, T. Swallow, Councillor Vaughan, and Mr. Corfield. The Rev. M. Dickinson, in responding, sincerely thanked all the brethren for their kind expressions and senti- ments. He observed that he had, after ally only done his duty to God and the Church of his early choice. Their good will and esteem he highly prized, for after so many years of ministerial life it was no small honour to feel that he was neither forsaken by God nor abandoned by his brethren. (Applause.) The proceedings then concluded.

div.head: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION.
div.p: VOLUNTEER INSPECTION.

The annual inspection of the 2nd L.E.V. (St. Helens) took place in Grange Park, Eccleston, on Saturday after- noon, the inspecting officer being Colonel G. W. Stockley, C.R•E. (York). The weather was extremely fine, and there was a large number of spectators. Out of a total strength of 560, there were 475 men on parade. Among the officers present were Colonel Bothwell, Lieut,ColOnel Wilcock, Captains Coode (adjutant), Duffy, and Pendlebury, Lieuts. Lyon, H. Bothwell. J. Bothwell, Brooker, and Gaudy, and Surgeon Hall. Arrived at the field, the battalion was put through a variety of evolutions lasting upwards of an hour. The men were drawn up in column and advanced by the in- specting officer. He afterwards addressed them, and said this was the sixth regiment of engineer Volunteers that he had seen during the past two months, and he was able to compare them with other battalions of the same branch of the service he had seen. There were a leY7 in the ranks who did not come up to the standard of the rest of the men. He fancied these men did not attend practice regularly and consequently on an occas;on like the present they spoiled the appearance of the detach- ment. He was glad to see so large a proportion of profi- ciente, and that some more only had a few drills to put in. But they all ought to be proficient when the inspecting officer came to see them, and he wished them to make an effort to become proficient. He did not want to see men coming out for the first time and spoiling the look of the battalion. He spotted a lot of such, some in each company. He did not want to see that again—it was not fair to the refit of them. He knew it was not easy for them to have battalion parade, when only 100 turned up as a rule, and consequently it was very difficult for them to move in large bodies when they were not accus- tomed to it; but if they went into camp it would do a great deal of good, besides giving them more practice in engineering work. He noticed a falling off in the modelling, there being this year only one model, whereas in former years there were several. He hoped they would have a little rifle practice. They had not a very good range. but still they had range which was handy, rend besides for the past two years they had had a very good rifle. On the whole he thought their appearance was very satisfactory and creditable. A great deal of credit was due to their colonel for his long services and for the strangtn and efficiency of the corps through his efforts. The corps was thee marched back to the drill ball, where the men dis- persed. In the course of the past few months earthworks have been constructed in the drill field, which have been , the practical outcome of a series of lectures delivered by the adjutant (Captain Goode) who was assisted by ergeant- Major Burns.

div.head: SHOCKING NEGLECT BY A MOTHER.
div.p: SHOCKING NEGLECT BY A MOTHER.

Mr. Brighouse; coroner, held an inquest at the Inn, Pocket Nook, on Fri-lay, on the body of Thomas Keenay, seven months old, son of James Keereay, 5, Barber- street.—The Coroner, in opening the inquiry, said it ap- peared from the police report that on Wedueeday Mrs. Keeney, who was a charwoman, went to the Legs of Mau beerhouse with the deceased. During the afternoon she was left in charge of the house for a short time, and when Mr. and Mrs. Owen, the occupiers, came back they found her in a helpless state of drunkenness. On going upstairs they found the child covered over with the bedclothes and al- most dead.—James Keenay, the father, then gave evidence of identification.—Mrs. Ann Owen stated that about eight o'clock on Wednesday morning Mrs. Keeney came to their house to wash and clean. She brought the child with her. About half-past two she fed the child, and then took it to bed. Witness saw it lyi.ng on its back, with its head on the pillow, covered over with a blanket, all right. She went out, leaving Mrs. Keeney, deceased, and two of her own children in the house. On returning at a quarter-past five she was met by her child, who said Mrs. Keenay was drunk again, and had gone home. Witness went to her house, and found her lying on the bed. She was drunk. On re- turning to her own house her husband asked her where Mrs. Keenay's child was. She sen.t her daughter upstairs, as she was busy. The child ran down again, and said "There is something under the clothes, but I cannot see its face." Witness went up, and found the child had worked itself down in the bed, and was rieht under the blanket. Its feet were cold, and it seemed to be taking its last breath. She fetched Mrs. Barn!" a Deighbour, and. they bathed its lips

with brandy and warmed its feet, and it seemed better. Later in the evening Mr. Mackonochie, assistant to Dr. Casey, was sent for, and he prescribed for it. At a quarter- , past eleven, Mrs. Keenay, who had recovered, came for it and took it home, but it died shortly afterwaid,.—Mrs. Keenay (who was present) emphatically protested that she i was not drunk, but only excited by some lads playing at the laack gate.—Mrs. Owen (witness) added that Mrs. Keenay bad previously appeared to care for her child.—Mr. Mackonochie (assistant to Dr. Casey) said he was called to the child about ten minutes to eight o'clock. It was almost completely collapsed, and he did not think it,would recover. It had previously suffered from croup and bronchitis, and had diseased lungs. There were no signs of suffocation as a primary cause of death. It ought to have bad medi- cal attendance there or four days prior to its death. He thought death was due to natural causes, but whether ac- celei ated by neglect he could not say positively. The child might have lived if it had had medical treatment pre- viously.—Alice Owen, ten years of age, who was left in the house, said Mrs. Keeney drew a quart of beer, and sold a pennyworth to a man. Witness believed she drank most of what was left. Her father came home first, and finding Mrs. Keenay drunk, sent her home.—The Coroner said the questions were—did the jury think they were justified in saying that the child died from natural causes, or in return- ing an open verdict, or saying that death had been caused by the negligence of the mother? He thought they were all agreed that Mrs. Keeney was in an undoubted state of intoxication, for which she was to be blamed. But they had to deal with the legal aspect of the case. On the evi- ' dence he did not think they could say with preciseness that she omitted or committed anything that had caueed death. —The jury were of opinion that death was due to natural causes, but that Mrs. Keenay was deserving of censure.— Mrs. Keenay was then called into the room, and repri- manded by the Coroner.

div.head: FRO DSHAM.
div.p: FRO DSHAM.

SHOCKING OccunapecE.—Mr. Henry Churton, coroner for West Chesi+ire, has held an inquest touching the death of Martin Logan, a private in the 6th Royal Lancashire Regi- ment. Mr. Fenna watched the case on behalf of the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company, and Mr. W. H. Linaker represented the inhabitants of Frodsham. From the evidence of the sergeant (who was in charge of the de- ceased) and tbe stationmaster, it transpired that Logan was being escorted back to Buxton from Chester, where he had been undergoing a term of imprisonment at the military prison. They travelled via Manchester, and on the train stepping at Frodsham station, Logan alighted. Before he regained his carriage the train was in motion, and in spite of the warn- ing of the stationmaster, he attempted to enter a carriage, but being prevented by an occupant he endeavoured to enter another compartment. In doing al he fell between the footboard of a coach and the platform. He was rolled over and then he fell on the metals, several wheels passing over his legs. When picked up his body was terribly mutilated. The injured man was removed to the waitiag-room, and every means were used to save his life, but be expired in anout a quarter of as hour, and before the arrival of the doctor. The jury expressed their dissatisfaction that no independent testimony was forthcoming. After a consulta- tion they found that the deceased met his death accident- ally, and added to their verdict the following rider—" That in the opinion of the jury the railway companies are open to censure in not having provided better platform and ether accommodation for the travelling public." The Coroner declined to accept the rider on the groand that it would stultify the verdict. There was a strong feeling of indig- nation on the part of the jury at the conduct of the coroner.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

FALSE PEETENCES.—Yesterday, at the Petty Sessions. John Burns, a young man, was charged with obtaining 9s 9d and two glasses of beer from Alice Gosling, of the Wheat sheaf Inn, by false pretences, on the 15th August.— Mr. Jenkins defended. Burns was alleged to have tendered a sham coin as a half-sovereign, for whieh he received two glasses of beer and 9s 9.1 in change. The defence was that the coin belonged to a friend, and that Burns had no bad intention.—He was c, mrnitted for trial to the Quarter Ses- sions.

div.head: COMPLAINT OF SUNDAY ROWDYISM.
div.p: COMPLAINT OF SUNDAY ROWDYISM.

At the; Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday morning, the Rev.. Canon Guest, Mr. Brown, and Mr. Skißing attended the court as a deputation and submitted to the magistrates a pe- tition signed by 52 residents. The petition read as follows : —" We, the undersigned inhabitants of Lymm, desire to ran the attention of your worships to the disorderly state of the village on Sundays. Lymm has become increasingly a re- sort of pleasure parties on the Sabbath. The arrival and departure of these parties is not unfrequently signalised by the blowing of trumpets and other disgraceful and offensive noises, while many of the visitors, if not intoxicated when they arrive, become so soon afterwards, they having as travellers access to the public-houses. Language often foul and shocking is used in our streets, and can be, and is. heard into the houses of some of us. In brief, the quiet and order which should, and used ter, characterise the village on the Sabbath day is fast giving place to noise and rowdyism. We have no desire to interfere in the least degree with the legitimate pleasure and enjoyment of the people, but the evil concerning which we make complaint has of late grown to such proportions that we feel that some action must, if possible, be taken to abate it. And we respectfully submit that we are entitled to ask your worships to secure, so far as you are able, that persons who visit this village on the Sabbath shall conduct themselves with moderation and decency. It is not for us to indicate by what means this obj.ct may be best attained, but if we might be permitted to offer a suggestion it would be this: That the laws against drunkenness, and the public use of obscene language, be vigorously and rigorously enforced, whether against visi- tors or the occupiers of public-houses who supply them w;th drink to excess.—The Clerk said that the police would be able to take action in regard to drunkenness and ob- scene language.—The Bench expressed sympathy with the obj,ct of the deputation, and said that they would confer with the police authorities regarding the matter.—The de- putation then withdrew.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

Han rows CommTroN.—At the Town Hall, on Monday. before Dr. Twyford and Mr. A. Sinclair, Elizabeth Tither, a middle.aged woman, was brought up on a charge of indecency. The magistrates were informed it was the prisoner's 109th appearance, and she was fined 5s and costs. TRANsFER OF LICENSES.—At St. Helens Town Hall, yesterday, the magistrates (Dr. Twyford and Mr. Sinelaii) granted the following transfers of licenses :—George and Dragon, Bold-street, Eccleston, from James Lindray to Jas. Highet : Derby Arms, Liverpool-road, from William Pye to George Hay; Half-mile House. Park-rd., from Samuel Woods to Ann Woods; and a beerhouse at Clock Face, from Richard Hill to Elizabeth Peel. A "DOG Fluirr."—At the Police Court, on Monday, before Dr. Twytord and Mr. Sinclair, John Hart, residing le Tentine-street, was charged with causing two dogs to be cruelly ill-treated by causing them to fight on the Bth inst. Police-constable Massey stated that on the Sunday night in question he was on duty in Tontine-street, and his atten- eion was attracted to a crowd of people in a passage off Bridge-street. He found two dogs were fighting, and de- fendant was in the midst of the people, with his coat off, " hissing " the dogs on, clapping his hands, and shouting, "Go on, Dick." Witness pulled him on one side. Both dogs were bleeding. The defendant, who denied that he urged the dogs to fight, was fined is and costs. ASSAULT ON A WIFE —At the Town Halt, on Wed- nesday, Joseph McGowan, a young man, of Eccleston, was summoned before Mr. H. S. Hall, Mr. A. Sinclair, and Aid. erman T. Cook, for assaulting his wife, Jane.—The prosecu- trix stated that on Saturday afternoon her husband came home and demanded his dinner. She gave him it as soon as possible, and asked him for his wages, when he struck her in the eye and three times upon the head. He then went to the public-house. After a short absence he returned and gave her 155, and stnl later in the evening be gave her another ss. After he had been in the house a short time he wanted to take the 5s from her again, and when she would not let him he struck and kicked her severely, and threat- ened to take her life with a knife. She had not been at home since. Defendant was bound over to keep the peace. DROWNED /N THE CANAL, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Merton Bank Inn, Park-road, on Thursday, on the body of Thomas Johnson, four years of age, son of Robert Johnson, a collier, residing at 174. Merton Bank-ro td. From the evidence given by deceased's mother, llee Johnson, a girl named Sarah Jane Burchall and James Lyon, it appeared that on Tuesday afternoon deceased was playine near the canal belonging the London and North-Western Railway Company, and while on the " staving " timber of a ternbridge felt into the water. The canal was afterwards dragged and the body recovered. Several jurors considered the canal insufficiently fenced on the opposite side to the towing path, and in returning a ver- dict of "Accidental death "added a recommendation that the Railway Company should extend and improve the fencing. Mescurevons Bevs.—On Friday, at the Town Hall, before Mr. H. S. Hall, Mr. A. Sinclair, and Alderman T. Cook, a boy named William Henry Campbell was sum- moned fir doing wilful damage to growing plants, belong- ing to Mr. C. j. Bishop. J.P., Cowley-hill, on the previous Saturday night. The defendant was seen cutting horse radiehes, and also doing damage to a number of cabbages and cauliflowers. He did not carry any of them away, but simnlv cut them and threw them down.—Mr. Hall said be would be fined 2s 61 and costs, and ordered to pay 2s for damagPs. They would have inflicted a heavier fine had it not been for the excellent character which the boy had re- ceived from the headmaster of Cowley Schools.—Two little boys, named John Taylor and George Johnson, both of Sut- ton, were summoned for doing damage to a crop of beans growing at Parr. belonging to Mr. A. C. McMiken. They were eech fined is and costs. SUDDEN DEATH IN A CHEMICAL WOEKS.-011 Mon- day morning, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Victoria Inn, Pocket Nook, touching the death of Thady Carb,?y, fifty-six years of age, formerly lodging, at 2, Bar- , her's-court, Parr, who died suddenly on Friday night whilo working at the St. Helens Chemical Company's Works. Mr. Robert Perry .Ittendee the inquest on behalf of Messrs. Chadwick and Co., owners of the works. The evi- dence showed that the deceased had been in the Union Workhouse at Present for some weeks, suffering from an injured foot, and came out about a week ago. He was severely ill about five months ago, when he was spitting blood and vomiting. Lest week he was assisting a labourir named Harkins at the chemical works, and while engaged wheeling a barrow of lime he was noticed to fall as if in a fit. Assistance was obtained, but the eleceas:A expired in a few minutes. The jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes."

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL COMMITTEE MEETINGS.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL COMMITTEE MEETINGS.

FREE LIBRARY COAIMITTEE.—The monthly meeting of the Free Library Committee was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday forenoon, when there were present Mr. H. R. Lacey (in the chair), Alderman T. Cook, Councillor Green- ough, Dr_ McNicoll, Mr. G. Webster, Mr. B. A. Dromgoole„ and Messrs. A. Lancaster (librarian), J. H. Craik (deputy town clerk.),-The Librarian (Mr.. A. Lancaster) reported that during the past month 6,747 books had been borrowed from the lending department, an increase of 721 on the corresponding month last year; reference department 225„ decrease 110. The cash received during the month amoun- ted to .£5 Sc 61 The Sunday attendances in July were 513, average 128 2; same month, last year 427, average 1067. The total number of visits to the reading•roonis was, 14,144, daily average 5238. The question of sending a re- presentative of the committee to the annual conference of the Library Association, to be held in London during Sep- tember, was briefly discussed.—Alderman Cook thought the Council would consider such appointment an unnecessary expense, and no representative to the conference was ap- pointed.—This was the only business. HIGHWAYS AND PAVING COMBILTTEB —This committee met at the Town Hall, on Wednesday afternoon. Present— Councillors C. J. Bishop (in the chair), F. J. Brown, W. Berchall„ W. H. Foster, J. Lowe, W. Longton, and Messrs. G. J. C. Broom (borough surveyor), J. H. Craik (deputy town clerk), and J. Johnson (borough treasurer).—The Repairs of Streets: Councillor Brown asked the reason why Traverse-street was kept in an unfinished state. Some por- tion was unpaved and another portion paved, and it wag in a very unsatisfactory state for nearly half its length—The Surveyor replied that Ana owing to their inability at the moment to get setts of the required size.—The Steam Rbller : Councillor Broeen celled attention to the fact that the steam roller was not in good condition, and the Surveyor said the tank was rather leaky. He submitted an estimate for its repair, which amounted to £l2 10s.—Street Gullzes: Coun- cillor Brown complained of certain street gullies being choked up with dirt, and said he thought their clearing out was being neglected by the Corporation men—The Sur- veyor promised to attend to the matter.—A 'Vets " Waggoz: The committee resolved to purchase a tip waggon at a cost of £4B from Messrs. Glover and Son, Norwich. A discussion had taken place as to the desirability of inviting tenders from local tradesmen, i but t was pointed out that if this were done only a pound or two would be saved, and as the " tip " waggon proposed to be purchased was a patent one, the committee might not get one to equal it for convenience.—The Streets:- The sur- veyor (Mr. Broom) submitted a tabulated statement as o the relative cost and maintenance of paved and macadam- ised roads in various boroughs. In the schedule it was shown that there were in St. Helens 21 miles of paved streets, which cost 6s per yard, and 301 miles of macadam- ised roads, which cost 4s 24 per square yard. In a lengthy report upon the matter, the surveyor suggested tbat the committee should consider the advisability of having two classes of atieets, first and second class; one for heavy traffic and another for light traffic. The chairman said there was the question of convenience and safety of the inhabitants to be considered as well as the cost. There was no doubt that ioaving in St. Helens in past years had been badly done, and they must alter their course for the future.. The committee decided to postpone the question for a month, and directed the surveyor to furnish each member of the committee with a copy of his report.—This was the only business.

The report of the Education Commissioners for 1885 i., states that there were 19,063 schools on the list for inspec- tion, having accommodation for 5,061 503 children. The ' number on the registers was 4,465,615, and the average number in attendance 3,406,076. PLEASANT TEEMINATION OF A DOMESTIC QUARREL, Before Messrs. R. Houghton and T. J. Gillespie, at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Thomas Aitken, a respect- ably dressed young man, was summoned for assaulting his wife, Mary, on the sth inst. Mr. T. 0. Swift appeared for the defendant—The complainant stated that they had been married seven years, and on the date named her hueband msaulted her. For two or three days she had a black face, which was also swollen. She could not tell why her hus- band struck her. He had assaulted her several times pre- viously during the time they bad been married. She could not live with him now and she had been living at her mother's. They had two children living.—ln reply to Mr. Swift, She said he did not slap her with his open hand, but struck her with his fist. She could not live quietly with him at his mother's houses as they had been doing, because they would not let them live quietly. It IVOS not the first nor the second time it hail been done.—ln reply to the magistrates' clerk (Mr. Nicholson), she said she would never go back with her husband to live at his mother's house.— The Chairman : You are inclined to quarrel then with his parents ?—Comnlainant : I will not go. back to live with them.—Mr. Swift said the defendant desired to live com- fortably with his wife and did not wish to hurt her. On the day in question they had a few words, as married couples did have occasionally, and he pushed her away. She went to her mother's house and a day or two later sent for her clothes, hut he would not send them,—The Bench asked if the parties could not settle and have a second courtship. (Laughter.) Complainant : I win go back to him if he will move out of his mother's house.—The Chairman : You might to try and live quietly and comfortably.—The Clerk: You promised to live with him when You married him, and it is not for you to say where you will live. (Laughter, in which the complainant joined).—The Chairman then re- commended the parties to live quietly Nether, and they Wt. the court. ThQ case ern dismissed,

GOOD DISCIPLINIL—A correspondent of an American paper tells an anecdote illustrating General Hancock's love of dignity and discipline. "He was in command of the tram which brought General Grant's remains from Mount Gilead to New York. General Hancock and his staff were in the coach next to the last. In the rear car was a party of Pennsylvania Militia officers, who were popping an occasional bottle of champagne and smoking quite sociably. General Hancock saw from his car what was going on in the rear. It did not comport with his ideas of the proprieties of so solemn an occasion; and, calling the conductor, he said, 'Will: you please present my compliments to those gentlemen, with the request that they cease smoking?' In a few moments the conductor returned with the announce- ment that the convivial officers returned -their compli- ments with a peremptory refusal to relinquish their cigars. 'Where is the net switch?' asked Hancock. 'About five miles below,' replied the conductor. 'When you reach it, if the smoking in that car has not ceased, switch it on to a side-track and leave it. You may tell the gentlemen what I have said.' In two minutes there was not a cigar to be seen in the last coach. Its occu- pants knew that Hancock meant just what he said." A NEPHEW'S PRESENT TO HIS MAIDEN AUNT.—A gentleman residing in Ceylon wished to make a pre- sent to a maiden aunt of his living in London • and he could think of nothing so suitable and likely to/be a source of amusement to her as a minor—a small bird corresponding in appearance and size to our common blackbird, and rivalling the parrot in power of imitation. Procuring a good specimen of the species fresh from the forest, he set a watch upon his own tongue, avoiding all slang and being very careful in 'respect of grammar.. Then, taking the bird on board a vessel about to sail for England, he gave it to the ship's cook, with a promise that, if the bird was delivered into the hands of the lady with its vocabulary undefiled, a bonus of ten shil- lings would be forthcoming; whereupon the cook pro- mised to take all possible care of the bird—to nourish him and watch over his morals. On the voyage the minor exercised a marked influence for good over one part, at least,of the vessel, and the cook's cuddy was a perfect hall of propriety; and in due course he received his ten shillings. A few weeks passed, and then the gentleman in Ceylon received a letter from his aunt. She thanked him for his gift, but said she had been obliged to part with the minor—not however on account of the expressions he made use of, for his language was correctness itself; but she could not endure all day long plaintive cries of "Steward !" with marvellous never- ceasing imitations of the distressful sound issuing from the lips of passengers suffering from rnal de rner. NOT ON SPHAXING TERMS.—In the San Francisco Custom-house there was employed as night-watchman a character called Barney McGlone. McGlone was known as a good-humoured, ready-witted fellow, and having had the misfortune to incur the enmity of his superior , officer, the latter eagerly sought, with persistent malice, ' to find grounds sufficient upon which to recommend Barney's removal. Night after night he watched, pouncing down at unexpected hours, only to find Barney vigilant at his post. Not a word would pass between them, the officer always retiring baffled and mortified. At length his persistency was rewarded. Barney had been putting in his time at "poker," instead of strength- ening himself by sleep for his weary vigil from midnight until morn, and the night beim,- very chilly he wrapped himself in his overcoat and tri'e'd to steal fitful snatches ' of sleep, hoping the night would be too cold for his re- lentless pursuer to continue his hunt. He reasoned directly opposite from the officer, who, guided by the music of Barney's snoring, with malignant joy stood watching the sleeper in triumph a moment, and then called out, "McGlone.' No answer. "McGlone !" he shouted. Barney awoke with a cold chill running down his back at the sound of his enemy's voice, but kept silent and simply stared at his interlocutor. "McGlone!" h "I've caught you 'exclaimed, Barney, now live t/3 his danger, exclaimed, "You neshtohuotredou agga hvin a, did not, sir !" " Then, why didn'tyou`answer me when I called you?" "Because, be jabers, I warn't on shpakin' terms wid you, sor." Barney- was reported, but his explanation as given was accepted as truth, and his presence of mind saved him.
